title: Ensemble Model Fitting
text:
In Fitting and Comparing Algorithms, we saw that a generalised linear model (GLM), a generalised additive model (GAM) and tree-based methods can describe different relationships between species records and environmental conditions. Their predictions may differ even when they use exactly the same occurrence data and predictors.
Ensemble modelling combines predictions from several fitted models. An ensemble may produce a more stable summary of the patterns suggested by different methods, but averaging models does not automatically make a prediction more accurate or ecologically correct. Models can share the same sampling bias, missing predictors and errors. Their predictions may also be strongly correlated.
This chapter explores both the average prediction and disagreement among models, using lesser horseshoe bat (Rhinolophus hipposideros) occurrence records and the same three environmental predictors as the earlier sections of the workshop.






TipLearning outcomes — optional research extension



This sections goes beyond the core practical excersises. You can complete the workshop’s GLM exercises without fitting an ensemble.
By the end of the examples, you should be able to:

Describe simple, weighted and threshold-based approaches to combining model predictions.
Produce an average ensemble from models fitted on the same training data.
Examine variation between individual model predictions and explain what it does—and does not—tell us about uncertainty.
Assess individual models and their ensemble using the same held-out test data.
Explain why ensemble weights must be chosen without using the final test observations.

The main example uses a GLM and a classification tree; a GAM and Random Forest are added when their packages are available. Additional biomod2 and sdm workflows are provided as research extensions and do not run automatically on the website.




Continue working in your own RStudio project and add the code to your annotated .R script. Reuse the training/test split and predictors created in GLM Model Fitting. If you continue in the same R session from Chapter 8, the fitted glm_multi, gam_model and rf_model can also be reused.
The website’s page can run independently. When necessary, its setup rebuilds the standard teaching dataset using scripts/prepare_glm_inputs.R, with the same background sampling and seed 2222 as Chapter 5, and creates the same stratified split with seed 2026 as Chapter 6. If you changed your occurrence cleaning, accessible area, background sampling or model formula, rerun your own preceding code rather than restoring the standard teaching example.

library(terra)
library(ggplot2)
library(pROC)

predictors <- c("bio_1", "bio_12", "elevation")

has_train <- exists("sdm_df_train", inherits = FALSE)
has_test <- exists("sdm_df_test", inherits = FALSE)
if (xor(has_train, has_test)) {
  stop("The training and test datasets must come from the same run.")
}
if (has_train && !exists("proj_stack", inherits = FALSE)) {
  stop("Restore proj_stack from the same analysis as your model data.")
}
if (exists("glm_multi", inherits = FALSE) && !has_train) {
  stop("A fitted glm_multi exists without its matching training data.")
}

if (!has_train) {
  has_data <- exists("sdm_df_clean", inherits = FALSE)
  has_raster <- exists("proj_stack", inherits = FALSE)
  if (xor(has_data, has_raster)) {
    stop("Complete the preceding data-preparation steps first; ",
         "do not mix a model table and raster from different runs.")
  }
  if (!has_data) {
    source("scripts/prepare_glm_inputs.R")
  }
  labels <- suppressWarnings(
    as.integer(as.character(sdm_df_clean$pa))
  )
  stopifnot(!anyNA(labels), all(labels %in% 0:1))
  set.seed(2026)
  p_rows <- which(labels == 1L)
  b_rows <- which(labels == 0L)
  stopifnot(length(p_rows) >= 5L, length(b_rows) >= 5L)
  train_rows <- sort(c(
    sample(p_rows, floor(0.7 * length(p_rows))),
    sample(b_rows, floor(0.7 * length(b_rows)))
  ))
  sdm_df_train <- sdm_df_clean[train_rows, , drop = FALSE]
  sdm_df_test <- sdm_df_clean[-train_rows, , drop = FALSE]
}

# Work with copies so factor conversions do not affect previous chapters.
model_train <- as.data.frame(
  sdm_df_train[, c("pa", predictors), drop = FALSE]
)
model_test <- as.data.frame(
  sdm_df_test[, c("pa", predictors), drop = FALSE]
)
model_train$pa <- suppressWarnings(
  as.integer(as.character(model_train$pa))
)
model_test$pa <- suppressWarnings(
  as.integer(as.character(model_test$pa))
)
stopifnot(
  all(stats::complete.cases(model_train)),
  all(stats::complete.cases(model_test)),
  all(model_train$pa %in% 0:1),
  all(model_test$pa %in% 0:1),
  all(c(0L, 1L) %in% model_train$pa),
  all(c(0L, 1L) %in% model_test$pa),
  inherits(proj_stack, "SpatRaster"),
  all(predictors %in% names(proj_stack))
)

table(Training = model_train$pa)

Training
  0   1 
216 216 

table(Test = model_test$pa)

Test
 0  1 
93 93 


The zeros in our dataset are sampled background locations, not confirmed species absences. All resulting 0–1 model outputs represent the fitted distinction between sampled presences and background under our particular sampling design; they must not be presented as independently calibrated occupancy probabilities.



For our first ensemble, we combine predictions from different types of model. A GLM describes specified regression relationships, whereas a classification tree divides environmental space into groups according to predictor values. We can also add the GAM and Random Forest from the preceding chapter.






NotePackages for the optional algorithms





This chapter uses terra, ggplot2, pROC and rpart for the main example. GAM and Random Forest are included when mgcv and randomForest are installed. No code on this page installs R packages automatically.

install.packages(c("rpart", "mgcv", "randomForest"))






All methods use bio_1, bio_12 and elevation. Their parameters are fitted only on the training subset.

if (!exists("glm_multi", inherits = FALSE)) {
  glm_multi <- stats::glm(
    pa ~ poly(elevation, 2) + poly(bio_1, 2) +
      poly(bio_12, 2),
    data = model_train,
    family = binomial(link = "logit")
  )
}
stopifnot(inherits(glm_multi, "glm"))

if (!requireNamespace("rpart", quietly = TRUE)) {
  stop("Install 'rpart' to complete this ensemble extension.")
}
set.seed(2026)
tree_model <- rpart::rpart(
  factor(pa, levels = c(0, 1)) ~ bio_1 + bio_12 + elevation,
  data = model_train,
  method = "class",
  control = rpart::rpart.control(
    cp = 0.01, minbucket = 8, xval = 0
  )
)

# Reuse the Chapter 8 models when present; otherwise fit them on
# exactly the same training observations, if packages are available.
if (!exists("gam_model", inherits = FALSE)) {
  gam_model <- NULL
}
if (is.null(gam_model) &&
    requireNamespace("mgcv", quietly = TRUE)) {
  gam_model <- mgcv::gam(
    pa ~ s(bio_1, k = 5) + s(bio_12, k = 5) +
      s(elevation, k = 5),
    data = model_train,
    family = binomial(link = "logit"), method = "REML"
  )
}

if (!exists("rf_model", inherits = FALSE)) {
  rf_model <- NULL
}
if (is.null(rf_model) &&
    requireNamespace("randomForest", quietly = TRUE)) {
  set.seed(2026)
  rf_model <- randomForest::randomForest(
    x = model_train[, predictors, drop = FALSE],
    y = factor(model_train$pa, levels = c(0, 1)),
    ntree = 250
  )
}

cat("Models available for the ensemble:",
    paste(c("GLM", "Tree",
            if (!is.null(gam_model)) "GAM",
            if (!is.null(rf_model)) "Random Forest"),
          collapse = ", "), "\n")

Models available for the ensemble: GLM, Tree, GAM, Random Forest 


Inspect: Which models assume an explicitly chosen mathematical response shape, and which split environmental space into groups? Different models can agree for different reasons, and they can all respond to the same biased training sample.



We need a column of predictions from each model in the same row order. The following code checks that every model provides one finite value for each held-out observation.

model_scores_test <- data.frame(
  GLM = as.numeric(predict(
    glm_multi, newdata = model_test, type = "response")),
  Tree = as.numeric(predict(
    tree_model, newdata = model_test, type = "prob")[, "1"])
)

if (!is.null(gam_model)) {
  model_scores_test$GAM <- as.numeric(predict(
    gam_model, newdata = model_test, type = "response"))
}
if (!is.null(rf_model)) {
  model_scores_test$RF <- as.numeric(predict(
    rf_model, newdata = model_test[, predictors, drop = FALSE],
    type = "prob")[, "1"])
}

stopifnot(nrow(model_scores_test) == nrow(model_test),
          ncol(model_scores_test) >= 2L,
          all(is.finite(as.matrix(model_scores_test))),
          all(as.matrix(model_scores_test) >= 0),
          all(as.matrix(model_scores_test) <= 1))
head(model_scores_test)

A common 0–1 numerical range does not guarantee that a GLM score and a tree’s class proportion have identical probabilistic interpretations. Averaging these values is an illustrative modelling choice, not an automatic statistical calibration.






A simple ensemble gives each included model the same influence. It is useful as a transparent starting point and does not require estimating extra performance weights.

ensemble_test_mean <- rowMeans(model_scores_test)
summary(ensemble_test_mean)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
 0.0030  0.1297  0.5404  0.4812  0.7434  0.9551 





The standard deviation of the model predictions measures how much the fitted algorithms disagree at each sampled location. It is not a confidence interval, and it does not include uncertainty about the occurrence records, background sampling, predictor data or future climate.

ensemble_test_sd <- apply(model_scores_test, 1, stats::sd)

comparison_df <- data.frame(
  mean_score = ensemble_test_mean,
  model_sd = ensemble_test_sd,
  sample_label = ifelse(model_test$pa == 1L,
                        "Recorded presence", "Background")
)

ggplot(comparison_df, aes(x = mean_score, y = model_sd,
                          colour = sample_label)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55) +
  labs(x = "Mean presence–background score",
       y = "Standard deviation among models",
       colour = "Sample type",
       title = "Mean ensemble score and model disagreement") +
  theme_minimal()








Inspect: Do high ensemble scores always correspond to high agreement? Find places with a similar average score but different levels of disagreement. What does that mean for interpretation?



We calculate AUC for each individual model and for the equal-weight ensemble using the same reserved test records. We do not choose models or weights based on these results. AUC measures ranking of the two sampled classes; it is not evidence of absolute occupancy probability or transferability to other regions.

heldout_auc <- function(scores) {
  as.numeric(pROC::auc(pROC::roc(
    response = model_test$pa,
    predictor = as.numeric(scores),
    levels = c(0, 1), direction = "<", quiet = TRUE
  )))
}

auc_table <- data.frame(
  Model = c(colnames(model_scores_test), "Equal-weight ensemble"),
  Test_AUC = c(
    vapply(model_scores_test, heldout_auc, numeric(1)),
    heldout_auc(ensemble_test_mean)
  )
)
auc_table$Test_AUC <- round(auc_table$Test_AUC, 3)
knitr::kable(auc_table,
             caption = "Held-out presence–background AUC")

Explain: Did averaging improve AUC in this example? If not, does that make the ensemble pointless? Think about differences in ecological interpretation, model agreement and the purpose of the analysis. Do not repeatedly change the ensemble to optimise this test-set AUC: doing so would make the test results overly optimistic.






WarningWhy we do not weight models by the test AUC



The final test subset is reserved for assessment. If we use its AUC values to set ensemble weights, and then report the same test AUC as evidence of independent performance, the assessment has been used twice.
To use performance-weighted averaging, estimate weights using a separate validation subset or cross-validation within the training data. Then lock the modelling and weighting procedure before assessing the final test subset. A fully annotated example appears below as an optional exercise.





This example splits the training subset into an internal calibration part and a validation part. It fits temporary models on calibration data, obtains validation AUCs and uses only those values to define non-negative weights. The final fitted models from Section 2 still use the entire training set. The original held-out test data do not enter weight calculation.
The code is not run during website rendering. It is intended for investigating weighting choices in your own RStudio script, rather than for demonstrating that a weighted ensemble is always preferable.

set.seed(2027)
inside_presence <- which(model_train$pa == 1L)
inside_background <- which(model_train$pa == 0L)
calibration_rows <- sort(c(
  sample(inside_presence, floor(0.8 * length(inside_presence))),
  sample(inside_background, floor(0.8 * length(inside_background)))
))
calibration <- model_train[calibration_rows, , drop = FALSE]
validation <- model_train[-calibration_rows, , drop = FALSE]

cal_glm <- glm(
  pa ~ poly(elevation, 2) + poly(bio_1, 2) +
    poly(bio_12, 2),
  data = calibration, family = binomial()
)
cal_tree <- rpart::rpart(
  factor(pa, levels = c(0, 1)) ~ bio_1 + bio_12 + elevation,
  data = calibration, method = "class",
  control = rpart::rpart.control(cp = 0.01, minbucket = 8,
                                 xval = 0)
)

validation_scores <- data.frame(
  GLM = as.numeric(predict(cal_glm, validation,
                           type = "response")),
  Tree = as.numeric(predict(cal_tree, validation,
                            type = "prob")[, "1"])
)

if ("GAM" %in% names(model_scores_test)) {
  cal_gam <- mgcv::gam(
    pa ~ s(bio_1, k = 5) + s(bio_12, k = 5) +
      s(elevation, k = 5),
    data = calibration, family = binomial(), method = "REML"
  )
  validation_scores$GAM <- as.numeric(predict(
    cal_gam, validation, type = "response"))
}
if ("RF" %in% names(model_scores_test)) {
  set.seed(2027)
  cal_rf <- randomForest::randomForest(
    x = calibration[, predictors, drop = FALSE],
    y = factor(calibration$pa, levels = c(0, 1)),
    ntree = 250
  )
  validation_scores$RF <- as.numeric(predict(
    cal_rf, validation[, predictors, drop = FALSE],
    type = "prob")[, "1"])
}

# Only the internal validation labels are used for the weights.
validation_auc <- vapply(validation_scores, function(scores) {
  as.numeric(pROC::auc(pROC::roc(
    validation$pa, scores, levels = c(0, 1),
    direction = "<", quiet = TRUE
  )))
}, numeric(1))

# Use discriminatory ability above 0.5; avoid negative weights.
weight_strength <- pmax(validation_auc - 0.5, 0)
if (sum(weight_strength) == 0) {
  ensemble_weights <- rep(1 / length(weight_strength),
                          length(weight_strength))
} else {
  ensemble_weights <- weight_strength / sum(weight_strength)
}
names(ensemble_weights) <- names(validation_scores)
print(ensemble_weights)

# Apply the FIXED weights to predictions from models fitted to
# the entire training subset, on the held-out test samples.
stopifnot(setequal(names(ensemble_weights),
                   colnames(model_scores_test)))
ensemble_test_weighted <- as.numeric(
  as.matrix(model_scores_test[, names(ensemble_weights)]) %*%
    ensemble_weights
)
heldout_auc(ensemble_test_weighted)

Think about: How sensitive might these weights be to the particular internal split? For more robust research analyses, consider repeated cross-validation, spatially separated folds and background-sampling sensitivity. Models with highly correlated errors do not become independent merely because their weights differ.




The individual models must predict from exactly the same environmental raster cells. We then take the mean and standard deviation across the aligned predictions. The second map shows algorithm disagreement, not a complete uncertainty assessment.

predictor_rasters <- proj_stack[[predictors]]

glm_ensemble_map <- terra::predict(
  predictor_rasters, glm_multi,
  type = "response", na.rm = TRUE
)
names(glm_ensemble_map) <- "GLM"

tree_ensemble_map <- terra::predict(
  predictor_rasters, tree_model,
  fun = function(model, data, ...) {
    as.numeric(predict(model, newdata = data,
                       type = "prob")[, "1"])
  },
  na.rm = TRUE
)
names(tree_ensemble_map) <- "Tree"

ensemble_model_maps <- c(glm_ensemble_map, tree_ensemble_map)

if (!is.null(gam_model)) {
  gam_ensemble_map <- terra::predict(
    predictor_rasters, gam_model,
    type = "response", na.rm = TRUE
  )
  names(gam_ensemble_map) <- "GAM"
  ensemble_model_maps <- c(ensemble_model_maps, gam_ensemble_map)
}
if (!is.null(rf_model)) {
  rf_ensemble_map <- terra::predict(
    predictor_rasters, rf_model,
    fun = function(model, data, ...) {
      as.numeric(predict(model, newdata = data,
                         type = "prob")[, "1"])
    },
    na.rm = TRUE
  )
  names(rf_ensemble_map) <- "RF"
  ensemble_model_maps <- c(ensemble_model_maps, rf_ensemble_map)
}

ensemble_mean_map <- terra::app(ensemble_model_maps,
                                fun = mean)
ensemble_sd_map <- terra::app(ensemble_model_maps,
                              fun = stats::sd)
names(ensemble_mean_map) <- "Ensemble_mean"
names(ensemble_sd_map) <- "Model_disagreement_SD"

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(ensemble_mean_map,
     main = "Mean presence–background score", zlim = c(0, 1))
plot(ensemble_sd_map,
     main = "Disagreement among algorithms (SD)")







par(old_par)

Inspect: Which regions have the strongest agreement between algorithms? Are there areas with intermediate mean suitability but substantial disagreement? Think about how differences in model structure and predictor relationships could produce these patterns.






NoteOptional: save an ensemble checkpoint





The following code saves the two derived raster maps without replacing the environmental inputs. The saved maps can be reopened in a later R session.

dir.create("data/checkpoints", recursive = TRUE,
           showWarnings = FALSE)
terra::writeRaster(
  c(ensemble_mean_map, ensemble_sd_map),
  "data/checkpoints/SDM_ensemble_current.tif",
  overwrite = TRUE
)

# Reopen in a fresh R session:
# ensemble_maps <- terra::rast(
#   "data/checkpoints/SDM_ensemble_current.tif")

Keep the fitting and model-combination code in your own annotated R script so that the maps can be recreated from the original workshop data.





A consensus map can also be produced by first classifying each model’s predicted score as above or below a threshold, and then calculating the proportion of models voting for the higher-score class. However, thresholds need justification and should be fixed without examining the final test set. Since the output scores of different algorithms are not necessarily calibrated to the same meaning, a single universal cutoff such as 0.5 is not automatically appropriate.






NoteResearch extension: calculate consensus using training-derived thresholds





Choose a threshold for each model using training-only cross-validation, classify that model’s spatial predictions using its chosen threshold, and average the resulting 0/1 rasters. The map then represents the proportion of models voting for a high-score class, not the probability of species occurrence. Avoid labelling the two classes as confirmed presence and absence.






The verified data/Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK.tif supplies the BCC-CSM2-MR projection for SSP1-2.6, 2041–2060. An ensemble can be projected to this scenario only if the predictors have the same definitions, units and compatible spatial grids as the training rasters. Elevation is held constant in this example. Future climate projections may contain conditions outside the calibration range, making extrapolated model scores especially uncertain.

future_climate <- terra::rast(
  "data/Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK.tif"
)
stopifnot(
  all(c("bio_1", "bio_12") %in% names(future_climate)),
  terra::compareGeom(future_climate[["bio_1"]],
                     predictor_rasters[["bio_1"]])
)

future_predictors <- c(
  future_climate[[c("bio_1", "bio_12")]],
  predictor_rasters[["elevation"]]
)
stopifnot(identical(names(future_predictors), predictors))

future_glm <- terra::predict(
  future_predictors, glm_multi, type = "response", na.rm = TRUE
)
future_tree <- terra::predict(
  future_predictors, tree_model,
  fun = function(model, data, ...) {
    as.numeric(predict(model, data, type = "prob")[, "1"])
  }, na.rm = TRUE
)
future_maps <- c(future_glm, future_tree)

if (!is.null(gam_model)) {
  future_maps <- c(future_maps, terra::predict(
    future_predictors, gam_model,
    type = "response", na.rm = TRUE
  ))
}
if (!is.null(rf_model)) {
  future_maps <- c(future_maps, terra::predict(
    future_predictors, rf_model,
    fun = function(model, data, ...) {
      as.numeric(predict(model, data, type = "prob")[, "1"])
    }, na.rm = TRUE
  ))
}

future_ensemble_mean <- terra::app(future_maps, fun = mean)
ensemble_score_difference <- future_ensemble_mean - ensemble_mean_map

plot(ensemble_score_difference,
     main = "Change in ensemble score: SSP1-2.6, 2041–2060")

This difference map shows a change in fitted model scores under one climate scenario, not a forecast of where bats will definitely occur or disappear. Agreement across algorithms does not measure agreement across GCMs, SSPs, background samples or dispersal assumptions.




Manually combining predictions is valuable for learning, but research projects often need multiple background samples, repeated or spatial cross-validation, hyperparameter tuning and more detailed output management. The specialised packages below support such workflows. These examples start a new analysis, rather than using the Chapter 6 held-out test set directly; their evaluation scores should not be placed alongside the manual ensemble AUC without a common independent assessment.


biomod2 can fit several SDM algorithms, manage pseudo-absence replicates, perform cross-validation and construct ensemble predictions. Its current interface uses SpatRaster environmental inputs and uses AUCroc to name the ROC/AUC metric. It also creates modelling files in the working directory, so a dedicated research project or subdirectory is recommended.
The example below uses presence locations and asks biomod2 to sample its own pseudo-absences. This is not the same background design or training/test partition used in the manual ensemble above, and the resulting scores are not directly comparable. The code requires the presence_sf object prepared in Chapter 5 and is not executed during website rendering.

library(biomod2)
library(sf)
library(terra)

if (!exists("presence_sf")) {
  stop("Recreate presence_sf from the Chapter 5 occurrence workflow.")
}
presence_on_grid <- sf::st_transform(
  presence_sf, terra::crs(predictor_rasters)
)
xy <- sf::st_coordinates(presence_on_grid)[, 1:2, drop = FALSE]

biomod_data <- biomod2::BIOMOD_FormatingData(
  resp.var = rep(1L, nrow(xy)),
  resp.xy = xy,
  expl.var = predictor_rasters,
  resp.name = "Rhinolophus_hipposideros",
  PA.nb.rep = 2,
  PA.nb.absences = nrow(xy),
  PA.strategy = "random"
)

biomod_models <- biomod2::BIOMOD_Modeling(
  bm.format = biomod_data,
  modeling.id = "EnsembleResearch",
  models = c("GLM", "GAM", "RF"),
  CV.strategy = "random",
  CV.nb.rep = 2,
  CV.perc = 0.7,
  OPT.strategy = "bigboss",
  metric.eval = "AUCroc",
  seed.val = 2026
)

# Use internal validation, not an external final test set, for weights.
biomod_ensemble <- biomod2::BIOMOD_EnsembleModeling(
  bm.mod = biomod_models,
  em.by = "PA+run",
  em.algo = c("EMmean", "EMcv", "EMwmean"),
  metric.select = "AUCroc",
  metric.select.dataset = "validation"
)

biomod_current <- biomod2::BIOMOD_Projection(
  bm.mod = biomod_models,
  new.env = predictor_rasters,
  proj.name = "current"
)

biomod_forecast <- biomod2::BIOMOD_EnsembleForecasting(
  bm.em = biomod_ensemble,
  bm.proj = biomod_current
)

# Inspect what biomod2 actually generated before selecting map layers.
print(biomod2::get_predictions(biomod_forecast))







WarningChoosing a pseudo-absence strategy in biomod2



biomod2 treats a supplied 0 in a binary response as an absence label. Opportunistically sampled background locations should not be passed to the package and described as confirmed survey absences. The example above supplies presences and generates pseudo-absence samples through the package, with their interpretation clearly stated.
For research, justify the accessible area, compare plausible pseudo-absence strategies and carry out appropriately spatial validation. Do not assume that a larger number of algorithms or pseudo-absence samples necessarily improves ecological inference.





The sdm package provides functions for defining environmental modelling data, fitting several algorithms and obtaining their evaluation results. It can accept training and independent test tables, but its model objects and evaluation conventions differ from those used in biomod2. Check which algorithms and package dependencies are available before fitting a large set of models.

library(sdm)

sdm_input <- sdm::sdmData(
  pa ~ bio_1 + bio_12 + elevation,
  train = model_train,
  test = model_test
)

# This fits new models; it does not reuse the Chapter 8 fitted objects.
sdm_models <- sdm::sdm(
  formula = pa ~ bio_1 + bio_12 + elevation,
  data = sdm_input,
  methods = c("glm", "gam", "rf")
)

# Distinguish training and independent-test evaluation in the results.
print(sdm::getEvaluation(sdm_models))

Research connection: A package can automate model fitting and evaluation, but it cannot decide whether the sampled background represents a defensible ecological comparison. Software also cannot make a randomly held-out observation spatially independent of nearby training observations.










NoteExercises — ensemble modelling




Read and inspect: Compare the GLM, tree, GAM and Random Forest scores at the same held-out sites. Which models agree most closely, and are their output scales equivalent in meaning?
Change: Refit the classification tree with a different cp value using training data only. Inspect how the ensemble mean and disagreement map change. This is a sensitivity exercise; do not use the held-out AUC repeatedly to tune cp.
Explain: Why might models agree on a misleading spatial pattern when all have been trained on the same biased occurrences and background locations?
Research extension: Calculate performance weights using the internal training-only example and compare their values with equal weighting. How do the fitted model structures, background design and spatial validation affect your conclusions?

Describe your modelling decisions and interpretations in your own annotated .R script. For independent research applications, report model settings, sampling design, spatial validation, algorithm agreement and all major sources of uncertainty.

title: Ensemble Model Fitting
text:
Continue working in your own RStudio project and add the code to your annotated .R script. Reuse the training/test split and predictors created in GLM Model Fitting. If you continue in the same R session from Chapter 8, the fitted glm_multi, gam_model and rf_model can also be reused.
The website’s page can run independently. When necessary, its setup rebuilds the standard teaching dataset using scripts/prepare_glm_inputs.R, with the same background sampling and seed 2222 as Chapter 5, and creates the same stratified split with seed 2026 as Chapter 6. If you changed your occurrence cleaning, accessible area, background sampling or model formula, rerun your own preceding code rather than restoring the standard teaching example.

library(terra)
library(ggplot2)
library(pROC)

predictors <- c("bio_1", "bio_12", "elevation")

has_train <- exists("sdm_df_train", inherits = FALSE)
has_test <- exists("sdm_df_test", inherits = FALSE)
if (xor(has_train, has_test)) {
  stop("The training and test datasets must come from the same run.")
}
if (has_train && !exists("proj_stack", inherits = FALSE)) {
  stop("Restore proj_stack from the same analysis as your model data.")
}
if (exists("glm_multi", inherits = FALSE) && !has_train) {
  stop("A fitted glm_multi exists without its matching training data.")
}

if (!has_train) {
  has_data <- exists("sdm_df_clean", inherits = FALSE)
  has_raster <- exists("proj_stack", inherits = FALSE)
  if (xor(has_data, has_raster)) {
    stop("Complete the preceding data-preparation steps first; ",
         "do not mix a model table and raster from different runs.")
  }
  if (!has_data) {
    source("scripts/prepare_glm_inputs.R")
  }
  labels <- suppressWarnings(
    as.integer(as.character(sdm_df_clean$pa))
  )
  stopifnot(!anyNA(labels), all(labels %in% 0:1))
  set.seed(2026)
  p_rows <- which(labels == 1L)
  b_rows <- which(labels == 0L)
  stopifnot(length(p_rows) >= 5L, length(b_rows) >= 5L)
  train_rows <- sort(c(
    sample(p_rows, floor(0.7 * length(p_rows))),
    sample(b_rows, floor(0.7 * length(b_rows)))
  ))
  sdm_df_train <- sdm_df_clean[train_rows, , drop = FALSE]
  sdm_df_test <- sdm_df_clean[-train_rows, , drop = FALSE]
}

# Work with copies so factor conversions do not affect previous chapters.
model_train <- as.data.frame(
  sdm_df_train[, c("pa", predictors), drop = FALSE]
)
model_test <- as.data.frame(
  sdm_df_test[, c("pa", predictors), drop = FALSE]
)
model_train$pa <- suppressWarnings(
  as.integer(as.character(model_train$pa))
)
model_test$pa <- suppressWarnings(
  as.integer(as.character(model_test$pa))
)
stopifnot(
  all(stats::complete.cases(model_train)),
  all(stats::complete.cases(model_test)),
  all(model_train$pa %in% 0:1),
  all(model_test$pa %in% 0:1),
  all(c(0L, 1L) %in% model_train$pa),
  all(c(0L, 1L) %in% model_test$pa),
  inherits(proj_stack, "SpatRaster"),
  all(predictors %in% names(proj_stack))
)

table(Training = model_train$pa)

Training

Test

The zeros in our dataset are sampled background locations, not confirmed species absences. All resulting 0–1 model outputs represent the fitted distinction between sampled presences and background under our particular sampling design; they must not be presented as independently calibrated occupancy probabilities.

title: Ensemble Model Fitting
text:
For our first ensemble, we combine predictions from different types of model. A GLM describes specified regression relationships, whereas a classification tree divides environmental space into groups according to predictor values. We can also add the GAM and Random Forest from the preceding chapter.






NotePackages for the optional algorithms





This chapter uses terra, ggplot2, pROC and rpart for the main example. GAM and Random Forest are included when mgcv and randomForest are installed. No code on this page installs R packages automatically.

install.packages(c("rpart", "mgcv", "randomForest"))






All methods use bio_1, bio_12 and elevation. Their parameters are fitted only on the training subset.

if (!exists("glm_multi", inherits = FALSE)) {
  glm_multi <- stats::glm(
    pa ~ poly(elevation, 2) + poly(bio_1, 2) +
      poly(bio_12, 2),
    data = model_train,
    family = binomial(link = "logit")
  )
}
stopifnot(inherits(glm_multi, "glm"))

if (!requireNamespace("rpart", quietly = TRUE)) {
  stop("Install 'rpart' to complete this ensemble extension.")
}
set.seed(2026)
tree_model <- rpart::rpart(
  factor(pa, levels = c(0, 1)) ~ bio_1 + bio_12 + elevation,
  data = model_train,
  method = "class",
  control = rpart::rpart.control(
    cp = 0.01, minbucket = 8, xval = 0
  )
)

# Reuse the Chapter 8 models when present; otherwise fit them on
# exactly the same training observations, if packages are available.
if (!exists("gam_model", inherits = FALSE)) {
  gam_model <- NULL
}
if (is.null(gam_model) &&
    requireNamespace("mgcv", quietly = TRUE)) {
  gam_model <- mgcv::gam(
    pa ~ s(bio_1, k = 5) + s(bio_12, k = 5) +
      s(elevation, k = 5),
    data = model_train,
    family = binomial(link = "logit"), method = "REML"
  )
}

if (!exists("rf_model", inherits = FALSE)) {
  rf_model <- NULL
}
if (is.null(rf_model) &&
    requireNamespace("randomForest", quietly = TRUE)) {
  set.seed(2026)
  rf_model <- randomForest::randomForest(
    x = model_train[, predictors, drop = FALSE],
    y = factor(model_train$pa, levels = c(0, 1)),
    ntree = 250
  )
}

cat("Models available for the ensemble:",
    paste(c("GLM", "Tree",
            if (!is.null(gam_model)) "GAM",
            if (!is.null(rf_model)) "Random Forest"),
          collapse = ", "), "\n")

Models available for the ensemble: GLM, Tree, GAM, Random Forest 


Inspect: Which models assume an explicitly chosen mathematical response shape, and which split environmental space into groups? Different models can agree for different reasons, and they can all respond to the same biased training sample.



We need a column of predictions from each model in the same row order. The following code checks that every model provides one finite value for each held-out observation.

model_scores_test <- data.frame(
  GLM = as.numeric(predict(
    glm_multi, newdata = model_test, type = "response")),
  Tree = as.numeric(predict(
    tree_model, newdata = model_test, type = "prob")[, "1"])
)

if (!is.null(gam_model)) {
  model_scores_test$GAM <- as.numeric(predict(
    gam_model, newdata = model_test, type = "response"))
}
if (!is.null(rf_model)) {
  model_scores_test$RF <- as.numeric(predict(
    rf_model, newdata = model_test[, predictors, drop = FALSE],
    type = "prob")[, "1"])
}

stopifnot(nrow(model_scores_test) == nrow(model_test),
          ncol(model_scores_test) >= 2L,
          all(is.finite(as.matrix(model_scores_test))),
          all(as.matrix(model_scores_test) >= 0),
          all(as.matrix(model_scores_test) <= 1))

A common 0–1 numerical range does not guarantee that a GLM score and a tree’s class proportion have identical probabilistic interpretations. Averaging these values is an illustrative modelling choice, not an automatic statistical calibration.

title: Ensemble Model Fitting
text:
A simple ensemble gives each included model the same influence. It is useful as a transparent starting point and does not require estimating extra performance weights.

ensemble_test_mean <- rowMeans(model_scores_test)
summary(ensemble_test_mean)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
 0.0030  0.1297  0.5404  0.4812  0.7434  0.9551 





The standard deviation of the model predictions measures how much the fitted algorithms disagree at each sampled location. It is not a confidence interval, and it does not include uncertainty about the occurrence records, background sampling, predictor data or future climate.

ensemble_test_sd <- apply(model_scores_test, 1, stats::sd)

comparison_df <- data.frame(
  mean_score = ensemble_test_mean,
  model_sd = ensemble_test_sd,
  sample_label = ifelse(model_test$pa == 1L,
                        "Recorded presence", "Background")
)

ggplot(comparison_df, aes(x = mean_score, y = model_sd,
                          colour = sample_label)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55) +
  labs(x = "Mean presence–background score",
       y = "Standard deviation among models",
       colour = "Sample type",
       title = "Mean ensemble score and model disagreement") +
  theme_minimal()








Inspect: Do high ensemble scores always correspond to high agreement? Find places with a similar average score but different levels of disagreement. What does that mean for interpretation?



We calculate AUC for each individual model and for the equal-weight ensemble using the same reserved test records. We do not choose models or weights based on these results. AUC measures ranking of the two sampled classes; it is not evidence of absolute occupancy probability or transferability to other regions.

heldout_auc <- function(scores) {
  as.numeric(pROC::auc(pROC::roc(
    response = model_test$pa,
    predictor = as.numeric(scores),
    levels = c(0, 1), direction = "<", quiet = TRUE
  )))
}

auc_table <- data.frame(
  Model = c(colnames(model_scores_test), "Equal-weight ensemble"),
  Test_AUC = c(
    vapply(model_scores_test, heldout_auc, numeric(1)),
    heldout_auc(ensemble_test_mean)
  )
)
auc_table$Test_AUC <- round(auc_table$Test_AUC, 3)
knitr::kable(auc_table,
             caption = "Held-out presence–background AUC")

Explain: Did averaging improve AUC in this example? If not, does that make the ensemble pointless? Think about differences in ecological interpretation, model agreement and the purpose of the analysis. Do not repeatedly change the ensemble to optimise this test-set AUC: doing so would make the test results overly optimistic.






WarningWhy we do not weight models by the test AUC



The final test subset is reserved for assessment. If we use its AUC values to set ensemble weights, and then report the same test AUC as evidence of independent performance, the assessment has been used twice.
To use performance-weighted averaging, estimate weights using a separate validation subset or cross-validation within the training data. Then lock the modelling and weighting procedure before assessing the final test subset. A fully annotated example appears below as an optional exercise.





This example splits the training subset into an internal calibration part and a validation part. It fits temporary models on calibration data, obtains validation AUCs and uses only those values to define non-negative weights. The final fitted models from Section 2 still use the entire training set. The original held-out test data do not enter weight calculation.
The code is not run during website rendering. It is intended for investigating weighting choices in your own RStudio script, rather than for demonstrating that a weighted ensemble is always preferable.

set.seed(2027)
inside_presence <- which(model_train$pa == 1L)
inside_background <- which(model_train$pa == 0L)
calibration_rows <- sort(c(
  sample(inside_presence, floor(0.8 * length(inside_presence))),
  sample(inside_background, floor(0.8 * length(inside_background)))
))
calibration <- model_train[calibration_rows, , drop = FALSE]
validation <- model_train[-calibration_rows, , drop = FALSE]

cal_glm <- glm(
  pa ~ poly(elevation, 2) + poly(bio_1, 2) +
    poly(bio_12, 2),
  data = calibration, family = binomial()
)
cal_tree <- rpart::rpart(
  factor(pa, levels = c(0, 1)) ~ bio_1 + bio_12 + elevation,
  data = calibration, method = "class",
  control = rpart::rpart.control(cp = 0.01, minbucket = 8,
                                 xval = 0)
)

validation_scores <- data.frame(
  GLM = as.numeric(predict(cal_glm, validation,
                           type = "response")),
  Tree = as.numeric(predict(cal_tree, validation,
                            type = "prob")[, "1"])
)

if ("GAM" %in% names(model_scores_test)) {
  cal_gam <- mgcv::gam(
    pa ~ s(bio_1, k = 5) + s(bio_12, k = 5) +
      s(elevation, k = 5),
    data = calibration, family = binomial(), method = "REML"
  )
  validation_scores$GAM <- as.numeric(predict(
    cal_gam, validation, type = "response"))
}
if ("RF" %in% names(model_scores_test)) {
  set.seed(2027)
  cal_rf <- randomForest::randomForest(
    x = calibration[, predictors, drop = FALSE],
    y = factor(calibration$pa, levels = c(0, 1)),
    ntree = 250
  )
  validation_scores$RF <- as.numeric(predict(
    cal_rf, validation[, predictors, drop = FALSE],
    type = "prob")[, "1"])
}

# Only the internal validation labels are used for the weights.
validation_auc <- vapply(validation_scores, function(scores) {
  as.numeric(pROC::auc(pROC::roc(
    validation$pa, scores, levels = c(0, 1),
    direction = "<", quiet = TRUE
  )))
}, numeric(1))

# Use discriminatory ability above 0.5; avoid negative weights.
weight_strength <- pmax(validation_auc - 0.5, 0)
if (sum(weight_strength) == 0) {
  ensemble_weights <- rep(1 / length(weight_strength),
                          length(weight_strength))
} else {
  ensemble_weights <- weight_strength / sum(weight_strength)
}
names(ensemble_weights) <- names(validation_scores)
print(ensemble_weights)

# Apply the FIXED weights to predictions from models fitted to
# the entire training subset, on the held-out test samples.
stopifnot(setequal(names(ensemble_weights),
                   colnames(model_scores_test)))
ensemble_test_weighted <- as.numeric(
  as.matrix(model_scores_test[, names(ensemble_weights)]) %*%
    ensemble_weights
)
heldout_auc(ensemble_test_weighted)

Think about: How sensitive might these weights be to the particular internal split? For more robust research analyses, consider repeated cross-validation, spatially separated folds and background-sampling sensitivity. Models with highly correlated errors do not become independent merely because their weights differ.

title: Ensemble Model Fitting
text:
The individual models must predict from exactly the same environmental raster cells. We then take the mean and standard deviation across the aligned predictions. The second map shows algorithm disagreement, not a complete uncertainty assessment.

predictor_rasters <- proj_stack[[predictors]]

glm_ensemble_map <- terra::predict(
  predictor_rasters, glm_multi,
  type = "response", na.rm = TRUE
)
names(glm_ensemble_map) <- "GLM"

tree_ensemble_map <- terra::predict(
  predictor_rasters, tree_model,
  fun = function(model, data, ...) {
    as.numeric(predict(model, newdata = data,
                       type = "prob")[, "1"])
  },
  na.rm = TRUE
)
names(tree_ensemble_map) <- "Tree"

ensemble_model_maps <- c(glm_ensemble_map, tree_ensemble_map)

if (!is.null(gam_model)) {
  gam_ensemble_map <- terra::predict(
    predictor_rasters, gam_model,
    type = "response", na.rm = TRUE
  )
  names(gam_ensemble_map) <- "GAM"
  ensemble_model_maps <- c(ensemble_model_maps, gam_ensemble_map)
}
if (!is.null(rf_model)) {
  rf_ensemble_map <- terra::predict(
    predictor_rasters, rf_model,
    fun = function(model, data, ...) {
      as.numeric(predict(model, newdata = data,
                         type = "prob")[, "1"])
    },
    na.rm = TRUE
  )
  names(rf_ensemble_map) <- "RF"
  ensemble_model_maps <- c(ensemble_model_maps, rf_ensemble_map)
}

ensemble_mean_map <- terra::app(ensemble_model_maps,
                                fun = mean)
ensemble_sd_map <- terra::app(ensemble_model_maps,
                              fun = stats::sd)
names(ensemble_mean_map) <- "Ensemble_mean"
names(ensemble_sd_map) <- "Model_disagreement_SD"

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(ensemble_mean_map,
     main = "Mean presence–background score", zlim = c(0, 1))
plot(ensemble_sd_map,
     main = "Disagreement among algorithms (SD)")







par(old_par)

Inspect: Which regions have the strongest agreement between algorithms? Are there areas with intermediate mean suitability but substantial disagreement? Think about how differences in model structure and predictor relationships could produce these patterns.






NoteOptional: save an ensemble checkpoint





The following code saves the two derived raster maps without replacing the environmental inputs. The saved maps can be reopened in a later R session.

dir.create("data/checkpoints", recursive = TRUE,
           showWarnings = FALSE)
terra::writeRaster(
  c(ensemble_mean_map, ensemble_sd_map),
  "data/checkpoints/SDM_ensemble_current.tif",
  overwrite = TRUE
)

# Reopen in a fresh R session:
# ensemble_maps <- terra::rast(
#   "data/checkpoints/SDM_ensemble_current.tif")

Keep the fitting and model-combination code in your own annotated R script so that the maps can be recreated from the original workshop data.





A consensus map can also be produced by first classifying each model’s predicted score as above or below a threshold, and then calculating the proportion of models voting for the higher-score class. However, thresholds need justification and should be fixed without examining the final test set. Since the output scores of different algorithms are not necessarily calibrated to the same meaning, a single universal cutoff such as 0.5 is not automatically appropriate.






NoteResearch extension: calculate consensus using training-derived thresholds





Choose a threshold for each model using training-only cross-validation, classify that model’s spatial predictions using its chosen threshold, and average the resulting 0/1 rasters. The map then represents the proportion of models voting for a high-score class, not the probability of species occurrence. Avoid labelling the two classes as confirmed presence and absence.






The verified data/Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK.tif supplies the BCC-CSM2-MR projection for SSP1-2.6, 2041–2060. An ensemble can be projected to this scenario only if the predictors have the same definitions, units and compatible spatial grids as the training rasters. Elevation is held constant in this example. Future climate projections may contain conditions outside the calibration range, making extrapolated model scores especially uncertain.

future_climate <- terra::rast(
  "data/Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK.tif"
)
stopifnot(
  all(c("bio_1", "bio_12") %in% names(future_climate)),
  terra::compareGeom(future_climate[["bio_1"]],
                     predictor_rasters[["bio_1"]])
)

future_predictors <- c(
  future_climate[[c("bio_1", "bio_12")]],
  predictor_rasters[["elevation"]]
)
stopifnot(identical(names(future_predictors), predictors))

future_glm <- terra::predict(
  future_predictors, glm_multi, type = "response", na.rm = TRUE
)
future_tree <- terra::predict(
  future_predictors, tree_model,
  fun = function(model, data, ...) {
    as.numeric(predict(model, data, type = "prob")[, "1"])
  }, na.rm = TRUE
)
future_maps <- c(future_glm, future_tree)

if (!is.null(gam_model)) {
  future_maps <- c(future_maps, terra::predict(
    future_predictors, gam_model,
    type = "response", na.rm = TRUE
  ))
}
if (!is.null(rf_model)) {
  future_maps <- c(future_maps, terra::predict(
    future_predictors, rf_model,
    fun = function(model, data, ...) {
      as.numeric(predict(model, data, type = "prob")[, "1"])
    }, na.rm = TRUE
  ))
}

future_ensemble_mean <- terra::app(future_maps, fun = mean)
ensemble_score_difference <- future_ensemble_mean - ensemble_mean_map

plot(ensemble_score_difference,
     main = "Change in ensemble score: SSP1-2.6, 2041–2060")

This difference map shows a change in fitted model scores under one climate scenario, not a forecast of where bats will definitely occur or disappear. Agreement across algorithms does not measure agreement across GCMs, SSPs, background samples or dispersal assumptions.

title: Ensemble Model Fitting
text:
Manually combining predictions is valuable for learning, but research projects often need multiple background samples, repeated or spatial cross-validation, hyperparameter tuning and more detailed output management. The specialised packages below support such workflows. These examples start a new analysis, rather than using the Chapter 6 held-out test set directly; their evaluation scores should not be placed alongside the manual ensemble AUC without a common independent assessment.


biomod2 can fit several SDM algorithms, manage pseudo-absence replicates, perform cross-validation and construct ensemble predictions. Its current interface uses SpatRaster environmental inputs and uses AUCroc to name the ROC/AUC metric. It also creates modelling files in the working directory, so a dedicated research project or subdirectory is recommended.
The example below uses presence locations and asks biomod2 to sample its own pseudo-absences. This is not the same background design or training/test partition used in the manual ensemble above, and the resulting scores are not directly comparable. The code requires the presence_sf object prepared in Chapter 5 and is not executed during website rendering.

library(biomod2)
library(sf)
library(terra)

if (!exists("presence_sf")) {
  stop("Recreate presence_sf from the Chapter 5 occurrence workflow.")
}
presence_on_grid <- sf::st_transform(
  presence_sf, terra::crs(predictor_rasters)
)
xy <- sf::st_coordinates(presence_on_grid)[, 1:2, drop = FALSE]

biomod_data <- biomod2::BIOMOD_FormatingData(
  resp.var = rep(1L, nrow(xy)),
  resp.xy = xy,
  expl.var = predictor_rasters,
  resp.name = "Rhinolophus_hipposideros",
  PA.nb.rep = 2,
  PA.nb.absences = nrow(xy),
  PA.strategy = "random"
)

biomod_models <- biomod2::BIOMOD_Modeling(
  bm.format = biomod_data,
  modeling.id = "EnsembleResearch",
  models = c("GLM", "GAM", "RF"),
  CV.strategy = "random",
  CV.nb.rep = 2,
  CV.perc = 0.7,
  OPT.strategy = "bigboss",
  metric.eval = "AUCroc",
  seed.val = 2026
)

# Use internal validation, not an external final test set, for weights.
biomod_ensemble <- biomod2::BIOMOD_EnsembleModeling(
  bm.mod = biomod_models,
  em.by = "PA+run",
  em.algo = c("EMmean", "EMcv", "EMwmean"),
  metric.select = "AUCroc",
  metric.select.dataset = "validation"
)

biomod_current <- biomod2::BIOMOD_Projection(
  bm.mod = biomod_models,
  new.env = predictor_rasters,
  proj.name = "current"
)

biomod_forecast <- biomod2::BIOMOD_EnsembleForecasting(
  bm.em = biomod_ensemble,
  bm.proj = biomod_current
)

# Inspect what biomod2 actually generated before selecting map layers.
print(biomod2::get_predictions(biomod_forecast))







WarningChoosing a pseudo-absence strategy in biomod2



biomod2 treats a supplied 0 in a binary response as an absence label. Opportunistically sampled background locations should not be passed to the package and described as confirmed survey absences. The example above supplies presences and generates pseudo-absence samples through the package, with their interpretation clearly stated.
For research, justify the accessible area, compare plausible pseudo-absence strategies and carry out appropriately spatial validation. Do not assume that a larger number of algorithms or pseudo-absence samples necessarily improves ecological inference.





The sdm package provides functions for defining environmental modelling data, fitting several algorithms and obtaining their evaluation results. It can accept training and independent test tables, but its model objects and evaluation conventions differ from those used in biomod2. Check which algorithms and package dependencies are available before fitting a large set of models.

library(sdm)

sdm_input <- sdm::sdmData(
  pa ~ bio_1 + bio_12 + elevation,
  train = model_train,
  test = model_test
)

# This fits new models; it does not reuse the Chapter 8 fitted objects.
sdm_models <- sdm::sdm(
  formula = pa ~ bio_1 + bio_12 + elevation,
  data = sdm_input,
  methods = c("glm", "gam", "rf")
)

# Distinguish training and independent-test evaluation in the results.
print(sdm::getEvaluation(sdm_models))

Research connection: A package can automate model fitting and evaluation, but it cannot decide whether the sampled background represents a defensible ecological comparison. Software also cannot make a randomly held-out observation spatially independent of nearby training observations.

title: Assessment and Projection
text:
In Fitting your first species distribution model, we fitted a binomial generalised linear model (GLM) to records of the lesser horseshoe bat (Rhinolophus hipposideros) and environmental conditions in the UK. We compared recorded presences with sampled background locations and mapped the fitted relative presence–background scores.
A fitted model is only the beginning. Before interpreting a map, we need to ask how well the model distinguishes observations it has not seen, what its evaluation measures actually represent, and how cautiously its relationships can be applied to another place or time.






TipLearning outcomes



By the end of the core practical, you should be able to:

Explain the difference between model fit on training data and assessment using held-out test data.
Calculate and interpret an ROC curve and AUC for a presence–background GLM.
Select a score threshold using training data, then calculate sensitivity, specificity and TSS on test data.
Interpret continuous and thresholded suitability maps without labelling background sites as confirmed absences.
Apply the same GLM to verified 2041–2060 SSP1-2.6 climate data, and explain limitations of that projection.

Optional research extensions introduce the Continuous Boyce Index, interactive mapping, checks for novel climate conditions and spatially separated validation.




Continue working in your own RStudio project and add the code to your annotated .R script. If you have completed Chapter 6 in the same R session, retain the fitted glm_multi and the objects sdm_df_train, sdm_df_test and proj_stack.
Each website page must also be able to run independently. The following setup reconstructs the standard teaching inputs and the same training split and model formula from Chapter 6 only when needed. It does not install packages, download data or fit unrelated algorithms. If you changed the background-sampling procedure or selected a different model in your own script, rerun your own preceding steps to preserve those choices.






NoteOptional: continue from a saved Chapter 6 checkpoint





If you saved the checkpoint described in Chapter 6, you can run this code first in your own RStudio script to restore the fitted model and test data from that analysis. The main setup below will then reuse these objects without refitting the standard GLM.

library(terra)
chapter6_checkpoint <- readRDS(
  "data/checkpoints/glm_chapter6_results.rds"
)
sdm_df_train <- chapter6_checkpoint$sdm_df_train
sdm_df_test <- chapter6_checkpoint$sdm_df_test
glm_multi <- chapter6_checkpoint$glm_multi
proj_stack <- terra::rast(
  "data/checkpoints/SDM_predictors_current.tif"
)

The files must come from the same Chapter 6 analysis; mixing a GLM with a different sampling design or raster predictor set would invalidate the comparison. If you did not save a checkpoint, simply continue with the standard setup.




library(terra)
library(ggplot2)

# Do not silently mix a model, split or predictor grid from different runs.
has_train <- exists("sdm_df_train", inherits = FALSE)
has_test <- exists("sdm_df_test", inherits = FALSE)
if (xor(has_train, has_test)) {
  stop("Only one of the Chapter 6 train/test objects is present. ",
       "Rerun Chapter 6 or restore both from the same checkpoint.")
}
if (has_train && !exists("proj_stack", inherits = FALSE)) {
  stop("Training/test records exist but proj_stack is missing. ",
       "Rerun Chapter 6 or restore its matching predictor checkpoint.")
}
if (exists("glm_multi", inherits = FALSE) && !has_train) {
  stop("A fitted glm_multi exists without the Chapter 6 training data. ",
       "Restore the full checkpoint or rerun the GLM practical.")
}

# If model inputs were not kept from the previous chapter,
# recreate its standard teaching data with the supplied helper.
if (!exists("proj_stack", inherits = FALSE) ||
    (!exists("sdm_df_train", inherits = FALSE) ||
     !exists("sdm_df_test", inherits = FALSE)) &&
    !exists("sdm_df_clean", inherits = FALSE)) {
  source("scripts/prepare_glm_inputs.R")
}

# Reproduce the SAME stratified 70/30 split as Chapter 6 when needed.
if (!exists("sdm_df_train", inherits = FALSE) ||
    !exists("sdm_df_test", inherits = FALSE)) {
  stopifnot(exists("sdm_df_clean", inherits = FALSE))
  set.seed(2026)
  presence_rows <- which(sdm_df_clean$pa == 1L)
  background_rows <- which(sdm_df_clean$pa == 0L)
  stopifnot(length(presence_rows) >= 5L,
            length(background_rows) >= 5L)
  trainIndex <- sort(c(
    sample(presence_rows, floor(0.7 * length(presence_rows))),
    sample(background_rows, floor(0.7 * length(background_rows)))
  ))
  sdm_df_train <- sdm_df_clean[trainIndex, , drop = FALSE]
  sdm_df_test <- sdm_df_clean[-trainIndex, , drop = FALSE]
}

# Refit the Chapter 6 teaching formula only if no fitted model exists.
if (!exists("glm_multi", inherits = FALSE)) {
  glm_multi <- glm(
    pa ~ poly(elevation, 2) + poly(bio_1, 2) +
      poly(bio_12, 2),
    data = sdm_df_train,
    family = binomial(link = "logit")
  )
}

model_predictors <- c("bio_1", "bio_12", "elevation")
stopifnot(
  inherits(glm_multi, "glm"),
  inherits(proj_stack, "SpatRaster"),
  all(model_predictors %in% names(proj_stack)),
  all(c("pa", model_predictors) %in% names(sdm_df_train)),
  all(c("pa", model_predictors) %in% names(sdm_df_test)),
  all(sdm_df_train$pa %in% c(0, 1)),
  all(sdm_df_test$pa %in% c(0, 1)),
  all(c(0, 1) %in% sdm_df_test$pa)
)

table(Training = sdm_df_train$pa)

Training
  0   1 
216 216 

table(Test = sdm_df_test$pa)

Test
 0  1 
93 93 


The test subset stays separate. Do not use its results to choose predictor variables, decide which GLM to keep or tune a classification threshold. The same distinction applies when you design spatial cross-validation for an independent research project.






NoteModel fit, assessment and projection





Model fit: How closely does the GLM describe the observations used to estimate its coefficients? Chapter 6 examined training-data results such as deviance and AIC.
Model assessment: How well does the fitted model distinguish the labels of previously unseen records? Here, our test data are held out from the same presence–background dataset.
Projection: What score does the fitted model assign to every grid cell when we supply environmental predictors for that location or a future scenario?
Our random split is a teaching demonstration. Nearby bat records and background cells can have similar conditions, so randomly held-out data may still overstate performance in an independent geographic region. Spatially separated evaluation and independent surveys are important research alternatives.








Our GLM was fitted with family = binomial(link = "logit"). Calling predict(..., type = "response") gives a value between 0 and 1 for each test record, representing the fitted presence-versus-background classification score under our sampling design. This is not a verified probability of species occurrence.

obs_test <- as.integer(as.character(sdm_df_test$pa))
glm_predict_test <- as.numeric(predict(
  glm_multi, newdata = sdm_df_test, type = "response"
))
stopifnot(all(is.finite(glm_predict_test)),
          all(glm_predict_test >= 0 & glm_predict_test <= 1))

head(data.frame(
  observed_label = obs_test,
  predicted_score = round(glm_predict_test, 3)
))

  observed_label predicted_score
1              1           0.671
2              1           0.366
3              1           0.448
4              1           0.683
5              1           0.606
6              1           0.740


Inspect: Do the test records labelled pa = 1 generally receive higher fitted scores than the test records labelled pa = 0? Remember that pa = 0 means a sampled background location, not that a bat was proven absent.



The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve compares sensitivity and the false-positive rate across possible score thresholds. The area under the curve (AUC) summarises how successfully the model ranks test presences above test background points.
An AUC of approximately 0.5 indicates little ranking discrimination; 1 indicates perfect separation for the evaluated sample. There is no universally reliable AUC cut-off that establishes ecological validity. Scores depend on the study region, sampling and test design.

if (!requireNamespace("pROC", quietly = TRUE)) {
  stop("Install the 'pROC' package using the workshop homepage instructions.")
}

roc_glm <- pROC::roc(
  response = obs_test,
  predictor = glm_predict_test,
  levels = c(0, 1),   # background = controls; presence = cases
  direction = "<",   # larger scores should indicate presence labels
  quiet = TRUE
)
auc_glm <- as.numeric(pROC::auc(roc_glm))
cat("Held-out test AUC:", round(auc_glm, 3), "\n")

Held-out test AUC: 0.883 

plot(roc_glm, col = "#426d8b", lwd = 2,
     main = "ROC curve: held-out presence/background records",
     legacy.axes = TRUE)
abline(0, 1, lty = 2, col = "grey50")








Interpret: What does AUC tell us about distinguishing sampled presences from sampled background locations? Could a spatially clustered dataset appear easier to predict when nearby sites are split at random between training and test sets?






NoteHow to read the ROC curve






Sensitivity is the fraction of recorded presences ranked above a chosen threshold.
Specificity is the fraction of sampled background locations ranked below that threshold. It is not the proportion of confirmed biological absences correctly identified.
The ROC curve shows the trade-off between sensitivity and 1 − specificity as the threshold changes.
AUC measures discrimination across these thresholds. It does not establish that a model is well calibrated, causally correct or transferable under future climate.








Some applications require a simplified classification such as higher versus lower modelled suitability. Converting a continuous GLM score into two classes requires a threshold, and different thresholds lead to different classifications.
Core practical. We choose the threshold using the training subset, then apply that fixed threshold to the held-out test subset. Choosing whichever threshold produces the best test result would make the assessment overly optimistic.


Here we select the threshold maximising sensitivity + specificity − 1 (Youden’s J, also equivalent to the training-set TSS). This is a convenient demonstration, not a universally preferable conservation threshold.

obs_train <- as.integer(as.character(sdm_df_train$pa))
train_scores <- as.numeric(predict(
  glm_multi, newdata = sdm_df_train, type = "response"
))
stopifnot(all(is.finite(train_scores)),
          all(c(0L, 1L) %in% obs_train))

# Consider each distinct score as a potential threshold.
candidate_thresholds <- sort(unique(train_scores))
training_sensitivity <- vapply(candidate_thresholds, function(t) {
  mean(train_scores[obs_train == 1L] >= t)
}, numeric(1))
training_specificity <- vapply(candidate_thresholds, function(t) {
  mean(train_scores[obs_train == 0L] < t)
}, numeric(1))

best_threshold_index <- which.max(
  training_sensitivity + training_specificity - 1
)
chosen_thresh <- candidate_thresholds[best_threshold_index]
cat("Training-selected score threshold:",
    round(chosen_thresh, 3), "\n")

Training-selected score threshold: 0.374 





We now compute a confusion table and the True Skill Statistic (TSS). With presence–background data, the calculation assesses discrimination of the assigned labels, not verified biological presence and absence.

pred_binary <- as.integer(glm_predict_test >= chosen_thresh)

cm <- table(
  Observed = factor(obs_test, levels = c(0, 1),
                    labels = c("Background", "Presence")),
  Predicted = factor(pred_binary, levels = c(0, 1),
                     labels = c("Lower score", "Higher score"))
)
print(cm)

            Predicted
Observed     Lower score Higher score
  Background          63           30
  Presence             5           88

test_sensitivity <- mean(pred_binary[obs_test == 1L] == 1L)
test_specificity <- mean(pred_binary[obs_test == 0L] == 0L)
test_tss <- test_sensitivity + test_specificity - 1

data.frame(
  Sensitivity = round(test_sensitivity, 3),
  Specificity = round(test_specificity, 3),
  TSS = round(test_tss, 3)
)

  Sensitivity Specificity   TSS
1       0.946       0.677 0.624


Inspect: How many recorded presences were classified above the threshold? What does an incorrectly classified background sample mean, given that the site may actually be suitable or occupied?
Change: Try a slightly higher or lower threshold in your own script without using this comparison to retune the model against the test set. What happens to the balance between sensitivity and specificity? For applied work, document the threshold-selection rule in advance or choose it on training/validation data according to the decision being made.






WarningWhy a threshold is not an ecological boundary





A binary map divides the model’s predicted scores into higher and lower categories. It does not demonstrate that a species is present on one side of the threshold and absent on the other. Thresholding also discards differences among locations with similar scores. Retain and interpret the continuous map alongside any binary classification.







The three predictors in proj_stack—annual mean temperature (bio_1), annual precipitation (bio_12) and elevation—have matching names and spatial grids. We can apply the same training-fitted GLM to each cell containing complete predictor data.



if (!exists("glm_suitability_map", inherits = FALSE)) {
  glm_suitability_map <- terra::predict(
    proj_stack, glm_multi, type = "response", na.rm = TRUE
  )
}
names(glm_suitability_map) <- "relative_suitability"

plot(glm_suitability_map,
     main = "Current-climate GLM: relative suitability score")








The continuous map represents relative scores conditional on the model and background-sampling design. It is not an independently observed bat distribution and is not a map of absolute occupancy probability.



We can apply the training-selected threshold to the same raster. The categories are labelled higher and lower relative scores, not presence and absence.

binary_map <- terra::ifel(
  glm_suitability_map >= chosen_thresh, 1, 0
)
names(binary_map) <- "score_class"

plot(binary_map,
     col = c("#e5e5e5", "#327c57"),
     breaks = c(-0.5, 0.5, 1.5),
     legend = FALSE,
     main = "Current climate: model score above/below threshold")
legend("bottomleft",
       legend = c("Below threshold", "At/above threshold"),
       fill = c("#e5e5e5", "#327c57"), bty = "n")








Inspect: Which parts of the UK receive higher modelled scores? Do the thresholded classes conceal important variation visible in the continuous map? Consider climate, observation effort and the model’s assumptions before drawing ecological conclusions.






TipResearch extension: explore an interactive map





The interactive map overlays the two model outputs, rather than displaying precise occurrence coordinates on a public website. It uses the standard OpenStreetMap basemap (addTiles()), which does not require a CARTO API key. Map tiles still require an internet connection, whereas the static maps above are available directly in the rendered page.






The map is for exploration. The reproducible static plots remain the primary figures in the core practical.







A temporal projection applies the fitted relationship between the sampled presences, background locations and environmental predictors to different environmental conditions. It is a conditional modelling exercise—not a prediction of exactly where bats will live in future decades.
The prepared future climate data were downloaded and verified in Environmental Data:



Dataset feature
Workshop example




Historical reference
WorldClim 2.1 bioclimatic data, 1970–2000


Global climate model
BCC-CSM2-MR


Future scenario
SSP1-2.6 (ssp = "126")


Future period
2041–2060


Resolution
5 arc-minutes, aligned to the historical teaching grid


File
data/Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK.tif



This is not the higher-emissions SSP5-8.5 scenario. The example reflects one model and one scenario, rather than the full range of climate-projection uncertainty.


The file supplied with the updated workshop data must contain actual future-climate values. If your copy of the GeoTIFF is missing or still contains the old, incorrect historical data, replace it with the verified file prepared in the Environmental Data chapter before proceeding.

future_file <- "data/Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK.tif"
historical_file <- "data/Clim_UK.tif"
stopifnot(file.exists(future_file), file.exists(historical_file))

Clim_UK <- terra::rast(historical_file)
Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK <- terra::rast(future_file)

stopifnot(
  terra::nlyr(Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK) == 19,
  identical(names(Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK), names(Clim_UK)),
  terra::compareGeom(Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK, Clim_UK),
  all(model_predictors[1:2] %in% names(Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK))
)

# A former teaching-file version duplicated the historical raster.
# Stop if the downloaded 'future' BIO1 is identical or contains no values.
temp_difference <- (
  Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK[["bio_1"]] - Clim_UK[["bio_1"]]
)
max_abs_temperature_change <- terra::global(
  abs(temp_difference), "max", na.rm = TRUE
)[[1]]
if (!is.finite(max_abs_temperature_change) ||
    max_abs_temperature_change < 1e-8) {
  stop("The future raster is empty or identical to historical BIO1. ",
       "Replace it with the verified SSP1-2.6 future GeoTIFF.")
}

# Inspect the observed range in the prepared comparison.
terra::global(temp_difference, "range", na.rm = TRUE)

           min      max
bio_1 1.164557 1.978635


In the verified preparation example, annual mean temperature increased by approximately 1.2–1.9°C across the mapped UK cells. Your displayed range should be checked against the actual GeoTIFF. The changes describe the selected climate-model scenario, not observed changes or a guaranteed regional forecast.



Our GLM uses temperature, precipitation and elevation. Only the two climate layers change in this example: elevation is kept fixed as a simplifying assumption. The predictor names, units and raster grid must match those used for model fitting.

future_stack <- c(
  Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK[[c("bio_1", "bio_12")]],
  proj_stack[["elevation"]]
)
names(future_stack) <- model_predictors

stopifnot(
  terra::compareGeom(future_stack, proj_stack),
  identical(names(future_stack), names(proj_stack))
)

# Apply the SAME Chapter 6 training-fitted GLM under future conditions.
future_suitability <- terra::predict(
  future_stack, glm_multi, type = "response", na.rm = TRUE
)
names(future_suitability) <- "relative_suitability_future"





plot(c(glm_suitability_map, future_suitability),
     main = c("Historical climate (1970–2000)",
              "SSP1-2.6 (2041–2060)"))








The two maps show modelled presence–background scores under different climate conditions. Their colours should be read with attention to the legends; for direct comparison, the difference map below is more informative than visually comparing separate automatic colour scales.

suitability_change <- future_suitability - glm_suitability_map
names(suitability_change) <- "future_minus_current"

plot(suitability_change,
     main = "Change in relative GLM score: SSP1-2.6 minus historical")








Inspect: Which areas show increasing or decreasing modelled suitability scores? Does an increase in the fitted score imply that lesser horseshoe bats will colonise those locations? Explain why factors such as dispersal, land use, roost availability and other ecological interactions also matter.
Important: The change map shows a difference between two model predictions. It does not estimate a change in occupancy probability, abundance, range size or conservation status.






NoteWhat makes future projections uncertain?






Climate scenario and GCM: Other SSPs or global climate models can produce different regional conditions.
Transferability: The relationships fitted using present-day presence–background samples may change through time.
Environmental novelty: Some future predictor combinations may fall outside conditions represented in training data; GLM response curves can extrapolate into these poorly supported regions.
Missing processes: Habitat management, roost availability, dispersal and biotic interactions are not included in this simple model.
Survey bias and resolution: Presence records, background selection and coarse climate grids influence the mapped relationships.

For an independent research assessment, consider multiple climate models, multiple scenarios and explicit spatial or temporal validation.






A simple first check asks whether projected temperature or precipitation falls outside the range represented in the training dataset. This does not detect every novel combination of variables, but it identifies one important type of extrapolation.

novel_temperature <-
  future_stack[["bio_1"]] < min(sdm_df_train$bio_1) |
  future_stack[["bio_1"]] > max(sdm_df_train$bio_1)

novel_precipitation <-
  future_stack[["bio_12"]] < min(sdm_df_train$bio_12) |
  future_stack[["bio_12"]] > max(sdm_df_train$bio_12)

novel_conditions <- novel_temperature | novel_precipitation
plot(novel_conditions,
     main = "Outside at least one training predictor range")

Explain: Why should predictions outside the training-data range be interpreted with greater caution even if terra::predict() successfully produces numbers?










TipContinuous Boyce Index (optional)





The Continuous Boyce Index (CBI) compares the distribution of suitability scores at known presences with the distribution of scores across the available study region. It is particularly relevant to presence-only SDMs, but its interpretation depends on the study extent, availability sample, sample size and spatial bias. It does not by itself provide independent proof that a model is ecologically accurate.
The optional code below uses scores across available raster cells as fit and held-out presence scores as obs. It does not incorrectly substitute a mixed vector of test presence/background predictions for study-region availability. This runs only when you choose to explore it in RStudio.

library(ecospat)

# Scores from the available study grid.
available_scores <- terra::values(
  glm_suitability_map, mat = FALSE, na.rm = TRUE
)
presence_scores <- glm_predict_test[obs_test == 1L]

boyce_res <- ecospat::ecospat.boyce(
  fit = available_scores,
  obs = presence_scores,
  nclass = 0,
  PEplot = TRUE
)
boyce_res$cor

A positive Boyce correlation suggests that observed presences tend to fall in cells with higher predicted scores than expected from the available region. Results can be unstable with few presences and are sensitive to availability and sampling design.









TipFinal model fitting after assessment (optional)





For an independent research analysis, a final GLM may be refitted to the full available dataset after the model structure, tuning decisions and evaluation procedure have been finalised. Its purpose is to use all suitable calibration data for subsequent projection. This does not change the previously obtained held-out AUC or TSS, and those evaluation measures must not be recalculated using the refitted model and the same test records.

# Only after model choices and held-out assessment are complete:
all_calibration_data <- rbind(sdm_df_train, sdm_df_test)
final_glm <- glm(
  formula(glm_multi),
  data = all_calibration_data,
  family = binomial(link = "logit")
)

# A full-data final map is a new product; preserve the assessed
# training-fitted model and its independent test results separately.
final_suitability <- terra::predict(
  proj_stack, final_glm, type = "response", na.rm = TRUE
)

Do not automatically carry over the earlier training-selected threshold to a different refitted model without checking the classification rule. For real-world SDMs, consider spatially separated evaluation, explicit predictor selection and external observations where available.
