       "Rerun Chapter 6 or restore both from the same checkpoint.")
}
if (has_train && !exists("proj_stack", inherits = FALSE)) {
  stop("Training/test records exist but proj_stack is missing. ",
       "Rerun Chapter 6 or restore its matching predictor checkpoint.")
}
if (exists("glm_multi", inherits = FALSE) && !has_train) {
  stop("A fitted glm_multi exists without the Chapter 6 training data. ",
       "Restore the full checkpoint or rerun the GLM practical.")
}

# If model inputs were not kept from the previous chapter,
# recreate its standard teaching data with the supplied helper.
if (!exists("proj_stack", inherits = FALSE) ||
    (!exists("sdm_df_train", inherits = FALSE) ||
     !exists("sdm_df_test", inherits = FALSE)) &&
    !exists("sdm_df_clean", inherits = FALSE)) {
  source("scripts/prepare_glm_inputs.R")
}

# Reproduce the SAME stratified 70/30 split as Chapter 6 when needed.
if (!exists("sdm_df_train", inherits = FALSE) ||
    !exists("sdm_df_test", inherits = FALSE)) {
  stopifnot(exists("sdm_df_clean", inherits = FALSE))
  set.seed(2026)
  presence_rows <- which(sdm_df_clean$pa == 1L)
  background_rows <- which(sdm_df_clean$pa == 0L)
  stopifnot(length(presence_rows) >= 5L,
            length(background_rows) >= 5L)
  trainIndex <- sort(c(
    sample(presence_rows, floor(0.7 * length(presence_rows))),
    sample(background_rows, floor(0.7 * length(background_rows)))
  ))
  sdm_df_train <- sdm_df_clean[trainIndex, , drop = FALSE]
  sdm_df_test <- sdm_df_clean[-trainIndex, , drop = FALSE]
}

# Refit the Chapter 6 teaching formula only if no fitted model exists.
if (!exists("glm_multi", inherits = FALSE)) {
  glm_multi <- glm(
    pa ~ poly(elevation, 2) + poly(bio_1, 2) +
      poly(bio_12, 2),
    data = sdm_df_train,
    family = binomial(link = "logit")
  )
}

model_predictors <- c("bio_1", "bio_12", "elevation")
stopifnot(
  inherits(glm_multi, "glm"),
  inherits(proj_stack, "SpatRaster"),
  all(model_predictors %in% names(proj_stack)),
  all(c("pa", model_predictors) %in% names(sdm_df_train)),
  all(c("pa", model_predictors) %in% names(sdm_df_test)),
  all(sdm_df_train$pa %in% c(0, 1)),
  all(sdm_df_test$pa %in% c(0, 1)),
  all(c(0, 1) %in% sdm_df_test$pa)
)

table(Training = sdm_df_train$pa)

Training
  0   1 
216 216 

table(Test = sdm_df_test$pa)

Test
 0  1 
93 93 


The test subset stays separate. Do not use its results to choose predictor variables, decide which GLM to keep or tune a classification threshold. The same distinction applies when you design spatial cross-validation for an independent research project.






NoteModel fit, assessment and projection





Model fit: How closely does the GLM describe the observations used to estimate its coefficients? Chapter 6 examined training-data results such as deviance and AIC.
Model assessment: How well does the fitted model distinguish the labels of previously unseen records? Here, our test data are held out from the same presence–background dataset.
Projection: What score does the fitted model assign to every grid cell when we supply environmental predictors for that location or a future scenario?
Our random split is a teaching demonstration. Nearby bat records and background cells can have similar conditions, so randomly held-out data may still overstate performance in an independent geographic region. Spatially separated evaluation and independent surveys are important research alternatives.

title: Assessment and Projection
text:
Our GLM was fitted with family = binomial(link = "logit"). Calling predict(..., type = "response") gives a value between 0 and 1 for each test record, representing the fitted presence-versus-background classification score under our sampling design. This is not a verified probability of species occurrence.

obs_test <- as.integer(as.character(sdm_df_test$pa))
glm_predict_test <- as.numeric(predict(
  glm_multi, newdata = sdm_df_test, type = "response"
))
stopifnot(all(is.finite(glm_predict_test)),
          all(glm_predict_test >= 0 & glm_predict_test <= 1))

head(data.frame(
  observed_label = obs_test,
  predicted_score = round(glm_predict_test, 3)
))

  observed_label predicted_score
1              1           0.671
2              1           0.366
3              1           0.448
4              1           0.683
5              1           0.606
6              1           0.740


Inspect: Do the test records labelled pa = 1 generally receive higher fitted scores than the test records labelled pa = 0? Remember that pa = 0 means a sampled background location, not that a bat was proven absent.



The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve compares sensitivity and the false-positive rate across possible score thresholds. The area under the curve (AUC) summarises how successfully the model ranks test presences above test background points.
An AUC of approximately 0.5 indicates little ranking discrimination; 1 indicates perfect separation for the evaluated sample. There is no universally reliable AUC cut-off that establishes ecological validity. Scores depend on the study region, sampling and test design.

if (!requireNamespace("pROC", quietly = TRUE)) {
  stop("Install the 'pROC' package using the workshop homepage instructions.")
}

roc_glm <- pROC::roc(
  response = obs_test,
  predictor = glm_predict_test,
  levels = c(0, 1),   # background = controls; presence = cases
  direction = "<",   # larger scores should indicate presence labels
  quiet = TRUE
)
auc_glm <- as.numeric(pROC::auc(roc_glm))
cat("Held-out test AUC:", round(auc_glm, 3), "\n")

Held-out test AUC: 0.883 

plot(roc_glm, col = "#426d8b", lwd = 2,
     main = "ROC curve: held-out presence/background records",
     legacy.axes = TRUE)
abline(0, 1, lty = 2, col = "grey50")








Interpret: What does AUC tell us about distinguishing sampled presences from sampled background locations? Could a spatially clustered dataset appear easier to predict when nearby sites are split at random between training and test sets?






NoteHow to read the ROC curve






Sensitivity is the fraction of recorded presences ranked above a chosen threshold.
Specificity is the fraction of sampled background locations ranked below that threshold. It is not the proportion of confirmed biological absences correctly identified.
The ROC curve shows the trade-off between sensitivity and 1 − specificity as the threshold changes.
AUC measures discrimination across these thresholds. It does not establish that a model is well calibrated, causally correct or transferable under future climate.

title: Assessment and Projection
text:
Some applications require a simplified classification such as higher versus lower modelled suitability. Converting a continuous GLM score into two classes requires a threshold, and different thresholds lead to different classifications.
Core practical. We choose the threshold using the training subset, then apply that fixed threshold to the held-out test subset. Choosing whichever threshold produces the best test result would make the assessment overly optimistic.


Here we select the threshold maximising sensitivity + specificity − 1 (Youden’s J, also equivalent to the training-set TSS). This is a convenient demonstration, not a universally preferable conservation threshold.

obs_train <- as.integer(as.character(sdm_df_train$pa))
train_scores <- as.numeric(predict(
  glm_multi, newdata = sdm_df_train, type = "response"
))
stopifnot(all(is.finite(train_scores)),
          all(c(0L, 1L) %in% obs_train))

# Consider each distinct score as a potential threshold.
candidate_thresholds <- sort(unique(train_scores))
training_sensitivity <- vapply(candidate_thresholds, function(t) {
  mean(train_scores[obs_train == 1L] >= t)
}, numeric(1))
training_specificity <- vapply(candidate_thresholds, function(t) {
  mean(train_scores[obs_train == 0L] < t)
}, numeric(1))

best_threshold_index <- which.max(
  training_sensitivity + training_specificity - 1
)
chosen_thresh <- candidate_thresholds[best_threshold_index]
cat("Training-selected score threshold:",
    round(chosen_thresh, 3), "\n")

Training-selected score threshold: 0.374 





We now compute a confusion table and the True Skill Statistic (TSS). With presence–background data, the calculation assesses discrimination of the assigned labels, not verified biological presence and absence.

pred_binary <- as.integer(glm_predict_test >= chosen_thresh)

cm <- table(
  Observed = factor(obs_test, levels = c(0, 1),
                    labels = c("Background", "Presence")),
  Predicted = factor(pred_binary, levels = c(0, 1),
                     labels = c("Lower score", "Higher score"))
)
print(cm)

            Predicted
Observed     Lower score Higher score
  Background          63           30
  Presence             5           88

test_sensitivity <- mean(pred_binary[obs_test == 1L] == 1L)
test_specificity <- mean(pred_binary[obs_test == 0L] == 0L)
test_tss <- test_sensitivity + test_specificity - 1

data.frame(
  Sensitivity = round(test_sensitivity, 3),
  Specificity = round(test_specificity, 3),
  TSS = round(test_tss, 3)
)

  Sensitivity Specificity   TSS
1       0.946       0.677 0.624


Inspect: How many recorded presences were classified above the threshold? What does an incorrectly classified background sample mean, given that the site may actually be suitable or occupied?
Change: Try a slightly higher or lower threshold in your own script without using this comparison to retune the model against the test set. What happens to the balance between sensitivity and specificity? For applied work, document the threshold-selection rule in advance or choose it on training/validation data according to the decision being made.






WarningWhy a threshold is not an ecological boundary





A binary map divides the model’s predicted scores into higher and lower categories. It does not demonstrate that a species is present on one side of the threshold and absent on the other. Thresholding also discards differences among locations with similar scores. Retain and interpret the continuous map alongside any binary classification.

title: Assessment and Projection
text:
The three predictors in proj_stack—annual mean temperature (bio_1), annual precipitation (bio_12) and elevation—have matching names and spatial grids. We can apply the same training-fitted GLM to each cell containing complete predictor data.



if (!exists("glm_suitability_map", inherits = FALSE)) {
  glm_suitability_map <- terra::predict(
    proj_stack, glm_multi, type = "response", na.rm = TRUE
  )
}
names(glm_suitability_map) <- "relative_suitability"

plot(glm_suitability_map,
     main = "Current-climate GLM: relative suitability score")








The continuous map represents relative scores conditional on the model and background-sampling design. It is not an independently observed bat distribution and is not a map of absolute occupancy probability.



We can apply the training-selected threshold to the same raster. The categories are labelled higher and lower relative scores, not presence and absence.

binary_map <- terra::ifel(
  glm_suitability_map >= chosen_thresh, 1, 0
)
names(binary_map) <- "score_class"

plot(binary_map,
     col = c("#e5e5e5", "#327c57"),
     breaks = c(-0.5, 0.5, 1.5),
     legend = FALSE,
     main = "Current climate: model score above/below threshold")
legend("bottomleft",
       legend = c("Below threshold", "At/above threshold"),
       fill = c("#e5e5e5", "#327c57"), bty = "n")








Inspect: Which parts of the UK receive higher modelled scores? Do the thresholded classes conceal important variation visible in the continuous map? Consider climate, observation effort and the model’s assumptions before drawing ecological conclusions.






TipResearch extension: explore an interactive map





The interactive map overlays the two model outputs, rather than displaying precise occurrence coordinates on a public website. It uses the standard OpenStreetMap basemap (addTiles()), which does not require a CARTO API key. Map tiles still require an internet connection, whereas the static maps above are available directly in the rendered page.






The map is for exploration. The reproducible static plots remain the primary figures in the core practical.

title: Assessment and Projection
text:
A temporal projection applies the fitted relationship between the sampled presences, background locations and environmental predictors to different environmental conditions. It is a conditional modelling exercise—not a prediction of exactly where bats will live in future decades.
The prepared future climate data were downloaded and verified in Environmental Data:



Dataset feature
Workshop example




Historical reference
WorldClim 2.1 bioclimatic data, 1970–2000


Global climate model
BCC-CSM2-MR


Future scenario
SSP1-2.6 (ssp = "126")


Future period
2041–2060


Resolution
5 arc-minutes, aligned to the historical teaching grid


File
data/Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK.tif



This is not the higher-emissions SSP5-8.5 scenario. The example reflects one model and one scenario, rather than the full range of climate-projection uncertainty.


The file supplied with the updated workshop data must contain actual future-climate values. If your copy of the GeoTIFF is missing or still contains the old, incorrect historical data, replace it with the verified file prepared in the Environmental Data chapter before proceeding.

future_file <- "data/Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK.tif"
historical_file <- "data/Clim_UK.tif"
stopifnot(file.exists(future_file), file.exists(historical_file))

Clim_UK <- terra::rast(historical_file)
Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK <- terra::rast(future_file)

stopifnot(
  terra::nlyr(Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK) == 19,
  identical(names(Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK), names(Clim_UK)),
  terra::compareGeom(Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK, Clim_UK),
  all(model_predictors[1:2] %in% names(Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK))
)

# A former teaching-file version duplicated the historical raster.
# Stop if the downloaded 'future' BIO1 is identical or contains no values.
temp_difference <- (
  Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK[["bio_1"]] - Clim_UK[["bio_1"]]
)
max_abs_temperature_change <- terra::global(
  abs(temp_difference), "max", na.rm = TRUE
)[[1]]
if (!is.finite(max_abs_temperature_change) ||
    max_abs_temperature_change < 1e-8) {
  stop("The future raster is empty or identical to historical BIO1. ",
       "Replace it with the verified SSP1-2.6 future GeoTIFF.")
}

# Inspect the observed range in the prepared comparison.
terra::global(temp_difference, "range", na.rm = TRUE)

           min      max
bio_1 1.164557 1.978635


In the verified preparation example, annual mean temperature increased by approximately 1.2–1.9°C across the mapped UK cells. Your displayed range should be checked against the actual GeoTIFF. The changes describe the selected climate-model scenario, not observed changes or a guaranteed regional forecast.



Our GLM uses temperature, precipitation and elevation. Only the two climate layers change in this example: elevation is kept fixed as a simplifying assumption. The predictor names, units and raster grid must match those used for model fitting.

future_stack <- c(
  Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK[[c("bio_1", "bio_12")]],
  proj_stack[["elevation"]]
)
names(future_stack) <- model_predictors

stopifnot(
  terra::compareGeom(future_stack, proj_stack),
  identical(names(future_stack), names(proj_stack))
)

# Apply the SAME Chapter 6 training-fitted GLM under future conditions.
future_suitability <- terra::predict(
  future_stack, glm_multi, type = "response", na.rm = TRUE
)
names(future_suitability) <- "relative_suitability_future"





plot(c(glm_suitability_map, future_suitability),
     main = c("Historical climate (1970–2000)",
              "SSP1-2.6 (2041–2060)"))








The two maps show modelled presence–background scores under different climate conditions. Their colours should be read with attention to the legends; for direct comparison, the difference map below is more informative than visually comparing separate automatic colour scales.

suitability_change <- future_suitability - glm_suitability_map
names(suitability_change) <- "future_minus_current"

plot(suitability_change,
     main = "Change in relative GLM score: SSP1-2.6 minus historical")








Inspect: Which areas show increasing or decreasing modelled suitability scores? Does an increase in the fitted score imply that lesser horseshoe bats will colonise those locations? Explain why factors such as dispersal, land use, roost availability and other ecological interactions also matter.
Important: The change map shows a difference between two model predictions. It does not estimate a change in occupancy probability, abundance, range size or conservation status.






NoteWhat makes future projections uncertain?






Climate scenario and GCM: Other SSPs or global climate models can produce different regional conditions.
Transferability: The relationships fitted using present-day presence–background samples may change through time.
Environmental novelty: Some future predictor combinations may fall outside conditions represented in training data; GLM response curves can extrapolate into these poorly supported regions.
Missing processes: Habitat management, roost availability, dispersal and biotic interactions are not included in this simple model.
Survey bias and resolution: Presence records, background selection and coarse climate grids influence the mapped relationships.

For an independent research assessment, consider multiple climate models, multiple scenarios and explicit spatial or temporal validation.






A simple first check asks whether projected temperature or precipitation falls outside the range represented in the training dataset. This does not detect every novel combination of variables, but it identifies one important type of extrapolation.

novel_temperature <-
  future_stack[["bio_1"]] < min(sdm_df_train$bio_1) |
  future_stack[["bio_1"]] > max(sdm_df_train$bio_1)

novel_precipitation <-
  future_stack[["bio_12"]] < min(sdm_df_train$bio_12) |
  future_stack[["bio_12"]] > max(sdm_df_train$bio_12)

novel_conditions <- novel_temperature | novel_precipitation
plot(novel_conditions,
     main = "Outside at least one training predictor range")

Explain: Why should predictions outside the training-data range be interpreted with greater caution even if terra::predict() successfully produces numbers?

title: Assessment and Projection
text:
TipContinuous Boyce Index (optional)





The Continuous Boyce Index (CBI) compares the distribution of suitability scores at known presences with the distribution of scores across the available study region. It is particularly relevant to presence-only SDMs, but its interpretation depends on the study extent, availability sample, sample size and spatial bias. It does not by itself provide independent proof that a model is ecologically accurate.
The optional code below uses scores across available raster cells as fit and held-out presence scores as obs. It does not incorrectly substitute a mixed vector of test presence/background predictions for study-region availability. This runs only when you choose to explore it in RStudio.

library(ecospat)

# Scores from the available study grid.
available_scores <- terra::values(
  glm_suitability_map, mat = FALSE, na.rm = TRUE
)
presence_scores <- glm_predict_test[obs_test == 1L]

boyce_res <- ecospat::ecospat.boyce(
  fit = available_scores,
  obs = presence_scores,
  nclass = 0,
  PEplot = TRUE
)
boyce_res$cor

A positive Boyce correlation suggests that observed presences tend to fall in cells with higher predicted scores than expected from the available region. Results can be unstable with few presences and are sensitive to availability and sampling design.









TipFinal model fitting after assessment (optional)





For an independent research analysis, a final GLM may be refitted to the full available dataset after the model structure, tuning decisions and evaluation procedure have been finalised. Its purpose is to use all suitable calibration data for subsequent projection. This does not change the previously obtained held-out AUC or TSS, and those evaluation measures must not be recalculated using the refitted model and the same test records.

# Only after model choices and held-out assessment are complete:
all_calibration_data <- rbind(sdm_df_train, sdm_df_test)
final_glm <- glm(
  formula(glm_multi),
  data = all_calibration_data,
  family = binomial(link = "logit")
)

# A full-data final map is a new product; preserve the assessed
# training-fitted model and its independent test results separately.
final_suitability <- terra::predict(
  proj_stack, final_glm, type = "response", na.rm = TRUE
)

Do not automatically carry over the earlier training-selected threshold to a different refitted model without checking the classification rule. For real-world SDMs, consider spatially separated evaluation, explicit predictor selection and external observations where available.

title: Background and Pseudo-Absence Data
text:
Species occurrence records tell us where a species has been observed, but often provide little information about where it was searched for and not found. To relate occurrences to environmental conditions, many species distribution models (SDMs) compare observed presences with conditions sampled elsewhere in a defined study region.
A background location is not a confirmed species absence. It represents an available location or environmental condition chosen for comparison. Some modelling approaches instead use pseudo-absences: locations assigned a working label of absence despite lacking direct evidence that the species was absent. The distinction, and the way these locations are selected, affects how we interpret model outputs.






TipLearning outcomes



By the end of the core practical, you should be able to:

Distinguish presence records, survey non-detections, confirmed absences, background locations and pseudo-absences.
Explain how the study area and observation effort influence the comparison between presences and background locations.
Generate reproducible random background samples in a specified sampling region.
Extract the same environmental predictors for presences and background locations, ready for the first GLM.

Optional research extensions: introduce distance-constrained background sampling and target-group records as alternative sampling strategies.




Open the project folder created on the workshop homepage, and continue adding code and explanatory comments to your own .R script. This chapter uses the supplied occurrence snapshot and the historical climate and elevation files. There is no need to query GBIF or download new rasters during the core practical.

library(terra)               # Raster alignment and extracting predictors
library(sf)                  # Spatial points and study-area boundaries
library(ggplot2)             # Maps and data exploration
library(CoordinateCleaner)   # Occurrence-coordinate checks

required_files <- c(
  "data/workshop_data.RData",
  "data/Clim_UK.tif",
  "data/Elev_UK.tif"
)
stopifnot(all(file.exists(required_files)))

load("data/workshop_data.RData")
Clim_UK <- terra::rast("data/Clim_UK.tif")
Elev_UK <- terra::rast("data/Elev_UK.tif")

stopifnot(inherits(UK_sf, "sf"))
stopifnot(all(c("bio_1", "bio_12") %in% names(Clim_UK)))
stopifnot(all(c("decimalLongitude", "decimalLatitude") %in%
              names(occ_df_rhinhipp)))

This setup is shown so that you can start this page independently, even if you did not run all the preceding chapters in the same R session.











Data type
What does it mean?
What should you not assume?




Presence
A species was detected or recorded at a location.
That other locations were surveyed equally thoroughly.


Survey non-detection
The species was not detected during a survey visit.
That the species was certainly absent.


Supported absence
Survey design and evidence support an absence interpretation for a defined place and time.
That detection is perfect under all circumstances.


Background
A sampled location representing environments available for comparison.
That the species was absent there.


Pseudo-absence
A model-assigned ‘absence’ label without a confirmed absence observation.
That the assigned label is biological ground truth.



The difference matters for the next chapter. Our introductory GLM uses a column called pa containing 1 for a recorded presence and 0 for a sampled background location. The 0 label is convenient for fitting a binary statistical model, but it does not turn a background point into a confirmed absence. The model learns a contrast between the particular presence and background samples; its fitted values should not automatically be interpreted as the true probability that the species occupies a location.






NoteWhy are reliable absences difficult to establish?






Detection is imperfect: A species may be present but not observed during a survey, particularly when it is cryptic, seasonal or mobile.
Survey design matters: Repeat visits, survey effort and sampling conditions determine how informative non-detections are.
Space and time matter: Absence at a site on one occasion does not imply absence at every time or spatial scale.

Field surveys designed to estimate detectability or occupancy can provide stronger evidence than opportunistic occurrence databases. In many presence-only SDMs, however, background points are used instead of verified absences.






The study region defines which conditions are treated as available to the species in our analysis. It should ultimately reflect accessible environments, biological history, dispersal, sampling processes and the study question, not just a convenient political boundary.
Core practical. For this teaching example, we use the supplied UK boundary. This is a transparent starting point and sensible for this national-scale example, not a claim that the UK is the biologically optimal accessible area for the lesser horseshoe bat (Rhinolophus hipposideros).


The Species Data chapter introduced the coordinate-cleaning decisions. The following code reproduces those same selected tests from the saved snapshot, so that this page can also run independently. Keep your raw data unchanged; automated flags are aids to review, not proof of ecological error.

occ_valid <- as.data.frame(occ_df_rhinhipp)

# Check geographic coordinate ranges before spatial conversion.
occ_valid$decimalLongitude <- suppressWarnings(
  as.numeric(as.character(occ_valid$decimalLongitude))
)
occ_valid$decimalLatitude <- suppressWarnings(
  as.numeric(as.character(occ_valid$decimalLatitude))
)

valid_coords <- with(occ_valid,
  is.finite(decimalLongitude) & is.finite(decimalLatitude) &
  decimalLongitude >= -180 & decimalLongitude <= 180 &
  decimalLatitude >= -90 & decimalLatitude <= 90
)
occ_valid <- occ_valid[valid_coords, , drop = FALSE]

if (!"species" %in% names(occ_valid)) {
  occ_valid$species <- "Rhinolophus hipposideros"
}
occ_valid$species <- as.character(occ_valid$species)
occ_valid$species[is.na(occ_valid$species) |
                    !nzchar(occ_valid$species)] <-
  "Rhinolophus hipposideros"

occ_rhinhipp_flags <- CoordinateCleaner::clean_coordinates(
  x = occ_valid,
  lon = "decimalLongitude",
  lat = "decimalLatitude",
  species = "species",
  tests = c("centroids", "duplicates", "equal",
            "gbif", "institutions", "zeros"),
  inst_rad = 10000,
  value = "spatialvalid",
  verbose = FALSE
)

flag_summary <- as.logical(occ_rhinhipp_flags$.summary)
flag_summary[is.na(flag_summary)] <- FALSE
occ_rhinhipp_cleaned <- occ_valid[flag_summary, , drop = FALSE]

cat("Records passing the selected checks:",
    nrow(occ_rhinhipp_cleaned), "\n")

Records passing the selected checks: 355 

stopifnot(nrow(occ_rhinhipp_cleaned) > 0)

Inspect: Compare this count with your result from the Species Data chapter. If it differs, have the starting snapshot or cleaning choices changed?



A location is usable for our three-predictor GLM only if it lies inside the study region and has valid environmental values. To make each page reproducible on its own, we also reproduce the environmental alignment from Environmental Data.

# Match continuous elevation to the historical climate grid.
climate_template <- Clim_UK[["bio_1"]]
if (!terra::same.crs(Elev_UK, climate_template)) {
  Elev_UK_aligned <- terra::project(
    Elev_UK, climate_template, method = "bilinear"
  )
} else {
  Elev_UK_aligned <- terra::resample(
    Elev_UK, climate_template, method = "bilinear"
  )
}
names(Elev_UK_aligned) <- "elevation"

Env_UK_stack <- c(Clim_UK, Elev_UK_aligned)
env_stack <- Env_UK_stack
model_predictors <- c("bio_1", "bio_12", "elevation")
proj_stack <- env_stack[[model_predictors]]

stopifnot(terra::compareGeom(proj_stack[[1]],
                             proj_stack[["elevation"]]))

study_area <- sf::st_transform(UK_sf, terra::crs(proj_stack))

# Only the columns needed for this model are carried forward.
presence_columns <- intersect(
  c("species", "key", "decimalLongitude", "decimalLatitude"),
  names(occ_rhinhipp_cleaned)
)
presence_sf <- sf::st_as_sf(
  occ_rhinhipp_cleaned[, presence_columns, drop = FALSE],
  coords = c("decimalLongitude", "decimalLatitude"),
  crs = 4326
)
presence_sf <- sf::st_transform(
  presence_sf, sf::st_crs(study_area)
)

# Retain points that intersect the UK study region.
inside_region <- lengths(sf::st_intersects(
  presence_sf, study_area
)) > 0
presence_sf <- presence_sf[inside_region, , drop = FALSE]

# Retain points with all three predictors available.
presence_values <- terra::extract(
  proj_stack, terra::vect(presence_sf), ID = FALSE
)
usable_presence <- stats::complete.cases(presence_values)
presence_sf <- presence_sf[usable_presence, , drop = FALSE]
presence_values <- presence_values[usable_presence, , drop = FALSE]

n_presence <- nrow(presence_sf)
stopifnot(n_presence > 0)

    n_presence, "\n")

Core practical. We start with a simple design: draw approximately as many background locations as we have usable presences, using a fixed random seed. This is a teaching choice that simplifies comparison, not a universal rule about the correct presence-to-background ratio.
We sample from cells inside the study region where all three predictors are available. Sampling from a bounding rectangle without checking the environmental layers could generate ‘ocean’ or missing-value locations that are later discarded without explanation.

# Identify cells with complete BIO1, BIO12 and elevation values.
valid_predictor_cells <- terra::ifel(
  !is.na(proj_stack[["bio_1"]]) &
    !is.na(proj_stack[["bio_12"]]) &
    !is.na(proj_stack[["elevation"]]),
  1, NA
)

# Restrict available cells to the UK boundary.
sampling_raster <- terra::mask(
  valid_predictor_cells, terra::vect(study_area)
)

# A fixed seed makes background selection reproducible.
set.seed(2026)
n_background <- n_presence

background_points <- terra::spatSample(
  sampling_raster,
  size = n_background,
  method = "random",
  replace = FALSE,
  na.rm = TRUE,
  as.points = TRUE,
  values = FALSE,
  exhaustive = TRUE
)
background_sf <- sf::st_as_sf(background_points)
background_sf$type <- "background"

# Verify the selected cells contain the required predictors.
background_values <- terra::extract(
  proj_stack, terra::vect(background_sf), ID = FALSE
)
stopifnot(nrow(background_sf) == n_background,
          all(stats::complete.cases(background_values)))

cat("Random background locations:", nrow(background_sf), "\n")

Random background locations: 309 


Inspect: What does set.seed(2026) achieve? Why did we sample only valid environmental cells? Why should we avoid claiming that a sampled background location is a confirmed absence? A background cell may even coincide with a cell containing a presence; that does not turn the background sample into a verified absence.
Change: Replace 2026 with another integer and rerun the background-sampling code. Do the selected locations change? Does the number of points change?


The map below shows background points and aggregated counts of focal-species records in approximate 0.25° cells. It does not publish exact bat occurrence coordinates or roost locations. The synthetic background points themselves are not species observations.

# Aggregate occurrence locations for a public teaching map.
pres_xy <- sf::st_coordinates(
  sf::st_transform(presence_sf, 4326)
)
grain <- 0.25
presence_cells <- data.frame(
  lon = floor(pres_xy[, 1] / grain) * grain + grain / 2,
  lat = floor(pres_xy[, 2] / grain) * grain + grain / 2
)
presence_counts <- stats::aggregate(
  rep(1L, nrow(presence_cells)),
  by = presence_cells, FUN = sum
)
names(presence_counts)[3] <- "n"

back_xy <- sf::st_coordinates(sf::st_transform(
  background_sf, 4326
))
background_map <- data.frame(
  lon = back_xy[, 1], lat = back_xy[, 2]
)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = sf::st_transform(study_area, 4326),
          fill = "grey94", colour = "grey55") +
  geom_point(data = background_map,
             aes(x = lon, y = lat),
             colour = "#287aa8", alpha = 0.35, size = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = presence_counts,
             aes(x = lon, y = lat, size = n),
             colour = "#7b3999", alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_size_continuous(name = "Records per cell", range = c(2, 7)) +
  coord_sf() +
  labs(title = "Observed presences and sampled background",
       subtitle = "Purple: aggregated occurrence counts; blue: simulated background",
       x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude") +
  theme_minimal()








Think about: If the occurrence data are concentrated around places where people look for bats, could a model confuse recording effort with environmental preference? What features of the map suggest that the two sampling processes may be different?




Core practical. The next GLM chapter will use the same three environmental variables for both sets of locations: annual mean temperature (bio_1), annual precipitation (bio_12) and elevation. The input labels are 1 for a recorded presence and 0 for a sampled background location.

# The predictor values were extracted above for the same grid.
# Keep spatial objects for maps and a plain data frame for modelling.
presence_data <- sf::st_sf(
  pa = rep(1L, nrow(presence_sf)),
  presence_values,
  geometry = sf::st_geometry(presence_sf)
)
background_data <- sf::st_sf(
  pa = rep(0L, nrow(background_sf)),
  background_values,
  geometry = sf::st_geometry(background_sf)

sdm_data <- rbind(presence_data, background_data)
sdm_df <- sf::st_drop_geometry(sdm_data)
sdm_df_clean <- sdm_df[stats::complete.cases(sdm_df), , drop = FALSE]
sdm_df_clean$pa <- as.integer(sdm_df_clean$pa)

stopifnot(all(c("pa", model_predictors) %in%
              names(sdm_df_clean)))

Here, sdm_df_clean is the model-ready data frame for the introductory GLM. It preserves the names expected by the next chapter. proj_stack contains the three aligned rasters needed to map the fitted model’s predictions. Students proceeding directly to the next chapter in the same R session can reuse these objects; the next chapter should also provide its own explicit setup for independent study.

  plot_df$pa == 1L, "Recorded presence", "Sampled background"
)

       aes(x = bio_1, fill = record_type)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4, na.rm = TRUE) +

Change: Replace bio_1 with bio_12 or elevation. Which contrast appears strongest? How could the sampling region or uneven survey effort contribute to that pattern?






TipOptional: save a modelling checkpoint





To resume the exercises in a fresh R session without repeating every background-sampling step, you may save the resulting teaching data and the three-predictor raster. Your own annotated R script remains the record of how those objects were created.

dir.create("data/checkpoints", recursive = TRUE,
           showWarnings = FALSE)

saveRDS(sdm_df_clean,
        "data/checkpoints/sdm_training_data.rds")

  proj_stack,
  "data/checkpoints/SDM_predictors_current.tif",
  overwrite = TRUE
)

# sdm_df_clean <- readRDS("data/checkpoints/sdm_training_data.rds")

The checkpoint is a convenience, not a substitute for retaining the code, selection criteria and data sources that produced it.







One alternative is to sample comparison locations within a specified distance of observed presences. This changes the environments regarded as available for comparison. It may better reflect the geographic footprint of sampling in some studies, but it can also restrict the contrast too strongly. A buffer around presences does not automatically correct observer bias or define the species’ accessible area.
The optional code below uses a 5 km buffer in a projected CRS with metre units.

# Use a metric coordinate system before measuring buffer distances.
metric_crs <- "EPSG:27700"  # British National Grid
presence_metric <- sf::st_transform(presence_sf, metric_crs)
uk_metric <- sf::st_transform(study_area, metric_crs)

# Construct a sampling region at most 5 km from a recorded presence.
buffer_5km <- sf::st_union(sf::st_buffer(presence_metric, dist = 5000))
buffer_domain <- sf::st_intersection(
  buffer_5km,
  sf::st_union(sf::st_geometry(uk_metric))
)

set.seed(2222)
candidate_points <- sf::st_sf(
  geometry = sf::st_sample(buffer_domain, size = n_background * 4)
)
candidate_points <- sf::st_transform(
  candidate_points, sf::st_crs(study_area)
)

# Keep only candidates with complete environmental predictors.
candidate_values <- terra::extract(
  proj_stack, terra::vect(candidate_points), ID = FALSE
)
candidate_points <- candidate_points[
  stats::complete.cases(candidate_values), , drop = FALSE
]
if (nrow(candidate_points) < n_background) {
  stop("Too few valid buffered candidates; revise the sampling design.")
}

background_constr_sf <- candidate_points[
  seq_len(n_background), , drop = FALSE
]

# Compare sampling regions; this does not automatically fit a new model.
plot(sf::st_geometry(uk_metric), col = "grey95")
plot(buffer_domain, add = TRUE, col = "lightblue", border = NA)
plot(sf::st_geometry(presence_metric), add = TRUE, pch = 16,
     col = "#7b3999", cex = 0.4)

Change: Try buffers of 1, 5 and 10 km. How do the geographical and environmental contrasts change? What biological or sampling information could justify one distance over another?



When records come from opportunistic observation systems such as GBIF, the locations where other species in a similarly surveyed group were recorded may help characterise observer effort. For example, we can compare focal lesser horseshoe bat records with occurrences of other bat species.
A target group should be selected based on similar recording methods, geography and time periods; taxonomic similarity alone is not sufficient. Target-group records are not confirmed absences of the focal species.


The workshop snapshot includes target_group_sf, created during data preparation. Using it avoids requiring a new GBIF query during the practical. This is a demonstration, not the background method used for the introductory GLM above.

stopifnot(exists("target_group_sf"), inherits(target_group_sf, "sf"))

target_group_uk <- sf::st_transform(
  target_group_sf, sf::st_crs(study_area)
)

# Review species identities; exclude any focal-species records.
if ("species" %in% names(target_group_uk)) {
  target_group_uk <- target_group_uk[
    is.na(target_group_uk$species) |
      target_group_uk$species != "Rhinolophus hipposideros", ,
    drop = FALSE
  ]
}

in_region <- lengths(sf::st_intersects(
  target_group_uk, study_area
)) > 0
target_group_uk <- target_group_uk[in_region, , drop = FALSE]

target_values <- terra::extract(
  proj_stack, terra::vect(target_group_uk), ID = FALSE
)
target_group_uk <- target_group_uk[
  stats::complete.cases(target_values), , drop = FALSE
]

nrow(target_group_uk)
# Compare spatial concentrations using aggregated maps,
# as in the Species Data chapter; avoid publishing precise roost locations.




The following optional query illustrates the independent acquisition route. Its results can change over time, and a small search result is not a complete or bias-free survey of British bats. Inspect names, dates, sources and duplicate records before treating this as a sampling-effort proxy.

library(rgbif)

bat_match <- rgbif::name_backbone(
  name = "Chiroptera", kingdom = "Animalia"
)
stopifnot("usageKey" %in% names(bat_match),
          !is.na(bat_match$usageKey[1]))

bat_search <- rgbif::occ_search(
  taxonKey = bat_match$usageKey[1],
  country = "GB",
  hasCoordinate = TRUE,
  limit = 500
)
bat_df <- bat_search$data

# Remove focal-species records and rows without coordinates.
bat_df <- bat_df[
  !is.na(bat_df$species) &
    bat_df$species != "Rhinolophus hipposideros" &
    !is.na(bat_df$decimalLongitude) &
    !is.na(bat_df$decimalLatitude), , drop = FALSE
]

# Inspect source, date, coordinate uncertainty and taxonomy
# before any use in an SDM.
head(bat_df)

For a research project, document the taxonomic checklist and rgbif version, select a defensible target group and preserve a citable GBIF download. See Species Data and Data Preparation.






NoteBackground choice is part of the scientific hypothesis





There is no universally optimal background or pseudo-absence strategy. Random sampling represents one definition of environmental availability; distance-constrained sampling changes that definition; target-group selection tries to reflect aspects of the recording process. Each can produce a different fitted relationship.
A research analysis should justify its geographic sampling region, background strategy, sample size and treatment of observation bias. It should then assess sensitivity to reasonable alternatives and, where feasible, use spatially separated evaluation. Comparing training accuracy alone does not resolve these choices.













NoteCore practical — complete these before fitting the GLM

Examine the supplied target-group data. Do the records represent a recording process comparable with the focal species?
Consider how a different accessible region, unequal sample sizes or spatially biased survey effort could change the estimated response curves.
For research using field survey non-detections, investigate methods that explicitly model detectability instead of relabelling all non-detections as absences.

Barbet-Massin et al. (2012). Selecting pseudo-absences for species distribution models: how, where and how many?.
Kramer-Schadt et al. (2013). The importance of correcting for sampling bias in MaxEnt species distribution models.

Open the project folder created on the workshop homepage, and continue adding code and explanatory comments to your own .R script. This chapter uses the supplied occurrence snapshot and the historical climate and elevation files. There is no need to query GBIF or download new rasters during the core practical.

Elev_UK <- terra::rast("data/Elev_UK.tif")

              names(occ_df_rhinhipp)))

title: Background and Pseudo-Absence Data
text:
Data type
What does it mean?
What should you not assume?




Presence
A species was detected or recorded at a location.
That other locations were surveyed equally thoroughly.


Survey non-detection
The species was not detected during a survey visit.
That the species was certainly absent.


Supported absence
Survey design and evidence support an absence interpretation for a defined place and time.
That detection is perfect under all circumstances.


Background
A sampled location representing environments available for comparison.
That the species was absent there.


Pseudo-absence
A model-assigned ‘absence’ label without a confirmed absence observation.
That the assigned label is biological ground truth.



The difference matters for the next chapter. Our introductory GLM uses a column called pa containing 1 for a recorded presence and 0 for a sampled background location. The 0 label is convenient for fitting a binary statistical model, but it does not turn a background point into a confirmed absence. The model learns a contrast between the particular presence and background samples; its fitted values should not automatically be interpreted as the true probability that the species occupies a location.






NoteWhy are reliable absences difficult to establish?






Detection is imperfect: A species may be present but not observed during a survey, particularly when it is cryptic, seasonal or mobile.
Survey design matters: Repeat visits, survey effort and sampling conditions determine how informative non-detections are.
Space and time matter: Absence at a site on one occasion does not imply absence at every time or spatial scale.

Field surveys designed to estimate detectability or occupancy can provide stronger evidence than opportunistic occurrence databases. In many presence-only SDMs, however, background points are used instead of verified absences.

title: Background and Pseudo-Absence Data
text:
The study region defines which conditions are treated as available to the species in our analysis. It should ultimately reflect accessible environments, biological history, dispersal, sampling processes and the study question, not just a convenient political boundary.
Core practical. For this teaching example, we use the supplied UK boundary. This is a transparent starting point and sensible for this national-scale example, not a claim that the UK is the biologically optimal accessible area for the lesser horseshoe bat (Rhinolophus hipposideros).


The Species Data chapter introduced the coordinate-cleaning decisions. The following code reproduces those same selected tests from the saved snapshot, so that this page can also run independently. Keep your raw data unchanged; automated flags are aids to review, not proof of ecological error.

occ_valid <- as.data.frame(occ_df_rhinhipp)

# Check geographic coordinate ranges before spatial conversion.
occ_valid$decimalLongitude <- suppressWarnings(
  as.numeric(as.character(occ_valid$decimalLongitude))
)
occ_valid$decimalLatitude <- suppressWarnings(
  as.numeric(as.character(occ_valid$decimalLatitude))
)

valid_coords <- with(occ_valid,
  is.finite(decimalLongitude) & is.finite(decimalLatitude) &
  decimalLongitude >= -180 & decimalLongitude <= 180 &
  decimalLatitude >= -90 & decimalLatitude <= 90
)
occ_valid <- occ_valid[valid_coords, , drop = FALSE]

if (!"species" %in% names(occ_valid)) {
  occ_valid$species <- "Rhinolophus hipposideros"
}
occ_valid$species <- as.character(occ_valid$species)
occ_valid$species[is.na(occ_valid$species) |
                    !nzchar(occ_valid$species)] <-
  "Rhinolophus hipposideros"

occ_rhinhipp_flags <- CoordinateCleaner::clean_coordinates(
  x = occ_valid,
  lon = "decimalLongitude",
  lat = "decimalLatitude",
  species = "species",
  tests = c("centroids", "duplicates", "equal",
            "gbif", "institutions", "zeros"),
  inst_rad = 10000,
  value = "spatialvalid",
  verbose = FALSE
)

flag_summary <- as.logical(occ_rhinhipp_flags$.summary)
flag_summary[is.na(flag_summary)] <- FALSE
occ_rhinhipp_cleaned <- occ_valid[flag_summary, , drop = FALSE]

cat("Records passing the selected checks:",
    nrow(occ_rhinhipp_cleaned), "\n")

Records passing the selected checks: 355 

stopifnot(nrow(occ_rhinhipp_cleaned) > 0)

if (!terra::same.crs(Elev_UK, climate_template)) {

    Elev_UK, climate_template, method = "bilinear"
  )
} else {
  Elev_UK_aligned <- terra::resample(
    Elev_UK, climate_template, method = "bilinear"
  )
}
names(Elev_UK_aligned) <- "elevation"

Env_UK_stack <- c(Clim_UK, Elev_UK_aligned)
env_stack <- Env_UK_stack
model_predictors <- c("bio_1", "bio_12", "elevation")

stopifnot(terra::compareGeom(proj_stack[[1]],
                             proj_stack[["elevation"]]))
names(proj_stack)

study_area <- sf::st_transform(UK_sf, terra::crs(proj_stack))

# Only the columns needed for this model are carried forward.
presence_columns <- intersect(
  c("species", "key", "decimalLongitude", "decimalLatitude"),
  names(occ_rhinhipp_cleaned)
)
presence_sf <- sf::st_as_sf(
  occ_rhinhipp_cleaned[, presence_columns, drop = FALSE],
  coords = c("decimalLongitude", "decimalLatitude"),
  crs = 4326
)
presence_sf <- sf::st_transform(
  presence_sf, sf::st_crs(study_area)
)

# Retain points that intersect the UK study region.
inside_region <- lengths(sf::st_intersects(
  presence_sf, study_area
)) > 0
presence_sf <- presence_sf[inside_region, , drop = FALSE]

# Retain points with all three predictors available.
presence_values <- terra::extract(
  proj_stack, terra::vect(presence_sf), ID = FALSE
)
usable_presence <- stats::complete.cases(presence_values)
presence_sf <- presence_sf[usable_presence, , drop = FALSE]
presence_values <- presence_values[usable_presence, , drop = FALSE]

n_presence <- nrow(presence_sf)
stopifnot(n_presence > 0)

    n_presence, "\n")

)
presence_counts <- stats::aggregate(
  rep(1L, nrow(presence_cells)),
  by = presence_cells, FUN = sum
)
names(presence_counts)[3] <- "n"

back_xy <- sf::st_coordinates(sf::st_transform(
  background_sf, 4326
))
background_map <- data.frame(
  lon = back_xy[, 1], lat = back_xy[, 2]
)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = sf::st_transform(study_area, 4326),
          fill = "grey94", colour = "grey55") +
  geom_point(data = background_map,
             aes(x = lon, y = lat),
             colour = "#287aa8", alpha = 0.35, size = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = presence_counts,
             aes(x = lon, y = lat, size = n),
             colour = "#7b3999", alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_size_continuous(name = "Records per cell", range = c(2, 7)) +
  coord_sf() +
  labs(title = "Observed presences and sampled background",
       subtitle = "Purple: aggregated occurrence counts; blue: simulated background",
       x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude") +
  theme_minimal()








Think about: If the occurrence data are concentrated around places where people look for bats, could a model confuse recording effort with environmental preference? What features of the map suggest that the two sampling processes may be different?

title: Background and Pseudo-Absence Data
text:
Core practical. The next GLM chapter will use the same three environmental variables for both sets of locations: annual mean temperature (bio_1), annual precipitation (bio_12) and elevation. The input labels are 1 for a recorded presence and 0 for a sampled background location.

# The predictor values were extracted above for the same grid.
# Keep spatial objects for maps and a plain data frame for modelling.
presence_data <- sf::st_sf(
  pa = rep(1L, nrow(presence_sf)),
  presence_values,
  geometry = sf::st_geometry(presence_sf)
)
background_data <- sf::st_sf(
  pa = rep(0L, nrow(background_sf)),
  background_values,
  geometry = sf::st_geometry(background_sf)
)

sdm_data <- rbind(presence_data, background_data)
sdm_df <- sf::st_drop_geometry(sdm_data)
sdm_df_clean <- sdm_df[stats::complete.cases(sdm_df), , drop = FALSE]
sdm_df_clean$pa <- as.integer(sdm_df_clean$pa)

stopifnot(all(c("pa", model_predictors) %in%
              names(sdm_df_clean)))
stopifnot(all(sdm_df_clean$pa %in% c(0L, 1L)))

Here, sdm_df_clean is the model-ready data frame for the introductory GLM. It preserves the names expected by the next chapter. proj_stack contains the three aligned rasters needed to map the fitted model’s predictions. Students proceeding directly to the next chapter in the same R session can reuse these objects; the next chapter should also provide its own explicit setup for independent study.



plot_df <- sdm_df_clean  # Keep the modelling data unchanged.
plot_df$record_type <- ifelse(
  plot_df$pa == 1L, "Recorded presence", "Sampled background"
)

ggplot(plot_df,
       aes(x = bio_1, fill = record_type)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4, na.rm = TRUE) +

Inspect: Are temperature values distributed in the same way among presences and background locations? This describes the sampled contrast, not a causal effect of temperature or a validated habitat preference.
Change: Replace bio_1 with bio_12 or elevation. Which contrast appears strongest? How could the sampling region or uneven survey effort contribute to that pattern?






TipOptional: save a modelling checkpoint





To resume the exercises in a fresh R session without repeating every background-sampling step, you may save the resulting teaching data and the three-predictor raster. Your own annotated R script remains the record of how those objects were created.

dir.create("data/checkpoints", recursive = TRUE,
           showWarnings = FALSE)

saveRDS(sdm_df_clean,
        "data/checkpoints/sdm_training_data.rds")
terra::writeRaster(
  proj_stack,
  "data/checkpoints/SDM_predictors_current.tif",
  overwrite = TRUE
)

# To load them in a new R session:
# sdm_df_clean <- readRDS("data/checkpoints/sdm_training_data.rds")
# proj_stack <- terra::rast("data/checkpoints/SDM_predictors_current.tif")

The checkpoint is a convenience, not a substitute for retaining the code, selection criteria and data sources that produced it.

title: Background and Pseudo-Absence Data
text:
One alternative is to sample comparison locations within a specified distance of observed presences. This changes the environments regarded as available for comparison. It may better reflect the geographic footprint of sampling in some studies, but it can also restrict the contrast too strongly. A buffer around presences does not automatically correct observer bias or define the species’ accessible area.
The optional code below uses a 5 km buffer in a projected CRS with metre units.

# Use a metric coordinate system before measuring buffer distances.
metric_crs <- "EPSG:27700"  # British National Grid
presence_metric <- sf::st_transform(presence_sf, metric_crs)
uk_metric <- sf::st_transform(study_area, metric_crs)

# Construct a sampling region at most 5 km from a recorded presence.
buffer_5km <- sf::st_union(sf::st_buffer(presence_metric, dist = 5000))
buffer_domain <- sf::st_intersection(
  buffer_5km,
  sf::st_union(sf::st_geometry(uk_metric))
)

set.seed(2222)
candidate_points <- sf::st_sf(
  geometry = sf::st_sample(buffer_domain, size = n_background * 4)
)
candidate_points <- sf::st_transform(
  candidate_points, sf::st_crs(study_area)
)

# Keep only candidates with complete environmental predictors.
candidate_values <- terra::extract(
  proj_stack, terra::vect(candidate_points), ID = FALSE
)
candidate_points <- candidate_points[
  stats::complete.cases(candidate_values), , drop = FALSE
]
if (nrow(candidate_points) < n_background) {
  stop("Too few valid buffered candidates; revise the sampling design.")
}

background_constr_sf <- candidate_points[
  seq_len(n_background), , drop = FALSE
]

# Compare sampling regions; this does not automatically fit a new model.
plot(sf::st_geometry(uk_metric), col = "grey95")
plot(buffer_domain, add = TRUE, col = "lightblue", border = NA)
plot(sf::st_geometry(presence_metric), add = TRUE, pch = 16,
     col = "#7b3999", cex = 0.4)

Change: Try buffers of 1, 5 and 10 km. How do the geographical and environmental contrasts change? What biological or sampling information could justify one distance over another?

title: Background and Pseudo-Absence Data
text:
When records come from opportunistic observation systems such as GBIF, the locations where other species in a similarly surveyed group were recorded may help characterise observer effort. For example, we can compare focal lesser horseshoe bat records with occurrences of other bat species.
A target group should be selected based on similar recording methods, geography and time periods; taxonomic similarity alone is not sufficient. Target-group records are not confirmed absences of the focal species.


The workshop snapshot includes target_group_sf, created during data preparation. Using it avoids requiring a new GBIF query during the practical. This is a demonstration, not the background method used for the introductory GLM above.

stopifnot(exists("target_group_sf"), inherits(target_group_sf, "sf"))

target_group_uk <- sf::st_transform(
  target_group_sf, sf::st_crs(study_area)
)

# Review species identities; exclude any focal-species records.
if ("species" %in% names(target_group_uk)) {
  target_group_uk <- target_group_uk[
    is.na(target_group_uk$species) |
      target_group_uk$species != "Rhinolophus hipposideros", ,
    drop = FALSE
  ]
}

in_region <- lengths(sf::st_intersects(
  target_group_uk, study_area
)) > 0
target_group_uk <- target_group_uk[in_region, , drop = FALSE]

target_values <- terra::extract(
  proj_stack, terra::vect(target_group_uk), ID = FALSE
)
target_group_uk <- target_group_uk[
  stats::complete.cases(target_values), , drop = FALSE
]

nrow(target_group_uk)
# Compare spatial concentrations using aggregated maps,
# as in the Species Data chapter; avoid publishing precise roost locations.




The following optional query illustrates the independent acquisition route. Its results can change over time, and a small search result is not a complete or bias-free survey of British bats. Inspect names, dates, sources and duplicate records before treating this as a sampling-effort proxy.

library(rgbif)

bat_match <- rgbif::name_backbone(
  name = "Chiroptera", kingdom = "Animalia"
)
stopifnot("usageKey" %in% names(bat_match),
          !is.na(bat_match$usageKey[1]))

bat_search <- rgbif::occ_search(
  taxonKey = bat_match$usageKey[1],
  country = "GB",
  hasCoordinate = TRUE,
  limit = 500
)
bat_df <- bat_search$data

# Remove focal-species records and rows without coordinates.
bat_df <- bat_df[
  !is.na(bat_df$species) &
    bat_df$species != "Rhinolophus hipposideros" &
    !is.na(bat_df$decimalLongitude) &
    !is.na(bat_df$decimalLatitude), , drop = FALSE
]

# Inspect source, date, coordinate uncertainty and taxonomy
# before any use in an SDM.
head(bat_df)

For a research project, document the taxonomic checklist and rgbif version, select a defensible target group and preserve a citable GBIF download. See Species Data and Data Preparation.






NoteBackground choice is part of the scientific hypothesis





There is no universally optimal background or pseudo-absence strategy. Random sampling represents one definition of environmental availability; distance-constrained sampling changes that definition; target-group selection tries to reflect aspects of the recording process. Each can produce a different fitted relationship.
A research analysis should justify its geographic sampling region, background strategy, sample size and treatment of observation bias. It should then assess sensitivity to reasonable alternatives and, where feasible, use spatially separated evaluation. Comparing training accuracy alone does not resolve these choices.

title: Background and Pseudo-Absence Data
text:
NoteCore practical — complete these before fitting the GLM




Explain in one or two sentences why a randomly sampled background point is not a confirmed absence.
Run the random background example twice with the same seed. Check that your points agree, then change the seed.
Inspect table(sdm_df_clean$pa) and names(sdm_df_clean). Which column identifies the modelling labels, and which columns contain environmental predictors?
Compare temperature or precipitation between presence and background samples. Record one ecological interpretation and one alternative explanation involving sampling in your R script.




Compare a random background with 1 km, 5 km and 10 km buffers. Which environments become available for comparison?
Examine the supplied target-group data. Do the records represent a recording process comparable with the focal species?
Consider how a different accessible region, unequal sample sizes or spatially biased survey effort could change the estimated response curves.
For research using field survey non-detections, investigate methods that explicitly model detectability instead of relabelling all non-detections as absences.
