Next: Continue to Model Fitting: GLMs. We will use sdm_df_clean to fit and assess a first model, while remembering that its 0 labels represent sampled background locations, not verified absences.

title: Species Data
text:
A species distribution model (SDM) relates observations of a species to environmental conditions across a study region. The conclusions depend as much on where, when and how the species was recorded as on the modelling algorithm.
Species occurrence data can come from different sources, including systematic field surveys, museum collections, citizen-science projects and biodiversity databases such as GBIF. While these records provide valuable information, some observations—particularly those collected opportunistically through citizen science—may not follow a standardised sampling design and therefore require careful checks for identification accuracy, coordinate quality and spatial sampling bias. Before fitting a model, we must decide which records are relevant, check their spatial accuracy and recognise where surveying has been uneven.
This chapter uses the lesser horseshoe bat (Rhinolophus hipposideros) in the United Kingdom. You will learn with a prepared snapshot so that the practical works without querying live biodiversity services, while also seeing how to obtain the original records in R. Never assume that a point on a map proves that a species is absent elsewhere.



Rhinolophus hipposideros (source: faluke, via iNaturalist, photo 102259155)








TipLearning outcomes



By the end of the core practical, you should be able to distinguish occurrence, non-detection and background records; load and inspect georeferenced observations; map their distribution; flag potentially unreliable coordinates; and explain how sampling bias can affect SDMs.
Optional research extensions demonstrate live GBIF queries, spatial thinning, importing your own survey data and documenting source-data provenance.




Continue working in the folder you created at the beginning of the workshop, using your own annotated .R script (see the workshop homepage). You can complete the practical using RStudio or R directly.


The student download contains a prepared snapshot of the species and spatial data used in this practical. Load these data before continuing.

library(sf)
library(ggplot2)

# Load the prepared workshop dataset.
stopifnot(file.exists("data/workshop_data.RData"))

load("data/workshop_data.RData")

# Verify the objects and essential fields used by this lesson.
stopifnot(inherits(UK_sf, "sf"))
stopifnot(exists("occ_df_rhinhipp"))
stopifnot(all(c("decimalLongitude", "decimalLatitude") %in%
              names(occ_df_rhinhipp)))




We will work with records of the lesser horseshoe bat (Rhinolophus hipposideros). Create a separate data frame called occ_raw so that the original downloaded snapshot remains unchanged.

# Create a working copy of the species occurrence records.
occ_raw <- as.data.frame(occ_df_rhinhipp)

# Check that the coordinate fields are present.
stopifnot(all(c("decimalLongitude", "decimalLatitude") %in%
              names(occ_raw)))

# How many occurrence records do we have?
nrow(occ_raw)

[1] 2000

# Inspect the coordinates of the first six records.
head(occ_raw[, c("decimalLongitude", "decimalLatitude")])

  decimalLongitude decimalLatitude
1        -4.166194        50.33011
2        -3.107454        52.54766
3        -3.280000        51.89000
4        -3.570000        51.76000
5        -3.990000        51.61000
6        -4.192260        53.23495


The object occ_raw will be our starting point for examining coordinate quality, identifying potentially problematic records and preparing the occurrence data for species distribution modelling.
Inspect: What do nrow(), names() and head() tell you? Find any available fields recording the species name, observation date, record identifier or source dataset. At this stage, have we established whether these coordinates are reliable? Which would you retain for a reproducible analysis?




An SDM may draw on several kinds of evidence:

Presence-only records: the species was recorded at a location; there is often no corresponding information about where it was sought but not detected.
Detection/non-detection surveys: sites were surveyed using a defined method. A non-detection is not automatically proof of true absence, because detectability can be imperfect.
Verified absence information: absence can be supported by a carefully designed survey, but certainty depends on timing, effort and detection probability.
Abundance or count data: numbers recorded at sites or visits, interpreted in relation to survey effort and detectability.
Background or pseudo-absence samples: locations constructed for modelling rather than confirmed field observations of absence. These will be examined later in the workshop.

Important fields commonly include scientific name, longitude, latitude, observation date, observation basis, record ID, coordinate uncertainty and data source. Spatial coordinates alone are not enough to establish that records are fit for modelling.






NoteWhere can you obtain species records?





Examples include GBIF, iNaturalist, eBird, OBIS, published survey datasets and original field surveys. Movebank provides movement-tracking records, which require different handling from independent species-occurrence points.
These sources differ in sampling design, taxonomic verification, temporal coverage, coordinate uncertainty and reuse conditions. Records from multiple sources should not be combined without checking duplicates and provenance.





The rgbif package allows you to check scientific names against a recognised taxonomy and retrieve georeferenced occurrence records from GBIF. The example below demonstrates how to access these data independently.
For research applications, occurrence records should be obtained through a documented and reproducible download. GBIF provides an occurrence search and download service that allows you to select records and obtain a persistent DOI for citing the downloaded dataset.
To download records for Rhinolophus hipposideros:

Open the GBIF occurrence search and search for Rhinolophus hipposideros.
Apply appropriate filters, such as country (United Kingdom), records with coordinates, and any relevant observation dates or data-quality criteria.
Select Download, sign in to your GBIF account if required, and request the occurrence dataset.
Save the downloaded data together with its DOI, search criteria and download date.

Before using these records in an SDM, examine their identification accuracy, coordinate uncertainty, duplication and spatial sampling bias. Keep a record of any data-cleaning decisions and excluded observations.
For further guidance, see GBIF’s citation guidelines.

library(rgbif)

species_name <- "Rhinolophus hipposideros"

# Resolve the name in the taxonomy used by rgbif.
match <- rgbif::name_backbone(
  name = species_name,
  kingdom = "Animalia"
)

# Examine the taxon match before sending a record query.
match[, intersect(c("usageKey", "scientificName", "matchType", "rank"),
                  names(match))]

# Use the returned usageKey; do not assume a numeric speciesKey.
stopifnot("usageKey" %in% names(match),
          !is.na(match$usageKey[1]))
taxon_key <- match$usageKey[1]

# A small exploratory search, not an exhaustive occurrence download.
live_result <- rgbif::occ_search(
  taxonKey = taxon_key,
  country = "GB",
  hasCoordinate = TRUE,
  limit = 300
)
occ_live <- live_result$data

nrow(occ_live)
head(occ_live[, intersect(c("species", "decimalLongitude",
                            "decimalLatitude", "eventDate"), names(occ_live))])

In rgbif 3.9.0 and later, the default taxonomic checklist changed from the GBIF Backbone to the Catalogue of Life Extended Release. Always inspect the match and document the checklist and package version rather than assuming taxon identifiers remain unchanged. See the rgbif migration guidance.
Change: For another species, modify species_name and inspect match before downloading. Consider adding a date filter. Compare: Why might the live result differ from the prepared workshop snapshot? A limit is a maximum returned by the search, not evidence of a complete or unbiased sample.






NoteData provenance and citation for research





For a thesis or publication, record the taxonomic checklist, query filters, date of retrieval, original dataset identifiers, licences and cleaning decisions. GBIF recommends DOI-assigned occurrence downloads (for example with rgbif::occ_download()) for citable research datasets; occ_search() by itself does not create a DOI for the result. See GBIF’s citation guidance and the optional Data Preparation chapter.







For the core practical, continue with occ_raw, not the optional occ_live object. First identify records with missing, non-numeric or impossible geographic coordinates. This is a basic plausibility check, not a complete cleaning procedure.

# Preserve the original fields; make the two coordinate columns numeric.
occ_check <- occ_raw
occ_check$decimalLongitude <- suppressWarnings(
  as.numeric(as.character(occ_check$decimalLongitude))
)
occ_check$decimalLatitude <- suppressWarnings(
  as.numeric(as.character(occ_check$decimalLatitude))
)

valid_coords <- with(occ_check,
  is.finite(decimalLongitude) & is.finite(decimalLatitude) &
  decimalLongitude >= -180 & decimalLongitude <= 180 &
  decimalLatitude >= -90 & decimalLatitude <= 90
)

# A copy containing valid longitude/latitude pairs.
occ_valid <- occ_check[valid_coords, , drop = FALSE]

count_check <- data.frame(
  stage = c("Snapshot", "Valid geographic coordinates"),
  records = c(nrow(occ_check), nrow(occ_valid))
)
count_check

                         stage records
1                     Snapshot    2000
2 Valid geographic coordinates    2000

stopifnot(nrow(occ_valid) > 0)

A valid pair of longitude/latitude values can still be wrong: the coordinates might fall in the sea, refer to a museum, have been rounded, or be inconsistent with the species’ recorded locality.



ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = UK_sf, fill = "grey94", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(data = occ_valid,
             aes(x = decimalLongitude, y = decimalLatitude),
             colour = "#65449b", size = 0.8, alpha = 0.45) +
  coord_sf() +
  labs(title = "Occurrence record snapshot",
       subtitle = "(unreviewed, georeferenced records)",
       x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude") +
  theme_minimal()








Inspect: Are the occurrences evenly distributed? Does a cluster prove that habitat is better in that area? Could survey effort, roads, local recording activity or repeated visits contribute to the pattern?
Research caution: The focal species may have sensitive roost locations. Check data-provider restrictions and relevant conservation guidance before distributing exact locations. The interactive web demonstration below uses an aggregated grid, not individual coordinates or precise roost metadata.




Data cleaning should be traceable and scientifically justified. A flagged coordinate is a candidate for inspection, not automatically an invalid ecological observation. Keep the original snapshot unchanged so every exclusion can be reconsidered.



# Are records repeated at the same coordinates?
# This is different from identical GBIF record IDs or repeated surveys.
coordinate_pair <- paste(occ_valid$decimalLongitude,
                         occ_valid$decimalLatitude, sep = "|")

sum(duplicated(coordinate_pair))

[1] 1431

# Inspect a few potentially repeated locations.
head(occ_valid[duplicated(coordinate_pair),
               c("decimalLongitude", "decimalLatitude"),
               drop = FALSE])

   decimalLongitude decimalLatitude
9         -3.107454        52.54766
22        -2.239404        51.55914
35        -1.550000        51.94000
36        -1.480000        51.99000
41        -2.000000        51.35000
43        -3.300000        51.94000


A repeated location may represent a duplicate import, a long-used roost or independent surveys at different times. Why would discarding every repeat without checking dates and record IDs be inappropriate?



Here we use CoordinateCleaner to flag several common problems, including duplicate coordinates within the same species, coordinates near country centroids, equal latitude/longitude values, coordinates near biodiversity institutions and the (0, 0) region. The checks are imperfect and some may flag genuine locations.

# This package is required for the core cleaning example.
library(CoordinateCleaner)

# The cleaning function requires a species field.
if (!"species" %in% names(occ_valid)) {
  occ_valid$species <- "Rhinolophus hipposideros"
}
occ_valid$species <- as.character(occ_valid$species)
occ_valid$species[is.na(occ_valid$species) |
                    !nzchar(as.character(occ_valid$species))] <-
  "Rhinolophus hipposideros"

# Keep flagging separate from deletion.
occ_rhinhipp_flags <- CoordinateCleaner::clean_coordinates(
  x = occ_valid,
  lon = "decimalLongitude",
  lat = "decimalLatitude",
  species = "species",
  tests = c("centroids", "duplicates", "equal",
            "gbif", "institutions", "zeros"),
  inst_rad = 10000,
  value = "spatialvalid",
  verbose = FALSE
)

# TRUE: passed the selected tests; FALSE: review the record.
flag_summary <- as.logical(occ_rhinhipp_flags$.summary)
flag_summary[is.na(flag_summary)] <- FALSE

summary_table <- data.frame(
  result = c("Passed selected tests", "Flagged for review"),
  records = c(sum(flag_summary), sum(!flag_summary))
)
summary_table

                 result records
1 Passed selected tests     355
2    Flagged for review    1645

# Retain a working copy for subsequent exercises.
occ_rhinhipp_cleaned <- occ_valid[flag_summary, , drop = FALSE]
stopifnot(nrow(occ_rhinhipp_cleaned) > 0)

Inspect: How many records were flagged? Which tests might remove legitimate observations? Should a 10 km institution radius make sense for this species and the underlying data sources? How might you report exclusions in a research paper?






NoteImportant limitations of automated cleaning





These tests do not prove species identification, absence of recording bias, suitability for the study period, or that coordinates correspond to the actual observation site. Check coordinate uncertainty, basisOfRecord, reported country, taxonomic status, occurrenceStatus, dates and relevant expert knowledge as part of a research-grade workflow. Review survey design before treating a non-detection as an absence.
The data used for later model fitting should be derived from a documented and consistently applied cleaning protocol. The automated flags shown here are an introductory exercise, not a universal filter.






For an interactive public map, we show counts per approximate 0.25-degree cell, rather than precise occurrence coordinates. These aggregated locations let you explore broad differences but are not appropriate for fine-scale habitat inference.

library(terra)

public_grid <- terra::rast(
  xmin = -12, xmax = 4, ymin = 49, ymax = 61,
  resolution = 0.25, crs = "EPSG:4326"
)

aggregate_for_map <- function(records, grid) {
  xy <- as.matrix(records[, c("decimalLongitude", "decimalLatitude")])
  cell <- terra::cellFromXY(grid, xy)
  counts <- table(cell[!is.na(cell)])
  if (length(counts) == 0) {
    return(data.frame(lon = numeric(), lat = numeric(), n = integer()))
  }
  grid_xy <- terra::xyFromCell(grid, as.integer(names(counts)))
  data.frame(lon = grid_xy[, 1], lat = grid_xy[, 2],
             n = as.integer(counts))
}

map_raw <- aggregate_for_map(occ_valid, public_grid)
map_clean <- aggregate_for_map(occ_rhinhipp_cleaned, public_grid)

nrow(map_raw)

[1] 119

nrow(map_clean)

[1] 93








Interact: Turn each layer on and off. What patterns persist? Why might removing flagged points affect interpretation of the apparent distribution? Background map tiles require an internet connection; the static map above still illustrates the records if tiles are unavailable.




Opportunistic records tend to reflect where observers go and where observations are reported. Their density is therefore not simply an index of species abundance or environmental suitability. Spatial thinning can reduce repeated sampling within a grid cell, but it cannot reconstruct the unsampled landscape and may discard useful data.


The following deterministic example selects one record per grid cell after randomising order. The random seed lets another student reproduce the same choices. The grid sizes are in degrees, not equal distances in kilometres; for serious analysis, a suitable projected CRS and ecologically justified scale are preferable.

library(terra)

thin_to_grid <- function(records, grain, seed = 123) {
  grid <- terra::rast(
    xmin = -12, xmax = 4, ymin = 49, ymax = 61,
    resolution = grain, crs = "EPSG:4326"
  )
  xy <- as.matrix(records[, c("decimalLongitude", "decimalLatitude")])
  cells <- terra::cellFromXY(grid, xy)

  set.seed(seed)
  shuffled <- sample(seq_len(nrow(records)))
  valid <- !is.na(cells[shuffled])
  shuffled <- shuffled[valid]
  selected <- shuffled[!duplicated(cells[shuffled])]
  records[sort(selected), , drop = FALSE]
}

thin_010 <- thin_to_grid(occ_rhinhipp_cleaned, grain = 0.10)
thin_025 <- thin_to_grid(occ_rhinhipp_cleaned, grain = 0.25)
thin_050 <- thin_to_grid(occ_rhinhipp_cleaned, grain = 0.50)

# Compare the number of records retained.
thinning_counts <- c(
  original = nrow(occ_rhinhipp_cleaned),
  grid_010 = nrow(thin_010),
  grid_025 = nrow(thin_025),
  grid_050 = nrow(thin_050)
)

print(thinning_counts)

# Label each dataset with its retained record count.
datasets <- list(
  paste0("No thinning (n = ", nrow(occ_rhinhipp_cleaned), ")") =
    NULL
)

# Build the comparison datasets.
datasets <- list(
  occ_rhinhipp_cleaned,
  thin_010,
  thin_025,
  thin_050
)

stage_labels <- c(
  paste0("No thinning (n = ", nrow(occ_rhinhipp_cleaned), ")"),
  paste0("0.10° thinning (n = ", nrow(thin_010), ")"),
  paste0("0.25° thinning (n = ", nrow(thin_025), ")"),
  paste0("0.50° thinning (n = ", nrow(thin_050), ")")
)

# Combine coordinates for faceted plotting.
plot_points <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(seq_along(datasets), function(i) {
    data.frame(
      lon = datasets[[i]]$decimalLongitude,
      lat = datasets[[i]]$decimalLatitude,
      stage = stage_labels[i]
    )
  })
)

plot_points$stage <- factor(
  plot_points$stage,
  levels = stage_labels
)

# Calculate the actual extent of cleaned occurrences.
clean_coords <- data.frame(
  lon = occ_rhinhipp_cleaned$decimalLongitude,
  lat = occ_rhinhipp_cleaned$decimalLatitude
)

clean_coords <- clean_coords[
  is.finite(clean_coords$lon) &
    is.finite(clean_coords$lat),
]

lon_range <- range(clean_coords$lon)
lat_range <- range(clean_coords$lat)

# Add a small margin around the observations.
lon_pad <- max(0.30, diff(lon_range) * 0.08)
lat_pad <- max(0.25, diff(lat_range) * 0.08)

map_xlim <- lon_range + c(-lon_pad, lon_pad)
map_ylim <- lat_range + c(-lat_pad, lat_pad)

# Compare the actual point patterns.
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(
    data = st_transform(UK_sf, 4326),
    fill = "grey94",
    colour = "grey65",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = plot_points,
    aes(x = lon, y = lat),
    colour = "#c94337",
    size = 0.7,
    alpha = 0.65
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~stage, ncol = 2) +
  coord_sf(
    default_crs = st_crs(4326),
    xlim = map_xlim,
    ylim = map_ylim,
    expand = FALSE
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Effects of spatial thinning",
    subtitle = "Comparison of original and thinned occurrence records",
    x = "Longitude",
    y = "Latitude"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

Change: Increase the grain, change the random seed or select a different extent. Explain: Why can different grid sizes change the apparent spatial pattern? Why is the number of retained records not a direct measure of ecological suitability?






TipResearch connection: bias correction is more than thinning





Other approaches include explicitly modelling sampling effort, using a target-group background, spatially structured evaluation or developing a better sampling design. No universal correction is optimal for every occurrence dataset. Compare alternatives against the research question and document the rationale.







You can also start from a field-survey table rather than GBIF. The example below assumes a file you provide yourself. It is not included in the student ZIP.

# Replace this filename with your own data file.
field_data <- read.csv("data/my_field_records.csv")

# Expected columns: decimalLongitude and decimalLatitude;
# additional columns might include species, date, detection, effort.
stopifnot(all(c("decimalLongitude", "decimalLatitude") %in%
              names(field_data)))

field_points <- sf::st_as_sf(
  field_data,
  coords = c("decimalLongitude", "decimalLatitude"),
  crs = 4326,
  remove = FALSE
)
plot(sf::st_geometry(field_points))

Verify that the coordinates are genuinely longitude/latitude in WGS84 before assigning crs = 4326. If your data use British National Grid or another projected CRS, specify that CRS and then transform the geometry when necessary. If the table includes non-detections, document the survey method and effort before interpreting these as absences.

The student download contains a prepared snapshot of the species and spatial data used in this practical. Load these data before continuing.

# Create a working copy of the species occurrence records.

stopifnot(all(c("decimalLongitude", "decimalLatitude") %in%

title: Species Data
text:
An SDM may draw on several kinds of evidence:

Presence-only records: the species was recorded at a location; there is often no corresponding information about where it was sought but not detected.
Detection/non-detection surveys: sites were surveyed using a defined method. A non-detection is not automatically proof of true absence, because detectability can be imperfect.
Verified absence information: absence can be supported by a carefully designed survey, but certainty depends on timing, effort and detection probability.
Abundance or count data: numbers recorded at sites or visits, interpreted in relation to survey effort and detectability.
Background or pseudo-absence samples: locations constructed for modelling rather than confirmed field observations of absence. These will be examined later in the workshop.

Important fields commonly include scientific name, longitude, latitude, observation date, observation basis, record ID, coordinate uncertainty and data source. Spatial coordinates alone are not enough to establish that records are fit for modelling.






NoteWhere can you obtain species records?





Examples include GBIF, iNaturalist, eBird, OBIS, published survey datasets and original field surveys. Movebank provides movement-tracking records, which require different handling from independent species-occurrence points.
These sources differ in sampling design, taxonomic verification, temporal coverage, coordinate uncertainty and reuse conditions. Records from multiple sources should not be combined without checking duplicates and provenance.





The rgbif package allows you to check scientific names against a recognised taxonomy and retrieve georeferenced occurrence records from GBIF. The example below demonstrates how to access these data independently.
For research applications, occurrence records should be obtained through a documented and reproducible download. GBIF provides an occurrence search and download service that allows you to select records and obtain a persistent DOI for citing the downloaded dataset.
To download records for Rhinolophus hipposideros:

Open the GBIF occurrence search and search for Rhinolophus hipposideros.
Apply appropriate filters, such as country (United Kingdom), records with coordinates, and any relevant observation dates or data-quality criteria.
Select Download, sign in to your GBIF account if required, and request the occurrence dataset.
Save the downloaded data together with its DOI, search criteria and download date.

Before using these records in an SDM, examine their identification accuracy, coordinate uncertainty, duplication and spatial sampling bias. Keep a record of any data-cleaning decisions and excluded observations.
For further guidance, see GBIF’s citation guidelines.

library(rgbif)

species_name <- "Rhinolophus hipposideros"

# Resolve the name in the taxonomy used by rgbif.
match <- rgbif::name_backbone(
  name = species_name,
  kingdom = "Animalia"
)

# Examine the taxon match before sending a record query.
match[, intersect(c("usageKey", "scientificName", "matchType", "rank"),
                  names(match))]

# Use the returned usageKey; do not assume a numeric speciesKey.
stopifnot("usageKey" %in% names(match),
          !is.na(match$usageKey[1]))
taxon_key <- match$usageKey[1]

# A small exploratory search, not an exhaustive occurrence download.
live_result <- rgbif::occ_search(
  taxonKey = taxon_key,
  country = "GB",
  hasCoordinate = TRUE,
  limit = 300
)
occ_live <- live_result$data

nrow(occ_live)
head(occ_live[, intersect(c("species", "decimalLongitude",
                            "decimalLatitude", "eventDate"), names(occ_live))])

In rgbif 3.9.0 and later, the default taxonomic checklist changed from the GBIF Backbone to the Catalogue of Life Extended Release. Always inspect the match and document the checklist and package version rather than assuming taxon identifiers remain unchanged. See the rgbif migration guidance.
Change: For another species, modify species_name and inspect match before downloading. Consider adding a date filter. Compare: Why might the live result differ from the prepared workshop snapshot? A limit is a maximum returned by the search, not evidence of a complete or unbiased sample.






NoteData provenance and citation for research





For a thesis or publication, record the taxonomic checklist, query filters, date of retrieval, original dataset identifiers, licences and cleaning decisions. GBIF recommends DOI-assigned occurrence downloads (for example with rgbif::occ_download()) for citable research datasets; occ_search() by itself does not create a DOI for the result. See GBIF’s citation guidance and the optional Data Preparation chapter.

title: Species Data
text:
For the core practical, continue with occ_raw, not the optional occ_live object. First identify records with missing, non-numeric or impossible geographic coordinates. This is a basic plausibility check, not a complete cleaning procedure.

# Preserve the original fields; make the two coordinate columns numeric.
occ_check <- occ_raw
occ_check$decimalLongitude <- suppressWarnings(
  as.numeric(as.character(occ_check$decimalLongitude))
)
occ_check$decimalLatitude <- suppressWarnings(
  as.numeric(as.character(occ_check$decimalLatitude))
)

valid_coords <- with(occ_check,
  is.finite(decimalLongitude) & is.finite(decimalLatitude) &
  decimalLongitude >= -180 & decimalLongitude <= 180 &
  decimalLatitude >= -90 & decimalLatitude <= 90
)

# A copy containing valid longitude/latitude pairs.
occ_valid <- occ_check[valid_coords, , drop = FALSE]

count_check <- data.frame(
  stage = c("Snapshot", "Valid geographic coordinates"),
  records = c(nrow(occ_check), nrow(occ_valid))
)
count_check

                         stage records
1                     Snapshot    2000
2 Valid geographic coordinates    2000

stopifnot(nrow(occ_valid) > 0)

A valid pair of longitude/latitude values can still be wrong: the coordinates might fall in the sea, refer to a museum, have been rounded, or be inconsistent with the species’ recorded locality.



ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = UK_sf, fill = "grey94", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(data = occ_valid,
             aes(x = decimalLongitude, y = decimalLatitude),
             colour = "#65449b", size = 0.8, alpha = 0.45) +
  coord_sf() +
  labs(title = "Occurrence record snapshot",
       subtitle = "(unreviewed, georeferenced records)",
       x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude") +
  theme_minimal()








Inspect: Are the occurrences evenly distributed? Does a cluster prove that habitat is better in that area? Could survey effort, roads, local recording activity or repeated visits contribute to the pattern?
Research caution: The focal species may have sensitive roost locations. Check data-provider restrictions and relevant conservation guidance before distributing exact locations. The interactive web demonstration below uses an aggregated grid, not individual coordinates or precise roost metadata.

title: Species Data
text:
Data cleaning should be traceable and scientifically justified. A flagged coordinate is a candidate for inspection, not automatically an invalid ecological observation. Keep the original snapshot unchanged so every exclusion can be reconsidered.



# Are records repeated at the same coordinates?
# This is different from identical GBIF record IDs or repeated surveys.
coordinate_pair <- paste(occ_valid$decimalLongitude,
                         occ_valid$decimalLatitude, sep = "|")

sum(duplicated(coordinate_pair))

[1] 1431

# Inspect a few potentially repeated locations.
head(occ_valid[duplicated(coordinate_pair),
               c("decimalLongitude", "decimalLatitude"),
               drop = FALSE])

   decimalLongitude decimalLatitude
9         -3.107454        52.54766
22        -2.239404        51.55914
35        -1.550000        51.94000
36        -1.480000        51.99000
41        -2.000000        51.35000
43        -3.300000        51.94000


A repeated location may represent a duplicate import, a long-used roost or independent surveys at different times. Why would discarding every repeat without checking dates and record IDs be inappropriate?



Here we use CoordinateCleaner to flag several common problems, including duplicate coordinates within the same species, coordinates near country centroids, equal latitude/longitude values, coordinates near biodiversity institutions and the (0, 0) region. The checks are imperfect and some may flag genuine locations.

# This package is required for the core cleaning example.
library(CoordinateCleaner)

# The cleaning function requires a species field.
if (!"species" %in% names(occ_valid)) {
  occ_valid$species <- "Rhinolophus hipposideros"
}
occ_valid$species <- as.character(occ_valid$species)
occ_valid$species[is.na(occ_valid$species) |
                    !nzchar(as.character(occ_valid$species))] <-
  "Rhinolophus hipposideros"

# Keep flagging separate from deletion.
occ_rhinhipp_flags <- CoordinateCleaner::clean_coordinates(
  x = occ_valid,
  lon = "decimalLongitude",
  lat = "decimalLatitude",
  species = "species",
  tests = c("centroids", "duplicates", "equal",
            "gbif", "institutions", "zeros"),
  inst_rad = 10000,
  value = "spatialvalid",
  verbose = FALSE
)

# TRUE: passed the selected tests; FALSE: review the record.
flag_summary <- as.logical(occ_rhinhipp_flags$.summary)
flag_summary[is.na(flag_summary)] <- FALSE

summary_table <- data.frame(
  result = c("Passed selected tests", "Flagged for review"),
  records = c(sum(flag_summary), sum(!flag_summary))
)
summary_table

                 result records
1 Passed selected tests     355
2    Flagged for review    1645

# Retain a working copy for subsequent exercises.
occ_rhinhipp_cleaned <- occ_valid[flag_summary, , drop = FALSE]
stopifnot(nrow(occ_rhinhipp_cleaned) > 0)

Inspect: How many records were flagged? Which tests might remove legitimate observations? Should a 10 km institution radius make sense for this species and the underlying data sources? How might you report exclusions in a research paper?






NoteImportant limitations of automated cleaning





These tests do not prove species identification, absence of recording bias, suitability for the study period, or that coordinates correspond to the actual observation site. Check coordinate uncertainty, basisOfRecord, reported country, taxonomic status, occurrenceStatus, dates and relevant expert knowledge as part of a research-grade workflow. Review survey design before treating a non-detection as an absence.
The data used for later model fitting should be derived from a documented and consistently applied cleaning protocol. The automated flags shown here are an introductory exercise, not a universal filter.






For an interactive public map, we show counts per approximate 0.25-degree cell, rather than precise occurrence coordinates. These aggregated locations let you explore broad differences but are not appropriate for fine-scale habitat inference.

library(terra)

public_grid <- terra::rast(
  xmin = -12, xmax = 4, ymin = 49, ymax = 61,
  resolution = 0.25, crs = "EPSG:4326"
)

aggregate_for_map <- function(records, grid) {
  xy <- as.matrix(records[, c("decimalLongitude", "decimalLatitude")])
  cell <- terra::cellFromXY(grid, xy)
  counts <- table(cell[!is.na(cell)])
  if (length(counts) == 0) {
    return(data.frame(lon = numeric(), lat = numeric(), n = integer()))
  }
  grid_xy <- terra::xyFromCell(grid, as.integer(names(counts)))
  data.frame(lon = grid_xy[, 1], lat = grid_xy[, 2],
             n = as.integer(counts))
}

map_raw <- aggregate_for_map(occ_valid, public_grid)
map_clean <- aggregate_for_map(occ_rhinhipp_cleaned, public_grid)

nrow(map_raw)

[1] 119

nrow(map_clean)

[1] 93








Interact: Turn each layer on and off. What patterns persist? Why might removing flagged points affect interpretation of the apparent distribution? Background map tiles require an internet connection; the static map above still illustrates the records if tiles are unavailable.

title: Species Data
text:
Opportunistic records tend to reflect where observers go and where observations are reported. Their density is therefore not simply an index of species abundance or environmental suitability. Spatial thinning can reduce repeated sampling within a grid cell, but it cannot reconstruct the unsampled landscape and may discard useful data.


The following deterministic example selects one record per grid cell after randomising order. The random seed lets another student reproduce the same choices. The grid sizes are in degrees, not equal distances in kilometres; for serious analysis, a suitable projected CRS and ecologically justified scale are preferable.

library(terra)

thin_to_grid <- function(records, grain, seed = 123) {
  grid <- terra::rast(
    xmin = -12, xmax = 4, ymin = 49, ymax = 61,
    resolution = grain, crs = "EPSG:4326"
  )
  xy <- as.matrix(records[, c("decimalLongitude", "decimalLatitude")])
  cells <- terra::cellFromXY(grid, xy)

  set.seed(seed)
  shuffled <- sample(seq_len(nrow(records)))
  valid <- !is.na(cells[shuffled])
  shuffled <- shuffled[valid]
  selected <- shuffled[!duplicated(cells[shuffled])]
  records[sort(selected), , drop = FALSE]
}

thin_010 <- thin_to_grid(occ_rhinhipp_cleaned, grain = 0.10)
thin_025 <- thin_to_grid(occ_rhinhipp_cleaned, grain = 0.25)
thin_050 <- thin_to_grid(occ_rhinhipp_cleaned, grain = 0.50)

# Compare the number of records retained.
thinning_counts <- c(
  original = nrow(occ_rhinhipp_cleaned),
  grid_010 = nrow(thin_010),
  grid_025 = nrow(thin_025),
  grid_050 = nrow(thin_050)
)

  paste0("0.25° thinning (n = ", nrow(thin_025), ")"),
  paste0("0.50° thinning (n = ", nrow(thin_050), ")")

  rbind,
  lapply(seq_along(datasets), function(i) {
    data.frame(
      lon = datasets[[i]]$decimalLongitude,
      lat = datasets[[i]]$decimalLatitude,
      stage = stage_labels[i]
    )
  })
)

  plot_points$stage,
  levels = stage_labels

  lon = occ_rhinhipp_cleaned$decimalLongitude,

map_ylim <- lat_range + c(-lat_pad, lat_pad)

title: Data Preparation
text:
This is an optional reference chapter. You can complete the core SDM practical using the prepared datasets supplied in the student materials. You do not need to download data from GBIF or WorldClim before fitting your first model.
The examples below show how the workshop inputs can be obtained and documented in R. They are intended for students who want to repeat the preparation workflow, test alternative data sources or develop their own research project. The download code is displayed but not executed when this page is built. If you try the examples, run them in RStudio from your own workshop project folder.






TipThree ways to obtain data for your own SDM




Collect your own observations: use field surveys, monitoring or systematic sampling; distinguish observed presences, credible absences and non-detections.
Reuse existing occurrence records: obtain suitably documented data from research collections, museums or biodiversity databases such as GBIF.
Use environmental information: obtain climate, elevation, land-cover or other predictors from existing datasets or measurements, at spatial and temporal resolutions appropriate to your question.

In every case, document where the data came from, what they represent, their limitations and any processing decisions. A downloaded presence record is not automatically a verified absence at any other location.




The proposed data download contains a data/ folder with the following existing workshop inputs:







File
Main contents and purpose




data/workshop_data.RData
Saved UK boundaries and occurrence-related objects, including the focal species Rhinolophus hipposideros


data/Clim_UK.tif
19 historical WorldClim bioclimatic layers for the UK example


data/Elev_UK.tif
Elevation raster for the UK example



These files must remain in the data/ folder inside the RStudio project you create.
Try loading and inspecting the supplied data:

# Run in your RStudio project (not in an arbitrary working directory)
getwd()
file.exists("data/workshop_data.RData")

The teaching example uses the lesser horseshoe bat, Rhinolophus hipposideros, in the United Kingdom (country = "GB" in GBIF). GBIF aggregates records from multiple publishers; downloaded coordinates can include duplicates, imprecise localities and sampling biases. Records must be inspected and cleaned before modelling.
The code below illustrates a limited GBIF search. It is appropriate for learning how an API query works, not as a complete or publication-ready occurrence dataset. Search results may change over time and limiting the number returned does not provide a representative sample.

species_name <- "Rhinolophus hipposideros"
match_species <- rgbif::name_backbone(name = species_name)
species_key <- match_species$speciesKey
stopifnot(length(species_key) == 1, !is.na(species_key))

occ_result <- rgbif::occ_search(
  taxonKey = species_key,
  country = "GB",
  hasCoordinate = TRUE,
  limit = 2000
)
occ_df_rhinhipp <- occ_result$data

# Explore the records and document what was actually retrieved
nrow(occ_df_rhinhipp)
names(occ_df_rhinhipp)
head(occ_df_rhinhipp[, intersect(
  c("species", "decimalLongitude", "decimalLatitude", "eventDate"),
  names(occ_df_rhinhipp)
)])
retrieval_date <- Sys.Date()
retrieval_date



The original workshop also retrieves other bat observations to illustrate target-group background sampling. These data are records of other bat species, not confirmed absences of the focal species. They must be filtered and assessed before use in a model.

bat_match <- rgbif::name_backbone(name = "Chiroptera")
bat_key <- bat_match$usageKey
stopifnot(length(bat_key) == 1, !is.na(bat_key))

bat_result <- rgbif::occ_search(
  taxonKey = bat_key,
  country = "GB",
  hasCoordinate = TRUE,
  limit = 10000
)
bat_df <- bat_result$data

# Retain records with coordinates and a taxon name
required_columns <- c("species", "decimalLongitude", "decimalLatitude")
stopifnot(all(required_columns %in% names(bat_df)))
target_group_df <- dplyr::filter(
  bat_df,
  !is.na(.data$species),
  .data$species != species_name,
  !is.na(.data$decimalLongitude),
  !is.na(.data$decimalLatitude)
)
target_group_df <- dplyr::select(
  target_group_df,
  dplyr::all_of(required_columns)
)
target_group_sf <- sf::st_as_sf(
  target_group_df,
  coords = c("decimalLongitude", "decimalLatitude"),
  crs = 4326
)







NoteGBIF citation and reproducible research





A GBIF occ_search() query does not automatically create a single DOI-assigned occurrence download. For research and publication, consider the GBIF download system and preserve the resulting DOI and download information. Keep the exact taxon and spatial filters, retrieval date, record-selection rules, quality-control steps, licences and attribution to original publishers.
A time-stamped saved snapshot is often more reproducible than repeatedly asking for the latest available records; the appropriate observation period depends on the ecological question. For detailed guidance, consult GBIF citation guidelines.







The code below illustrates the same object names used in the original workshop, so the subsequent SDM chapters can locate prepared boundaries and species records. Run the relevant optional examples above first. Saving to data/rebuilt/ protects the distributed student files.

needed_objects <- c(
  "World_sf", "UK_sf", "UK_admin_sf", "WalesEast_admin_sf",
  "species_name", "occ_df_rhinhipp", "target_group_sf"
)
missing_objects <- needed_objects[
  !vapply(needed_objects, function(x) {
    exists(x, envir = .GlobalEnv, inherits = FALSE)
  }, logical(1))
]
if (length(missing_objects)) {
  stop("First create these objects: ", paste(missing_objects, collapse = ", "))
}

dir.create("data/rebuilt", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
save(
  World_sf, UK_sf, UK_admin_sf, WalesEast_admin_sf,
  species_name, occ_df_rhinhipp, target_group_sf,
  file = "data/rebuilt/workshop_data.RData"
)

# Inspect the saved object names in a separate environment
check_snapshot <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
load("data/rebuilt/workshop_data.RData", envir = check_snapshot)
ls(check_snapshot)

For independent research, it is often clearer to save individual .rds or .csv tables plus raster files, with a short data dictionary and provenance file, rather than relying entirely on a single .RData workspace. Never overwrite the original field records or downloaded snapshot without preserving the source and processing history.



Before presenting results in a dissertation or publication, document the following decisions:

Ecological question and study extent: species, time period, spatial boundary and the area accessible to the species.
Occurrence provenance: surveys or database sources, retrieval date, persistent citations, filters and coordinate uncertainty.
Environmental predictors: source, baseline, resolution, units, projections, and the ecological justification for selection.
Sampling and quality control: duplicated observations, sampling bias, presence/absence/background definitions, and missing-data handling.
Modelling and validation: training/test separation, spatial dependence, tuning, evaluation measures and uncertainty.
Reproducible outputs: input snapshots, processing scripts, package versions and enough metadata to reconstruct results.

The ODMAP reporting framework is a useful reference for organising these decisions. Detailed modelling choices are introduced throughout the workshop’s practical and advanced chapters.

Natural Earth boundary data and the rnaturalearth package.
GBIF occurrence records and citation guidance.
geodata R package for retrieving environmental datasets.






Zurrell et al. (2020). A standard protocol for reporting species distribution models.

For this workshop release: replace any unvalidated climate projection file before publishing future-suitability demonstrations or distributing it to students.

title: SDM Workshop
text:
This workshop introduces Species Distribution Modelling using R and open datasets. Explore spatial data, species occurrences, environmental predictors, and learn to fit, assess, and compare species distribution models including GLMs, Random Forests, and MaxEnt. Build your skills to generate predictions and ensemble models confidently.




Konstans Wells


Biodiversity, Animal Health and Ecosystems (BAHE) Group, Swansea University

title: SDM Workshop
section: How to use the code and interactive outputs
text:
How to use the code and interactive outputs
Read → run → inspect → change → explain.
The aim is not simply to reproduce the examples shown on the website, but to develop your own understanding of R coding and the ecological reasoning behind each step.
Build your own R script as you work through the tutorial:

Read the ecological question and explanation.
Copy and run the R code in your own script.
Inspect the resulting figures, tables and maps.
Change a predictor, model formula or plotting option and rerun the code.
Explain the result in your own comments, including any ecological interpretation or limitations.

Add short comments to your script using # to explain what you are doing and why.






TipMore guidance: examples, demonstrations and exercises












On the website
What to do




R code with results
Copy the code into your script, run it and compare the results.


A figure or interactive map without code
Explore the demonstration and consider its ecological interpretation.


An exercise without displayed results
Modify and execute the code independently.


An example using prepared datasets
Load the required files and continue without repeating lengthy downloads.



Interactive maps allow you to zoom, pan and explore spatial patterns directly on the website, but they cannot execute new R analyses in your browser.
Use RStudio to modify datasets, fit models or generate new predictions.
If an example relies on prepared objects, follow the loading instructions provided in that chapter.

title: SDM Workshop
text:
Beyond the core practical
After completing the introductory GLM workflow, the workshop provides further material for independent MRes, PhD and other research projects:

Fitting & Comparing Algorithms — GAMs, BRTs, Random Forests, MaxEnt and the assumptions behind model comparisons.
Ensemble Modelling — model combination, differences among predictions and uncertainty.
Assessment & Projection — spatial validation, transferability, extrapolation and environmental novelty.
Data Preparation — data sources, reproducible preparation and documentation for independent research.

For research, the aim is not simply to fit additional algorithms but to justify scientific decisions about sampling bias, accessible areas, predictors, evaluation, transferability and uncertainty. Useful references include the ODMAP reporting framework and Valavi et al. on spatially separated cross-validation.






NoteSoftware, data sources and image credits





The online workshop was developed with Quarto and R. Its published pages contain the tutorial and copyable R examples; the separate student materials supply the practical files.
The workshop illustration and favicon incorporate a photograph of the lesser horseshoe bat (Rhinolophus hipposideros). Credits supplied with the original workshop: Oriol Massana Valeriano and Adrià López-Baucells. Third-party image rights should be checked separately from the licence covering the workshop text and code.

title: Spatial Data in R
section: Start in your own R project
text:
Start in your own R project
Follow the homepage instructions to download the student files and create your own RStudio project. Save your code in your own .R script (for example, 01_SDM_practical.R), and add comments explaining what each command does.
Copy and run this first example. It loads the packages used in this chapter and the prepared workshop datasets. You do not need to download data from online services.

library(terra)     # Vector and raster operations
library(sf)        # Spatial objects and geometry
library(ggplot2)   # Plotting maps with ggplot2

# Check that you are working in the workshop project folder
stopifnot(file.exists("data/workshop_data.RData"))
stopifnot(file.exists("data/Clim_UK.tif"))

# Load the prepared boundaries and environmental raster
load("data/workshop_data.RData")
Clim_UK <- terra::rast("data/Clim_UK.tif")

# Confirm the expected data are available
stopifnot(inherits(UK_sf, "sf"))
stopifnot(inherits(UK_admin_sf, "sf"))
stopifnot(inherits(WalesEast_admin_sf, "sf"))
stopifnot("bio_12" %in% names(Clim_UK))

names(Clim_UK)

 [1] "bio_1"  "bio_2"  "bio_3"  "bio_4"  "bio_5"  "bio_6"  "bio_7"  "bio_8" 
 [9] "bio_9"  "bio_10" "bio_11" "bio_12" "bio_13" "bio_14" "bio_15" "bio_16"
[17] "bio_17" "bio_18" "bio_19"

terra::nlyr(Clim_UK)

[1] 19


If a file cannot be found, return to the project folder and setup check on the homepage. Do not use setwd() to conceal an incorrect project location. The chapter’s setup is shown deliberately, so you can reproduce its later plots in your own R session.

title: Spatial Data in R
section: 1. Vector data: points, lines and polygons
text:
1. Vector data: points, lines and polygons
A vector represents individual spatial features:

Points represent species observations, survey locations or weather stations.
Lines represent features such as rivers, transects or movements.
Polygons represent areas such as survey boundaries, habitats or administrative regions.

Each feature can have attributes (for example, species, observation date or habitat type). A spatial dataset therefore combines a geometry with a data table.

1.1 Create and map point locations
Let’s create six point locations from longitude and latitude. Longitude is the first coordinate; latitude is the second.

city_coords <- matrix(c(
  -1.2577, 51.7520,   # Oxford
  12.4964, 41.9028,   # Rome
  -3.9440, 51.6214,   # Swansea
   8.6821, 50.1109,   # Frankfurt
   8.5417, 47.3769,   # Zurich
   2.3522, 48.8566    # Paris
), ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)

city_points <- terra::vect(
  city_coords,
  type = "points",
  crs = "EPSG:4326"
)
city_points$city <- c(
  "Oxford", "Rome", "Swansea",
  "Frankfurt", "Zurich", "Paris"
)

plot(city_points, col = "steelblue", pch = 16,
     xlim = c(-6, 16), ylim = c(38, 56),
     main = "Illustrative city locations")
text(city_points, labels = city_points$city,
     pos = 4, cex = 0.75)







class(city_points)

[1] "SpatVector"
attr(,"package")
[1] "terra"

terra::crs(city_points, describe = TRUE)

    name authority code  area             extent
1 WGS 84      EPSG 4326 World -180, 180, -90, 90


Inspect: Which R class stores these points? How are the city names attached to the coordinates?
Change: Add one city with its longitude and latitude. Remember to update the city-name vector as well.


1.2 Coordinate reference systems (CRSs)
A coordinate reference system (CRS) describes how coordinates relate to the Earth. EPSG:4326 is a geographic CRS using longitude and latitude in degrees. Projected CRSs generally express coordinates in linear units, such as metres, and are useful for some distance- and area-based analyses.
It is essential to distinguish assigning a CRS from transforming coordinates:

# Inspect the original CRS
terra::crs(city_points, describe = TRUE)

    name authority code  area             extent
1 WGS 84      EPSG 4326 World -180, 180, -90, 90

# Transform the point coordinates to a European projected CRS
city_points_europe <- terra::project(city_points, "EPSG:3035")

# Compare coordinates before and after transformation
head(terra::crds(city_points))

           x       y
[1,] -1.2577 51.7520
[2,] 12.4964 41.9028
[3,] -3.9440 51.6214
[4,]  8.6821 50.1109
[5,]  8.5417 47.3769
[6,]  2.3522 48.8566

head(terra::crds(city_points_europe))

           x       y
[1,] 3547145 3242304
[2,] 4528867 2092277
[3,] 3362083 3259926
[4,] 4226726 3000691
[5,] 4210798 2697007
[6,] 3760772 2889485


Do not use terra::crs(city_points) <- "EPSG:3035" to reproject the points. This would incorrectly relabel the existing coordinates without moving them. Use terra::project() (or sf::st_transform() for sf objects). https://rspatial.github.io/terra/reference/project.html






NoteWhy choosing a CRS matters






EPSG:4326: longitude and latitude in degrees; convenient for global occurrence records.
EPSG:27700: British National Grid; often suitable for detailed UK mapping.
EPSG:3035: a European equal-area projection, useful for some regional area comparisons.
EPSG:3857: Web Mercator, common for online maps but not a suitable general-purpose equal-area system.

Always inspect the CRS before combining layers. Where possible, transform vector geometries to match a raster rather than needlessly reprojecting the raster and resampling its values.





1.3 Lines and polygons: an illustrative movement route
We will draw a hypothetical bird movement route and an illustrative polygon. These are teaching geometries, not observed tracking data or a recognised protected-area boundary.

# Illustrative route through Europe (longitude, latitude)
route_coords <- matrix(c(
  15.0, 60.0,
   9.0, 56.0,
   5.0, 52.0,
   2.0, 48.0,
  -1.0, 44.0,
   0.0, 40.0
), ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)

# A line is an ordered series of coordinates
route_sf <- sf::st_sf(
  label = "Illustrative route",
  geometry = sf::st_sfc(
    sf::st_linestring(route_coords), crs = 4326
  )
)
migration_line <- terra::vect(route_sf)

# A polygon is a closed ring: last point = first point
area_coords <- matrix(c(
  1.0, 48.4,
  1.0, 47.2,
  2.2, 47.2,
  3.0, 47.4,
  3.0, 48.4,
  1.0, 48.4
), ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)

area_sf <- sf::st_sf(
  label = "Illustrative area",
  geometry = sf::st_sfc(
    sf::st_polygon(list(area_coords)), crs = 4326
  )
)
illustrative_area <- terra::vect(area_sf)

# Plot the route and area in the same coordinate system
plot(illustrative_area, col = "lightblue", border = "blue",
     xlim = c(-3, 17), ylim = c(38, 62),
     main = "Illustrative movement route and area")
lines(migration_line, col = "darkgreen", lwd = 2)








Inspect: How do the geometries of the line and polygon differ? What does closing the ring accomplish?
Research connection: Real tracking data may also require timestamps and analysis of movement uncertainty. A drawn route alone is not evidence of a species’ migration pathway.






TipChange and explore: Movement paths and tortuosity






Add waypoints: Create a new movement path by inserting additional points between the existing waypoints. Experiment with changing their positions to make the route more or less winding. Plot the original and modified paths together.
Sample fewer locations: Randomly remove some intermediate waypoints from the modified path, keeping the start and end points and preserving the original sequence of the remaining points. Plot the resulting routes.
Compare: How do the apparent movement patterns, total path lengths and path tortuosity change as you retain fewer or more waypoints?

Think about: How might the frequency of GPS observations influence estimates of animal movement distances and habitat use? Why could different sampling intervals lead to different ecological interpretations?





1.4 Obtaining and mapping UK administrative boundaries
Administrative boundaries provide a geographic context for ecological observations. These are examples of polygon vector data.
In R, we can obtain country and regional boundaries directly from Natural Earth using the rnaturalearth package.
We will explore two approaches:

Retrieve the original spatial data using R.
Load prepared spatial data supplied with the workshop.

Both approaches allow us to construct the same type of map. During the practical, the prepared data provide a convenient starting point, but learning how to retrieve new spatial datasets is valuable for independent research.

Option A: Obtain administrative boundaries using R
The following code demonstrates how to retrieve UK country and administrative boundaries.

library(sf)
library(rnaturalearth)

# Retrieve country boundaries
World_sf <- rnaturalearth::ne_countries(
  scale = "medium",
  returnclass = "sf"
)

# Retrieve the United Kingdom boundary
UK_sf <- rnaturalearth::ne_countries(
  scale = "medium",
  country = "United Kingdom",
  returnclass = "sf"
)

# Retrieve UK administrative boundaries
UK_admin_sf <- rnaturalearth::ne_states(
  country = "United Kingdom",
  returnclass = "sf"
)

# Inspect the data structure and attributes
names(UK_admin_sf)
head(sf::st_drop_geometry(UK_admin_sf))

# Explore the regional classifications, if available
if ("region" %in% names(UK_admin_sf)) {
  unique(UK_admin_sf$region)
}

# Select East Wales using the regional attribute
if (!"region" %in% names(UK_admin_sf)) {
  stop("The regional attribute is unavailable. Inspect the data or use the workshop snapshot.")
}

WalesEast_admin_sf <- UK_admin_sf[
  !is.na(UK_admin_sf$region) &
    UK_admin_sf$region == "East Wales",
]

# Check that the selection returned a polygon
if (nrow(WalesEast_admin_sf) == 0) {
  stop("East Wales was not found. Check the boundary classification or use the supplied data.")
}

Understanding the code

ne_countries() retrieves country boundaries.
ne_states() retrieves subnational administrative boundaries.
returnclass = "sf" requests spatial objects compatible with the sf package.
names() and head() allow us to inspect the attributes.
Subsetting selects features matching a particular regional classification.

Important: Administrative classifications and attribute names can vary between data sources and versions. Inspect the downloaded attributes before selecting a region. The UK administrative-boundary example may require additional high-resolution Natural Earth data.






TipExplore: Choosing another region





Try selecting another administrative region using the available attributes.

Which attribute identifies the region?
How many polygons are returned?
What happens if you choose a region that does not exist?
How might differences in administrative boundaries affect ecological analyses?






Option B: Load the prepared workshop boundaries
For the core practical, the same spatial objects have been prepared and saved with the workshop datasets.
This avoids repeated downloads and ensures that everyone can continue even when online data services are unavailable.

library(sf)
library(ggplot2)

# Load prepared spatial data
load("data/workshop_data.RData")

# Inspect the spatial objects
class(UK_sf)

[1] "sf"         "data.frame"

class(WalesEast_admin_sf)

Note: Options A and B are alternative starting points. If you retrieved the boundaries successfully using Option A, you can continue with those objects without reloading the prepared data.


Visualise East Wales within the United Kingdom
We can now map the UK boundary and highlight East Wales.

# Use copies to preserve the original objects
uk_map <- UK_sf
east_wales_map <- WalesEast_admin_sf

# Ensure both objects use the same CRS
east_wales_map <- sf::st_transform(
  east_wales_map,
  sf::st_crs(uk_map)
)

# Create the map
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(
    data = uk_map,
    fill = "grey90",
    colour = "grey30"
  ) +
  geom_sf(
    data = east_wales_map,
    fill = "steelblue",
    colour = "darkblue",
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "East Wales within the United Kingdom",
    subtitle = "(Administrative boundaries from Natural Earth)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()














TipChange and explore






Change the map: Modify the polygon fill colours, border colours and line widths.
Explore spatial attributes: Use names() and head() to examine the associated geographic information.
Change the region: Select and plot another UK region from the administrative-boundary dataset.
Compare: What differences might arise when using administrative boundaries from another source or at a different spatial resolution?

Research connection: Administrative boundaries can define study areas, but they are not necessarily ecologically meaningful boundaries. How might the choice of study extent influence the interpretation of a species distribution model?









TipOther ways to obtain vector data





Vector data may be supplied as GeoPackage (.gpkg), GeoJSON (.geojson), or as shapefiles (a group of related files, not just .shp). For example, terra::vect("path/to/boundaries.gpkg") reads a GeoPackage. The optional Data Preparation chapter explains the boundary sources and how to obtain them independently.

title: Spatial Data in R
text:
2. Raster data: continuous environmental information
A raster is a regular grid. Each cell contains a value for a particular layer: temperature, elevation or precipitation may be continuous, while land-cover classes are categorical. A raster can contain multiple layers for the same grid.
A raster’s spatial properties include its extent, cell resolution, origin, CRS and its pattern of missing (NA) values. In a longitude/latitude CRS, resolution is expressed in degrees rather than metres. A finer cell size does not necessarily mean the source data are more accurate or ecologically appropriate.

2.1 Make a simple raster and change its resolution

raster_fine <- terra::rast(
  ncols = 50, nrows = 50,
  xmin = 0, xmax = 50, ymin = 0, ymax = 50,
  crs = "EPSG:3857"
)

set.seed(42)  # Repeatable example
terra::values(raster_fine) <- stats::rnorm(terra::ncell(raster_fine))

terra::res(raster_fine)

[1] 1 1

plot(raster_fine, main = "Illustrative raster values")








Now aggregate neighbouring cells into a coarser grid. To compare fine and coarse data on identical cells, we also resample the aggregated layer back to the original grid. Resampling does not recreate the detail that was lost during aggregation.

raster_coarse <- terra::aggregate(
  raster_fine, fact = 2, fun = mean
)
raster_coarse_on_fine <- terra::resample(
  raster_coarse, raster_fine, method = "bilinear"
)

raster_comparison <- c(raster_fine, raster_coarse_on_fine)
names(raster_comparison) <- c("Fine", "Coarse_resampled")

plot(raster_comparison)







terra::res(raster_fine)

[1] 1 1

terra::res(raster_coarse)

[1] 2 2


Inspect: Compare the maps. Why are the values smoother in the aggregated version? Would a fine-resolution raster always be the best environmental predictor for a wide-ranging species?


2.2 Read the prepared WorldClim raster
For our UK example, the supplied Clim_UK.tif contains 19 WorldClim bioclimatic variables at 5 arc-minute resolution. They are named bio_1 through bio_19 in the prepared file. The climate values represent environmental summaries, not direct measurements at every animal observation point.

Clim_UK <- terra::rast("data/Clim_UK.tif")

# Check the data, its CRS and spatial resolution
names(Clim_UK)

 [1] "bio_1"  "bio_2"  "bio_3"  "bio_4"  "bio_5"  "bio_6"  "bio_7"  "bio_8" 
 [9] "bio_9"  "bio_10" "bio_11" "bio_12" "bio_13" "bio_14" "bio_15" "bio_16"
[17] "bio_17" "bio_18" "bio_19"

terra::nlyr(Clim_UK)

[1] 19

terra::crs(Clim_UK, describe = TRUE)

    name authority code  area             extent
1 WGS 84      EPSG 4326 World -180, 180, -90, 90

terra::res(Clim_UK)

[1] 0.08333333 0.08333333

# BIO12: annual precipitation (mm)
precip_UK <- Clim_UK[["bio_12"]]
plot(precip_UK, main = "Annual precipitation (BIO12) — UK")








The prepared climate layers are downloaded from WorldClim; you do not need to download them again for this practical. See Data Preparation for source details, temporal coverage and reproducible download code.


2.3 Transform and manipulate raster data
Here we project the precipitation raster to a new CRS. Raster transformation involves estimating cell values on a new grid and should not be repeated unnecessarily in a research workflow.

precip_UK_projected <- terra::project(
  precip_UK, "EPSG:27700", method = "bilinear"
)
plot(precip_UK_projected,
     main = "Precipitation in British National Grid")








We can also convert units and calculate a neighbourhood mean. Notice that we keep missing values as missing rather than treating them as zero precipitation.

# Convert millimetres to centimetres
precip_cm <- precip_UK / 10

# A 3-by-3-cell neighbourhood mean (illustrative smoothing)
precip_smoothed <- terra::focal(
  precip_UK, w = 3, fun = "mean",
  na.rm = TRUE, na.policy = "omit"
)

plot(c(precip_UK, precip_smoothed),
     main = c("Original BIO12 (mm)", "Smoothed BIO12 (mm)"))








Research connection: Resampling, projection and smoothing can affect the environmental values assigned to occurrence points. Before modelling, decide on a defensible spatial resolution and ensure that predictors share a consistent grid.


2.4 Summarise precipitation within administrative areas
A zonal summary calculates a statistic for each spatial polygon. Here, we estimate mean BIO12 annual precipitation for the supplied UK administrative regions. Some regions may have no valid raster cells and therefore retain NA.

# Work with a copy of the boundaries
uk_zones <- sf::st_transform(
  UK_admin_sf, sf::st_crs(terra::crs(precip_UK))
)

zone_means <- terra::extract(
  precip_UK, terra::vect(uk_zones),
  fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE, ID = TRUE
)

# ID refers to the polygon's row position in the input SpatVector
uk_zones$mean_precip_mm <- zone_means$bio_12[
  match(seq_len(nrow(uk_zones)), zone_means$ID)
]

ggplot(uk_zones) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = mean_precip_mm), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Annual precipitation (mm)",
                       na.value = "grey90") +
  labs(title = "Mean BIO12 by UK administrative region",
       caption = "Source: prepared WorldClim and Natural Earth datasets") +
  theme_minimal()








Inspect: Why might some regions have missing values? Why should those not automatically be replaced with zero?






NoteInterpreting zonal averages





A regional average can conceal strong environmental variation within a polygon. This is relevant when combining species records collected at fine spatial scales with predictors summarised at coarser scales. The administrative boundaries in this demonstration are not necessarily ecologically appropriate modelling regions.





2.5 Extract environmental values at points
A fundamental SDM operation is associating an environmental value with an observation location. First, we sample illustrative random points, not actual bat observations. Later chapters will use genuine occurrence records.

set.seed(123)
uk_vect <- terra::vect(
  sf::st_transform(UK_sf, sf::st_crs(terra::crs(Clim_UK)))
)

# These are random teaching points, NOT species records
sample_points <- terra::spatSample(
  uk_vect, size = 100, method = "random"
)

# Extract BIO12; the first returned column is the point ID
sample_precip <- terra::extract(precip_UK, sample_points)

# Combine coordinates and extracted precipitation
sample_results <- data.frame(
  terra::crds(sample_points),
  precip_mm = sample_precip$bio_12
)
head(sample_results)

Inspect: Do all points have a precipitation value? What might cause a missing value? Why is it important that the point coordinates and environmental raster have compatible CRSs?
Change: Use Clim_UK[["bio_1"]] to extract annual mean temperature at the same points. Examine the map and compare its spatial pattern with precipitation.






TipWhy this matters for SDMs





The next chapters use this same operation to associate measured or derived environmental conditions with species presences and background or pseudo-absence locations. Those extracted variables become candidate predictors in a statistical model. Random sample points used for illustration here must not be mistaken for species absence observations.

title: Spatial Data in R
text:
3. Practise, interpret and extend






NoteCore practice




Plot Clim_UK[["bio_1"]] (annual mean temperature) and Clim_UK[["bio_12"]] (annual precipitation). Which variable appears to have the stronger north–south gradient in the supplied UK data?
Change the aggregation factor in the synthetic raster example from 2 to 5. Describe what happens to spatial detail.
Compare precipitation values at several sampled points. Add a comment in your R script explaining why a point may have a missing environmental value.


Research extension

How would you choose a meaningful spatial resolution for a species that moves kilometres per day compared with one whose movements are measured in metres?
How can spatial coordinate uncertainty affect extraction of predictors at observation locations?
When would you use a projected CRS to calculate distances or areas, and why?
