title: Environmental Data
text:
Species distribution models (SDMs) relate species records to environmental conditions. Climate, topography, land cover, soils and habitat structure can all be informative predictors, but a predictor should be chosen because of an ecological hypothesis—not simply because a raster is available.
This chapter follows Spatial Data in R and Species Data. You will explore prepared environmental layers, learn how to obtain your own data, align rasters and extract environmental values for modelling.






TipLearning outcomes



By the end of the core practical, you should be able to:

Read and inspect environmental rasters and identify important BIO variables.
Explain why spatial resolution, time period and predictor units matter.
Align continuous elevation with a climate grid and assemble a named predictor stack.
Explore relationships between predictors and extract raster values at locations.

A further example compares historical climate with a supplied future climate projection. Optional research extensions show how to download the original data independently and document your choices.




Follow the homepage instructions to create your own RStudio project. Copy the examples into your own .R script and add comments as you work. The supplied datasets are used for the practical, while the optional download examples show how to obtain data for independent research. The website does not install packages or download data when it is built.

library(terra)     # Read, inspect and align environmental rasters
library(sf)        # Handle supplied UK boundaries
library(ggplot2)   # Explore extracted environmental values

# Check your project folder and the supplied data
required_files <- c(
  "data/workshop_data.RData",
  "data/Clim_UK.tif",
  "data/Elev_UK.tif"
)
stopifnot(all(file.exists(required_files)))

# Load the prepared UK boundaries and historical predictors
load("data/workshop_data.RData")
Clim_UK <- terra::rast("data/Clim_UK.tif")
Elev_UK <- terra::rast("data/Elev_UK.tif")

stopifnot(inherits(UK_sf, "sf"))
stopifnot(terra::nlyr(Clim_UK) == 19)
stopifnot(all(c("bio_1", "bio_12") %in% names(Clim_UK)))

message("Environmental input files loaded successfully.")

If the file check fails: open the correct RStudio project and check the data/ folder. Do not change your working directory with setwd() as a workaround. If you are continuing from Chapter 2, some of these objects may already exist; running this setup again is safe.



Climate can influence species physiology, food availability, phenology and habitat suitability. WorldClim 2.1 provides historical climate summaries for 1970–2000. These are long-term climatological summaries, not current weather and not conditions measured on the exact date of every species observation.
WorldClim’s 19 bioclimatic (BIO) variables summarise annual means, variation, seasonality and extremes. For example:



Layer
Ecological interpretation
Units in the supplied raster




bio_1
Annual mean temperature
°C


bio_4
Temperature seasonality
Standard deviation × 100


bio_12
Annual precipitation
mm


bio_15
Precipitation seasonality
Coefficient of variation



For the complete variable definitions, consult WorldClim’s BIO variable guide.


The supplied Clim_UK.tif contains 19 named layers at 5 arc-minute resolution (approximately 9 km north–south; actual east–west distances vary with latitude).

names(Clim_UK)

 [1] "bio_1"  "bio_2"  "bio_3"  "bio_4"  "bio_5"  "bio_6"  "bio_7"  "bio_8" 
 [9] "bio_9"  "bio_10" "bio_11" "bio_12" "bio_13" "bio_14" "bio_15" "bio_16"
[17] "bio_17" "bio_18" "bio_19"

terra::nlyr(Clim_UK)

[1] 19

terra::res(Clim_UK)   # Cell size in degrees, not metres

[1] 0.08333333 0.08333333

terra::crs(Clim_UK, describe = TRUE)

    name authority code  area             extent
1 WGS 84      EPSG 4326 World -180, 180, -90, 90

# Select variables by name rather than by layer number
clim_example <- Clim_UK[[c("bio_1", "bio_12")]]
plot(clim_example,
     main = c("Annual mean temperature (BIO1)",
              "Annual precipitation (BIO12)"))








Inspect: How do temperature and precipitation vary across the UK? What could explain the patterns?
Change: Plot bio_4 and bio_15 instead. What new ecological information do they provide?






NoteResearch extension: download WorldClim yourself





The code below shows the original acquisition route using geodata. It is visible so you can copy it into RStudio, but it is not run while the website is built. An internet connection and time for the global download are required.

library(geodata)

# Keep optional downloads separate from supplied workshop files
dir.create("data/optional_downloads", recursive = TRUE,
           showWarnings = FALSE)

clim_global <- geodata::worldclim_global(
  var = "bio", res = 5, path = "data/optional_downloads"
)

# UK_sf was loaded in the chapter setup
uk_vector <- terra::vect(UK_sf)
clim_uk_downloaded <- terra::mask(
  terra::crop(clim_global, uk_vector), uk_vector
)

# Verify that the original data contain BIO1 ... BIO19
names(clim_uk_downloaded)
stopifnot(terra::nlyr(clim_uk_downloaded) == 19)

# Match the documented source order to the workshop naming convention
names(clim_uk_downloaded) <- paste0("bio_", 1:19)

plot(clim_uk_downloaded[["bio_12"]])
# Optional: save a NEW file, without replacing data/Clim_UK.tif
terra::writeRaster(clim_uk_downloaded,
  "data/optional_downloads/Clim_UK_downloaded.tif", overwrite = TRUE)

Compare: Do your download and the teaching snapshot have matching extent, resolution and missing-value patterns? Document data product, version, baseline period, download date and any crop/mask decisions. For the full provenance workflow, see Data Preparation.







Elevation may describe thermal and moisture gradients, exposure or topographic constraints. It can also be correlated with climate. Including both elevation and temperature therefore requires ecological justification, not just statistical convenience.

names(Elev_UK)

[1] "GBR_elv_msk"

terra::res(Elev_UK)

[1] 0.008333333 0.008333333

terra::crs(Elev_UK, describe = TRUE)

    name authority code  area             extent
1 WGS 84      EPSG 4326 World -180, 180, -90, 90

plot(Elev_UK, main = "Prepared UK elevation raster (m)")








Inspect: Compare the elevation cell size with terra::res(Clim_UK). Can rasters with different resolutions be stacked directly for SDM prediction? What information would be lost if elevation is aggregated to the climate resolution?






NoteResearch extension: obtain elevation independently





The geodata package can retrieve elevation data without using the supplied file. This is an optional download, and coverage should be checked carefully for the intended study area.

library(geodata)
dir.create("data/optional_downloads", recursive = TRUE,
           showWarnings = FALSE)

elev_downloaded <- geodata::elevation_30s(
  country = "GB", path = "data/optional_downloads"
)
plot(elev_downloaded)

# For research, check coverage, source, vertical units and datum.
# Do not overwrite the supplied data/Elev_UK.tif.

Remember that a dataset’s geographical coverage may not exactly match the polygon you choose as your SDM study area.






Climate is not the only ecologically relevant environmental information. Local vegetation, built-up areas, wetland extent, soils, habitat fragmentation and land-use history can influence species distributions. Such predictors may be particularly relevant for a species whose fine-scale habitat use is poorly represented by coarse climate grids.
Land-cover classes (forest, cropland, built-up land) are categorical, whereas tree-cover fractions and vegetation indices may be continuous. This distinction matters when you choose a resampling method.
Potential sources include ESA WorldCover, Copernicus Land Monitoring and MODIS land products.






TipResearch extension: download a tree-cover fraction layer





The geodata::landcover() function retrieves a derived fractional land-cover product at 30-arc-second resolution. This example is not a download of the original 10-m categorical ESA WorldCover map.

library(geodata)
dir.create("data/optional_downloads", recursive = TRUE,
           showWarnings = FALSE)

tree_fraction_global <- geodata::landcover(
  var = "trees", path = "data/optional_downloads"
)

# Crop and mask to the prepared UK boundary
uk_vector <- terra::vect(UK_sf)
tree_fraction_uk <- terra::mask(
  terra::crop(tree_fraction_global, uk_vector), uk_vector
)
plot(tree_fraction_uk, main = "Tree-cover fraction (illustrative)")

Think about: Would a tree-cover fraction or a binary forest/non-forest class best represent your ecological hypothesis? How do the product date, resolution and accuracy relate to the occurrence data?






Core practical. Before combining environmental variables in an SDM, we need to make sure their spatial data are properly aligned. For example, climate and elevation rasters may cover the same geographic area but have different cell sizes or spatial grids.
We will use R to align these datasets so that environmental values can be combined and compared at the same locations.



# Use BIO1 as the exact grid template
climate_template <- Clim_UK[["bio_1"]]

# Reproject if the CRSs differ; otherwise only resample
if (!terra::same.crs(Elev_UK, climate_template)) {
  Elev_UK_aligned <- terra::project(
    Elev_UK, climate_template, method = "bilinear"
  )
} else {
  Elev_UK_aligned <- terra::resample(
    Elev_UK, climate_template, method = "bilinear"
  )
}

names(Elev_UK_aligned) <- "elevation"

# Verify that the output matches the climate grid
terra::compareGeom(climate_template, Elev_UK_aligned)

[1] TRUE

terra::res(Elev_UK_aligned)

[1] 0.08333333 0.08333333

# These rasters have different geometries: plot separately, not c(x, y)
original_par <- graphics::par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(Elev_UK, main = "Original elevation")
plot(Elev_UK_aligned, main = "Elevation on climate grid")







graphics::par(original_par)

Inspect: Compare the original and aligned elevation maps. Does a finer original resolution guarantee greater accuracy when combined with coarser climate data? Why not?




# Preserve the original bioclimatic layer names
Env_UK_stack <- c(Clim_UK, Elev_UK_aligned)
stopifnot(terra::nlyr(Env_UK_stack) == 20)

# A small three-predictor subset used in subsequent modelling chapters
model_predictors <- c("bio_1", "bio_12", "elevation")
proj_stack <- Env_UK_stack[[model_predictors]]
env_stack <- Env_UK_stack  # Consistent name for later exercises

names(Env_UK_stack)

 [1] "bio_1"     "bio_2"     "bio_3"     "bio_4"     "bio_5"     "bio_6"    
 [7] "bio_7"     "bio_8"     "bio_9"     "bio_10"    "bio_11"    "bio_12"   
[13] "bio_13"    "bio_14"    "bio_15"    "bio_16"    "bio_17"    "bio_18"   
[19] "bio_19"    "elevation"

names(proj_stack)

[1] "bio_1"     "bio_12"    "elevation"

terra::compareGeom(Clim_UK[[1]], proj_stack[["elevation"]])

[1] TRUE


Research connection: Later chapters use temperature, precipitation and elevation to demonstrate SDM fitting. These three variables provide a manageable teaching example; for independent research, predictor selection should be justified by the species’ ecology, the question and the available data.






TipOptional: save an environmental checkpoint





To avoid recomputing aligned elevation in your own project, save a reusable checkpoint without changing the original inputs:

dir.create("data/checkpoints", recursive = TRUE,
           showWarnings = FALSE)
terra::writeRaster(
  proj_stack, "data/checkpoints/SDM_predictors_current.tif",
  overwrite = TRUE
)

# Reopen it in a fresh R session:
# proj_stack <- terra::rast("data/checkpoints/SDM_predictors_current.tif")

The saved file provides a useful checkpoint: you can reload the prepared environmental predictors in a later R session without repeating the alignment steps.
Keep the code used to prepare these predictors in your own R script, together with comments explaining each step. This allows you to reproduce the workflow from the original datasets whenever needed.







Core practical. The same extraction procedure will later link environmental predictors to the cleaned species occurrences and to background locations. Here we use random illustrative locations with valid precipitation values. These are not bat observations or confirmed absences.

set.seed(123)
sample_points <- terra::spatSample(
  proj_stack[["bio_12"]], size = 40, method = "random",
  na.rm = TRUE, as.points = TRUE
)

# Extract all three predictor values at exactly the same locations
env_at_points <- terra::extract(
  proj_stack, sample_points, ID = FALSE
)

head(env_at_points)

5  7.278125   1244 392.97672
6  8.382441   2015        NA

summary(env_at_points)

 Min.   : 5.453   Min.   : 567   Min.   : 16.43  
 1st Qu.: 8.562   1st Qu.: 744   1st Qu.: 50.36

ggplot(env_at_points, aes(x = bio_1, y = bio_12)) +
  geom_point(colour = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Annual mean temperature (°C)",
       y = "Annual precipitation (mm)",
       title = "Environmental variation at sampled UK grid cells") +
  theme_minimal()








Inspect: Are temperature and precipitation independent across the sampled locations?
Change: Replace the scatterplot’s y = bio_12 with y = elevation. Which ecological explanations might account for their association?


Strong correlations can complicate model interpretation because different predictors may provide overlapping information. However, removing predictors solely because they are correlated may discard biologically important variables. Predictor choice should reflect the question, species ecology and modelling method.

# Small demonstration using complete raster cells in the study grid
# For formal model selection, use the training/calibration data only.
all_predictor_cells <- terra::as.data.frame(proj_stack, na.rm = TRUE)

round(stats::cor(all_predictor_cells), 2)

          bio_1 bio_12 elevation
bio_1      1.00  -0.65     -0.83
bio_12    -0.65   1.00      0.70
elevation -0.83   0.70      1.00


Research connection: A correlation between rasters is a spatial pattern, not proof of a causal biological mechanism. Later chapters will introduce model evaluation and spatially separated validation to assess whether relationships generalise beyond the locations used for model training.




Climate-model projections allow us to explore how environmental conditions might differ under a specified future scenario. Here, we compare the supplied WorldClim historical climate data (1970–2000) with a prepared future projection for 2041–2060.
The future dataset was obtained from WorldClim CMIP6 using geodata, cropped to the UK and aligned to the historical climate grid. It is supplied as data/Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK.tif so that everyone can reproduce the comparison without downloading global climate data. The preparation settings and source information should be retained with the dataset for future research use.







Climate data
Source and setting




Historical baseline
WorldClim 2.1, 1970–2000


Future period
2041–2060


Global climate model (GCM)
BCC-CSM2-MR


Emissions and development scenario
SSP1-2.6, specified in geodata as ssp = "126"


Spatial resolution
5 arc-minutes, aligned with the historical UK grid


Variables
19 comparable bioclimatic layers, bio_1 to bio_19



The future data are conditional projections, not observations or predictions of exactly what the UK climate will be. Other climate models and scenarios can produce different results.


Further exploration using prepared data. Subtracting historical BIO1 from future BIO1 gives the projected change in annual mean temperature for each grid cell. This works because the supplied rasters have matching spatial grids and variable definitions.

# Load the prepared CMIP6 projection
future_file <- "data/Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK.tif"
stopifnot(file.exists(future_file))

Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK <- terra::rast(future_file)

# Verify that both rasters describe the same variables and grid
stopifnot(terra::nlyr(Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK) == 19)
stopifnot(identical(names(Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK),
                    names(Clim_UK)))
stopifnot(terra::compareGeom(Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK,
                            Clim_UK, lyrs = TRUE))

# Subtract historical from future annual mean temperature
bio1_change <- Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK[["bio_1"]] -
  Clim_UK[["bio_1"]]

# Map the difference, in degrees Celsius
plot(bio1_change,
     main = "Projected change in annual mean temperature (°C)\n2041–2060 minus 1970–2000; SSP1-2.6")







# Inspect the range of projected differences
terra::global(bio1_change, "range", na.rm = TRUE)

           min      max
bio_1 1.164557 1.978635


Interpret: Positive values indicate higher annual mean temperature in the future projection than in the historical baseline. In the prepared workshop example, the mapped differences are approximately +1.2 to +1.9°C, depending on location. These differences describe one model and one scenario, not an observed warming trend or a range of uncertainty across climate models.
Inspect: Where are the largest and smallest projected changes? Are they distributed evenly across the UK? What other evidence would you need before drawing conclusions about future bat distributions?






TipChange and explore: precipitation projections





BIO12 is annual precipitation, measured in millimetres. Compare the future and historical BIO12 layers with the same subtraction approach:

bio12_change <- Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK[["bio_12"]] -
  Clim_UK[["bio_12"]]

plot(bio12_change,
     main = "Projected annual precipitation change (mm)\n2041–2060 minus 1970–2000")
terra::global(bio12_change, "range", na.rm = TRUE)

Where does projected annual precipitation increase or decrease? Could a change in total precipitation conceal changes in seasonality or extreme events? Why might different environmental variables have different implications for species ecology?






Optional research extension. The example below shows how the original CMIP6 data can be downloaded, cropped and aligned using R. This requires an internet connection and can take time (it is not required for the core practical and is not executed when the website is built).
The code saves an independently generated file under data/optional_downloads/. It does not overwrite the prepared data/Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK.tif used elsewhere in the workshop.

library(geodata)
dir.create("data/optional_downloads", recursive = TRUE,
           showWarnings = FALSE)

# WorldClim CMIP6: BCC-CSM2-MR, SSP1-2.6, 2041–2060
future_global <- geodata::cmip6_world(
  var = "bioc",
  ssp = "126",          # SSP1-2.6 (not SSP5-8.5)
  model = "BCC-CSM2-MR",
  time = "2041-2060",
  res = 5,
  path = "data/optional_downloads"
)

stopifnot(inherits(future_global, "SpatRaster"),
          terra::nlyr(future_global) == 19)

# Check the original names rather than assuming their order
names(future_global)
source_ids <- suppressWarnings(as.integer(
  sub("^bio_?0*", "", names(future_global))
))
stopifnot(!anyNA(source_ids),
          setequal(source_ids, 1:19),
          !anyDuplicated(source_ids))

future_global <- future_global[[match(1:19, source_ids)]]
names(future_global) <- paste0("bio_", 1:19)

# Crop the downloaded future layers to the UK
uk_vector <- terra::project(terra::vect(UK_sf),
                             terra::crs(future_global))
future_uk <- terra::crop(future_global, uk_vector, mask = TRUE)

# Match the historical raster's spatial grid
if (terra::same.crs(future_uk, Clim_UK)) {
  future_rebuilt <- terra::resample(
    future_uk, Clim_UK[[1]], method = "bilinear"
  )
} else {
  future_rebuilt <- terra::project(
    future_uk, Clim_UK[[1]], method = "bilinear"
  )
}
future_rebuilt <- terra::mask(future_rebuilt, Clim_UK[[1]])
names(future_rebuilt) <- names(Clim_UK)
stopifnot(terra::compareGeom(future_rebuilt,
                            Clim_UK, lyrs = TRUE))

# Verify the temperature values and compare them with the baseline
terra::global(Clim_UK[["bio_1"]], "range", na.rm = TRUE)
terra::global(future_rebuilt[["bio_1"]], "range", na.rm = TRUE)

rebuilt_change <- future_rebuilt[["bio_1"]] -
  Clim_UK[["bio_1"]]
terra::global(rebuilt_change, "range", na.rm = TRUE)
plot(rebuilt_change,
     main = "Independently generated BIO1 change (°C)")

# Save a separate file without replacing the workshop dataset
terra::writeRaster(
  future_rebuilt,
  "data/optional_downloads/CMIP6_SSP126_BCC_2041_2060_UK_rebuilt.tif",
  overwrite = TRUE
)

For a reproducible research analysis, record the source and version, download date, GCM, SSP, time period, resolution, units and spatial processing steps. These decisions are as important as the final map. See Data Preparation.



A future climate raster can be used as an input when projecting a fitted SDM, but a change in climate does not automatically imply a corresponding change in species occurrence. Such projections depend on the model’s assumptions, the species’ ability to disperse, habitat availability, land-use change and whether the future environmental conditions lie within the range represented by the model-training data.






TipResearch questions: climate scenarios and uncertainty






What would changing ssp = "126" (SSP1-2.6) to ssp = "585" (SSP5-8.5) mean for the scenario being explored?
Why might two GCMs produce different changes in UK temperature or precipitation under the same SSP?
How could seasonal climate variables reveal ecological changes that annual averages conceal?
Why is a predicted change in climatic suitability not evidence that a species will colonise a newly suitable location?
What limitations arise if occurrence records and climate predictors refer to different decades?

Research projections should consider multiple GCMs and SSPs, model evaluation, environmental novelty and uncertainty. These topics are developed further in Assessment and Projection.













NoteCore practical — complete these before modelling




Plot Clim_UK[["bio_1"]], Clim_UK[["bio_12"]] and Elev_UK_aligned. Explain one spatial pattern for each.
Check terra::compareGeom() for climate and aligned elevation. Why does this matter for predicting suitability at every grid cell?
Extract bio_1, bio_12 and elevation at the same illustrative sample points. Which relationships appear strongest? Are they ecologically causal?
Add a short comment to your own R script explaining why all environmental predictor layers must be aligned before model fitting.




Inspect the prepared BIO1 change map in Section 6. Explain what a positive value represents and why one climate scenario cannot establish how species distributions will change.
Download WorldClim or elevation data independently and document their provenance.
Identify a land-cover product appropriate to the focal species and justify how it should be resampled.
Obtain the CMIP6 projection independently and compare its values, spatial grid and provenance with the supplied workshop raster.
Discuss how spatial scale, temporal mismatch and correlated predictors could bias an SDM.

WorldClim CMIP6 climate projections

# Optional: save a NEW file, without replacing data/Clim_UK.tif
terra::writeRaster(clim_uk_downloaded,
  "data/optional_downloads/Clim_UK_downloaded.tif", overwrite = TRUE)

Compare: Do your download and the teaching snapshot have matching extent, resolution and missing-value patterns? Document data product, version, baseline period, download date and any crop/mask decisions. For the full provenance workflow, see Data Preparation.

title: Environmental Data
text:
Elevation may describe thermal and moisture gradients, exposure or topographic constraints. It can also be correlated with climate. Including both elevation and temperature therefore requires ecological justification, not just statistical convenience.

names(Elev_UK)

[1] "GBR_elv_msk"

terra::res(Elev_UK)

[1] 0.008333333 0.008333333

terra::crs(Elev_UK, describe = TRUE)

    name authority code  area             extent
1 WGS 84      EPSG 4326 World -180, 180, -90, 90

plot(Elev_UK, main = "Prepared UK elevation raster (m)")








Inspect: Compare the elevation cell size with terra::res(Clim_UK). Can rasters with different resolutions be stacked directly for SDM prediction? What information would be lost if elevation is aggregated to the climate resolution?






NoteResearch extension: obtain elevation independently





The geodata package can retrieve elevation data without using the supplied file. This is an optional download, and coverage should be checked carefully for the intended study area.

library(geodata)
dir.create("data/optional_downloads", recursive = TRUE,
           showWarnings = FALSE)

elev_downloaded <- geodata::elevation_30s(
  country = "GB", path = "data/optional_downloads"
)
plot(elev_downloaded)

# For research, check coverage, source, vertical units and datum.
# Do not overwrite the supplied data/Elev_UK.tif.

Remember that a dataset’s geographical coverage may not exactly match the polygon you choose as your SDM study area.

title: Environmental Data
text:
Climate is not the only ecologically relevant environmental information. Local vegetation, built-up areas, wetland extent, soils, habitat fragmentation and land-use history can influence species distributions. Such predictors may be particularly relevant for a species whose fine-scale habitat use is poorly represented by coarse climate grids.
Land-cover classes (forest, cropland, built-up land) are categorical, whereas tree-cover fractions and vegetation indices may be continuous. This distinction matters when you choose a resampling method.
Potential sources include ESA WorldCover, Copernicus Land Monitoring and MODIS land products.






TipResearch extension: download a tree-cover fraction layer





The geodata::landcover() function retrieves a derived fractional land-cover product at 30-arc-second resolution. This example is not a download of the original 10-m categorical ESA WorldCover map.

library(geodata)
dir.create("data/optional_downloads", recursive = TRUE,
           showWarnings = FALSE)

tree_fraction_global <- geodata::landcover(
  var = "trees", path = "data/optional_downloads"
)

# Crop and mask to the prepared UK boundary
uk_vector <- terra::vect(UK_sf)
tree_fraction_uk <- terra::mask(
  terra::crop(tree_fraction_global, uk_vector), uk_vector
)
plot(tree_fraction_uk, main = "Tree-cover fraction (illustrative)")

Think about: Would a tree-cover fraction or a binary forest/non-forest class best represent your ecological hypothesis? How do the product date, resolution and accuracy relate to the occurrence data?

title: Environmental Data
text:
Core practical. Before combining environmental variables in an SDM, we need to make sure their spatial data are properly aligned. For example, climate and elevation rasters may cover the same geographic area but have different cell sizes or spatial grids.
We will use R to align these datasets so that environmental values can be combined and compared at the same locations.



# Use BIO1 as the exact grid template
climate_template <- Clim_UK[["bio_1"]]

# Reproject if the CRSs differ; otherwise only resample
if (!terra::same.crs(Elev_UK, climate_template)) {
  Elev_UK_aligned <- terra::project(
    Elev_UK, climate_template, method = "bilinear"
  )
} else {
  Elev_UK_aligned <- terra::resample(
    Elev_UK, climate_template, method = "bilinear"
  )
}

names(Elev_UK_aligned) <- "elevation"

# Verify that the output matches the climate grid
terra::compareGeom(climate_template, Elev_UK_aligned)

[1] TRUE

terra::res(Elev_UK_aligned)

[1] 0.08333333 0.08333333

# These rasters have different geometries: plot separately, not c(x, y)
original_par <- graphics::par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(Elev_UK, main = "Original elevation")
plot(Elev_UK_aligned, main = "Elevation on climate grid")







graphics::par(original_par)

Inspect: Compare the original and aligned elevation maps. Does a finer original resolution guarantee greater accuracy when combined with coarser climate data? Why not?




# Preserve the original bioclimatic layer names
Env_UK_stack <- c(Clim_UK, Elev_UK_aligned)
stopifnot(terra::nlyr(Env_UK_stack) == 20)

# A small three-predictor subset used in subsequent modelling chapters
model_predictors <- c("bio_1", "bio_12", "elevation")
proj_stack <- Env_UK_stack[[model_predictors]]
env_stack <- Env_UK_stack  # Consistent name for later exercises

Research connection: Later chapters use temperature, precipitation and elevation to demonstrate SDM fitting. These three variables provide a manageable teaching example; for independent research, predictor selection should be justified by the species’ ecology, the question and the available data.






TipOptional: save an environmental checkpoint





To avoid recomputing aligned elevation in your own project, save a reusable checkpoint without changing the original inputs:

dir.create("data/checkpoints", recursive = TRUE,
           showWarnings = FALSE)
terra::writeRaster(
  proj_stack, "data/checkpoints/SDM_predictors_current.tif",
  overwrite = TRUE
)

# Reopen it in a fresh R session:
# proj_stack <- terra::rast("data/checkpoints/SDM_predictors_current.tif")

The saved file provides a useful checkpoint: you can reload the prepared environmental predictors in a later R session without repeating the alignment steps.
Keep the code used to prepare these predictors in your own R script, together with comments explaining each step. This allows you to reproduce the workflow from the original datasets whenever needed.

title: Environmental Data
text:
Core practical. The same extraction procedure will later link environmental predictors to the cleaned species occurrences and to background locations. Here we use random illustrative locations with valid precipitation values. These are not bat observations or confirmed absences.

set.seed(123)
sample_points <- terra::spatSample(
  proj_stack[["bio_12"]], size = 40, method = "random",
  na.rm = TRUE, as.points = TRUE
)

# Extract all three predictor values at exactly the same locations
env_at_points <- terra::extract(
  proj_stack, sample_points, ID = FALSE
)

Change: Replace the scatterplot’s y = bio_12 with y = elevation. Which ecological explanations might account for their association?


Strong correlations can complicate model interpretation because different predictors may provide overlapping information. However, removing predictors solely because they are correlated may discard biologically important variables. Predictor choice should reflect the question, species ecology and modelling method.

# Small demonstration using complete raster cells in the study grid
# For formal model selection, use the training/calibration data only.
all_predictor_cells <- terra::as.data.frame(proj_stack, na.rm = TRUE)

Research connection: A correlation between rasters is a spatial pattern, not proof of a causal biological mechanism. Later chapters will introduce model evaluation and spatially separated validation to assess whether relationships generalise beyond the locations used for model training.

title: Environmental Data
text:
Climate-model projections allow us to explore how environmental conditions might differ under a specified future scenario. Here, we compare the supplied WorldClim historical climate data (1970–2000) with a prepared future projection for 2041–2060.
The future dataset was obtained from WorldClim CMIP6 using geodata, cropped to the UK and aligned to the historical climate grid. It is supplied as data/Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK.tif so that everyone can reproduce the comparison without downloading global climate data. The preparation settings and source information should be retained with the dataset for future research use.







Climate data
Source and setting




Historical baseline
WorldClim 2.1, 1970–2000


Future period
2041–2060


Global climate model (GCM)
BCC-CSM2-MR


Emissions and development scenario
SSP1-2.6, specified in geodata as ssp = "126"


Spatial resolution
5 arc-minutes, aligned with the historical UK grid


Variables
19 comparable bioclimatic layers, bio_1 to bio_19



The future data are conditional projections, not observations or predictions of exactly what the UK climate will be. Other climate models and scenarios can produce different results.


Further exploration using prepared data. Subtracting historical BIO1 from future BIO1 gives the projected change in annual mean temperature for each grid cell. This works because the supplied rasters have matching spatial grids and variable definitions.

# Load the prepared CMIP6 projection
future_file <- "data/Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK.tif"
stopifnot(file.exists(future_file))

Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK <- terra::rast(future_file)

# Verify that both rasters describe the same variables and grid
stopifnot(terra::nlyr(Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK) == 19)
stopifnot(identical(names(Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK),
                    names(Clim_UK)))
stopifnot(terra::compareGeom(Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK,
                            Clim_UK, lyrs = TRUE))

# Subtract historical from future annual mean temperature
bio1_change <- Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK[["bio_1"]] -
  Clim_UK[["bio_1"]]

# Map the difference, in degrees Celsius
plot(bio1_change,
     main = "Projected change in annual mean temperature (°C)\n2041–2060 minus 1970–2000; SSP1-2.6")







# Inspect the range of projected differences
terra::global(bio1_change, "range", na.rm = TRUE)

           min      max
bio_1 1.164557 1.978635


Interpret: Positive values indicate higher annual mean temperature in the future projection than in the historical baseline. In the prepared workshop example, the mapped differences are approximately +1.2 to +1.9°C, depending on location. These differences describe one model and one scenario, not an observed warming trend or a range of uncertainty across climate models.
Inspect: Where are the largest and smallest projected changes? Are they distributed evenly across the UK? What other evidence would you need before drawing conclusions about future bat distributions?






TipChange and explore: precipitation projections





BIO12 is annual precipitation, measured in millimetres. Compare the future and historical BIO12 layers with the same subtraction approach:

bio12_change <- Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK[["bio_12"]] -
  Clim_UK[["bio_12"]]

plot(bio12_change,
     main = "Projected annual precipitation change (mm)\n2041–2060 minus 1970–2000")
terra::global(bio12_change, "range", na.rm = TRUE)

Where does projected annual precipitation increase or decrease? Could a change in total precipitation conceal changes in seasonality or extreme events? Why might different environmental variables have different implications for species ecology?






Optional research extension. The example below shows how the original CMIP6 data can be downloaded, cropped and aligned using R. This requires an internet connection and can take time (it is not required for the core practical and is not executed when the website is built).
The code saves an independently generated file under data/optional_downloads/. It does not overwrite the prepared data/Clim_cmip6_2041_2060_UK.tif used elsewhere in the workshop.

library(geodata)
dir.create("data/optional_downloads", recursive = TRUE,
           showWarnings = FALSE)

# WorldClim CMIP6: BCC-CSM2-MR, SSP1-2.6, 2041–2060
future_global <- geodata::cmip6_world(
  var = "bioc",
  ssp = "126",          # SSP1-2.6 (not SSP5-8.5)
  model = "BCC-CSM2-MR",
  time = "2041-2060",
  res = 5,
  path = "data/optional_downloads"
)

stopifnot(inherits(future_global, "SpatRaster"),
          terra::nlyr(future_global) == 19)

# Check the original names rather than assuming their order
names(future_global)
source_ids <- suppressWarnings(as.integer(
  sub("^bio_?0*", "", names(future_global))
))
stopifnot(!anyNA(source_ids),
          setequal(source_ids, 1:19),
          !anyDuplicated(source_ids))

future_global <- future_global[[match(1:19, source_ids)]]
names(future_global) <- paste0("bio_", 1:19)

# Crop the downloaded future layers to the UK
uk_vector <- terra::project(terra::vect(UK_sf),
                             terra::crs(future_global))
future_uk <- terra::crop(future_global, uk_vector, mask = TRUE)

# Match the historical raster's spatial grid
if (terra::same.crs(future_uk, Clim_UK)) {
  future_rebuilt <- terra::resample(
    future_uk, Clim_UK[[1]], method = "bilinear"
  )
} else {
  future_rebuilt <- terra::project(
    future_uk, Clim_UK[[1]], method = "bilinear"
  )
}
future_rebuilt <- terra::mask(future_rebuilt, Clim_UK[[1]])
names(future_rebuilt) <- names(Clim_UK)
stopifnot(terra::compareGeom(future_rebuilt,
                            Clim_UK, lyrs = TRUE))

# Verify the temperature values and compare them with the baseline
terra::global(Clim_UK[["bio_1"]], "range", na.rm = TRUE)
terra::global(future_rebuilt[["bio_1"]], "range", na.rm = TRUE)

rebuilt_change <- future_rebuilt[["bio_1"]] -
  Clim_UK[["bio_1"]]
terra::global(rebuilt_change, "range", na.rm = TRUE)
plot(rebuilt_change,
     main = "Independently generated BIO1 change (°C)")

# Save a separate file without replacing the workshop dataset
terra::writeRaster(
  future_rebuilt,
  "data/optional_downloads/CMIP6_SSP126_BCC_2041_2060_UK_rebuilt.tif",
  overwrite = TRUE
)

For a reproducible research analysis, record the source and version, download date, GCM, SSP, time period, resolution, units and spatial processing steps. These decisions are as important as the final map. See Data Preparation.



A future climate raster can be used as an input when projecting a fitted SDM, but a change in climate does not automatically imply a corresponding change in species occurrence. Such projections depend on the model’s assumptions, the species’ ability to disperse, habitat availability, land-use change and whether the future environmental conditions lie within the range represented by the model-training data.






TipResearch questions: climate scenarios and uncertainty






What would changing ssp = "126" (SSP1-2.6) to ssp = "585" (SSP5-8.5) mean for the scenario being explored?
Why might two GCMs produce different changes in UK temperature or precipitation under the same SSP?
How could seasonal climate variables reveal ecological changes that annual averages conceal?
Why is a predicted change in climatic suitability not evidence that a species will colonise a newly suitable location?
What limitations arise if occurrence records and climate predictors refer to different decades?

Research projections should consider multiple GCMs and SSPs, model evaluation, environmental novelty and uncertainty. These topics are developed further in Assessment and Projection.

title: Fitting your first species distribution model - GLMs
text:
We now fit our first species distribution model (SDM). In the preceding chapters, we inspected species records, selected background locations, and associated both sets of locations with environmental predictors. Here, we will use a generalised linear model (GLM) to investigate relationships between the occurrence records of the lesser horseshoe bat (Rhinolophus hipposideros) and environmental conditions across the UK.
Binomial generalised linear models (GLMs), fitted using logistic regression, are widely used in species distribution modelling because they provide a relatively simple and interpretable way to relate a binary response variable—coded as 1 for species presence and 0 for absence—to environmental conditions. In this chapter, we use binomialGLMs to explore the principles of multiple regression, examine how different environmental predictors contribute to a model, and consider why careful variable selection is important for producing ecologically meaningful and interpretable results.






TipLearning outcomes



By the end of the core practical, you should be able to:

Explain the difference between a binary training label and confirmed species absence.
Fit a binomial GLM using glm() and inspect its main results.
Compare a straight-line and a curved response to elevation.
Extend a GLM to temperature, precipitation and elevation.
Interpret a map of relative presence–background suitability scores, without treating it as a map of confirmed occupancy probabilities.
Explain why training data and held-out test data have different purposes.

Optional research activities explore predictor correlations, model complexity, AIC and residual checks. The next chapter covers formal model assessment and projection.




Keep adding the code and your own explanatory comments to the R script you created for the workshop. If you just completed Background and Pseudo-Absence Data, the objects sdm_df_clean and proj_stack should already be available in your R session.
To make this page work independently, the workshop also provides a short recovery script that reproduces the same data-cleaning, predictor-alignment and random-background choices as Chapter 5. It does not download files or fit models. This avoids unexpectedly replacing the dataset that you constructed yourself.

library(ggplot2)
library(terra)

# If the two objects are unavailable, reproduce the Chapter 5
# CORE data preparation using the supplied files.
# This does not replace the code in your own annotated script.
has_model_data <- exists("sdm_df_clean", inherits = FALSE)
has_predictors <- exists("proj_stack", inherits = FALSE)

if (!has_model_data || !has_predictors) {
  message("Preparing the standard Chapter 5 teaching inputs. ",
          "If you changed the background-sampling design, ",
          "rerun your own Chapter 5 code instead.")
  source("scripts/prepare_glm_inputs.R")
}

# Check the inputs that will be used for the first model
model_predictors <- c("bio_1", "bio_12", "elevation")
stopifnot(
  is.data.frame(sdm_df_clean),
  all(c("pa", model_predictors) %in% names(sdm_df_clean)),
  all(model_predictors %in% names(proj_stack)),
  all(stats::complete.cases(sdm_df_clean[, c("pa", model_predictors)])),
  inherits(proj_stack, "SpatRaster")
)

# Safely convert 0/1 labels, even if a previous exercise made a factor.
pa_numeric <- suppressWarnings(
  as.integer(as.character(sdm_df_clean$pa))
)
stopifnot(!anyNA(pa_numeric), all(pa_numeric %in% c(0L, 1L)))
sdm_df_clean$pa <- pa_numeric

table(sdm_df_clean$pa)

The recovery script reproduces the Chapter 5 teaching using the supplied data, fixed background-sampling seed (2222) and the same coordinate-cleaning choices. If you changed the sampling region, background method or cleaning decisions, rerun those steps from your own annotated R script rather than using the standard recovery script. This also lets you reproduce your modified analysis after restarting R.






NoteWhat is in the model data?





sdm_df_clean is a table containing:



Column
Meaning




pa = 1
Recorded presence of the focal species


pa = 0
Sampled background location, not a confirmed absence


bio_1
Annual mean temperature (°C)


bio_12
Annual precipitation (mm)


elevation
Elevation (m)



proj_stack is a three-layer raster with the same predictor names. We will later apply the fitted model to each grid cell using these layers.
Note: Because the background points have artificially assigned zero labels, the GLM’s fitted numbers are not automatically the absolute probability that a bat occurs at a given location. They are scores representing the contrast between the supplied presence and background samples. Their values depend on the sampling design and presence–background ratio.






Core practical. Before fitting the GLMs, we will set aside some records for later evaluation. This helps avoid presenting model performance measured on the same observations that were used to fit it.
For a first teaching example, we use a 70% training / 30% test split, retaining records from both labelled groups. The test observations will not be used to choose the model formula or fit its coefficients.

set.seed(2026)
presence_rows <- which(sdm_df_clean$pa == 1L)
background_rows <- which(sdm_df_clean$pa == 0L)
stopifnot(length(presence_rows) >= 5L,
          length(background_rows) >= 5L)

trainIndex <- sort(c(
  sample(presence_rows, floor(0.7 * length(presence_rows))),
  sample(background_rows, floor(0.7 * length(background_rows)))
))

sdm_df_train <- sdm_df_clean[trainIndex, , drop = FALSE]
sdm_df_test <- sdm_df_clean[-trainIndex, , drop = FALSE]

# Compare the numbers of presence/background labels in both subsets
table(Training = sdm_df_train$pa)

Training
  0   1 
216 216 

table(Test = sdm_df_test$pa)

Test
 0  1 
93 93 


Inspect: Which subset is used for fitting models? Why should you avoid repeatedly checking the test results and then altering the model to improve them?
Research connection: Random splitting is easy to demonstrate but does not account for spatial autocorrelation or neighbouring observations that share environmental conditions. Independent SDM research should assess whether spatially separated validation is appropriate. We return to this in Assessment and Projection.





A binomial GLM models a binary response using a mathematical transformation called the logit link. A simple model has the form:
[ () = _0 + _1,. ]
Here, (p) is the model’s fitted probability of the training label pa = 1, given the particular presence–background sampling design. In our example, it must not be described as the species’ true occupancy probability.
The fitted intercept describes the log-odds at elevation zero. The slope describes how the log-odds change with elevation; neither coefficient is directly an ordinary probability.



Conceptual illustration of bat observations and environmental predictors. This is a schematic teaching illustration, not the workshop’s actual survey design.



glm_elev <- glm(
  pa ~ elevation,
  data = sdm_df_train,
  family = binomial(link = "logit")
)

summary(glm_elev)


Call:
glm(formula = pa ~ elevation, family = binomial(link = "logit"), 
    data = sdm_df_train)

Coefficients:
              Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept)  0.0563937  0.1674901   0.337    0.736
elevation   -0.0003363  0.0008175  -0.411    0.681

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 598.88  on 431  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 598.71  on 430  degrees of freedom
AIC: 602.71

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 3

# Convert the fitted log-odds to a 0–1 response score
stats::plogis(coef(glm_elev)["(Intercept)"])

(Intercept) 
  0.5140947 

# Odds ratio for a 100-m increase in elevation, conditional on the
# sampled presence/background labels (not population occupancy odds)
exp(100 * coef(glm_elev)["elevation"])

elevation 
0.9669322 


Inspect: Is the elevation coefficient positive or negative? What does the odds ratio for a 100-m elevation change suggest about the sampled contrast between presences and background locations? Does it establish that elevation causes the observed distribution?






NoteGLM refresher: Understanding predictions from a binomial GLM





When we fit a binomial GLM with a logit link (family = binomial(link = "logit")), we are using logistic regression. The model estimates how the response changes in relation to an environmental predictor, such as elevation. The fitted coefficients describe this relationship on the log-odds scale.
Using predict() with type = "response" converts the model’s predictions into values between 0 and 1. By calculating these predictions across a range of elevation values, we can draw a response curve showing how the fitted relationship changes along the environmental gradient.
In our workshop, we compare species presence records (pa = 1) with randomly selected background locations (pa = 0), rather than confirmed absences. Therefore, the predicted values should be interpreted as relative presence–background suitability scores, not as the actual probability that the species occurs at a particular location.
The model intercept represents the fitted log-odds when elevation equals 0 m. If this is not representative of the sampled locations, we can centre elevation around its mean to make the intercept easier to interpret.






Visualising the fitted response helps connect an R model to an ecological question. Here, the horizontal axis is elevation and the vertical axis is the fitted presence–background score.

elev_seq <- data.frame(
  elevation = seq(min(sdm_df_train$elevation),
                  max(sdm_df_train$elevation),
                  length.out = 200)
)
elev_seq$score_linear <- predict(
  glm_elev, newdata = elev_seq, type = "response"
)

ggplot(sdm_df_train, aes(x = elevation, y = pa)) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.035, width = 0,
              alpha = 0.25, colour = "grey35") +
  geom_line(data = elev_seq,
            aes(x = elevation, y = score_linear),
            linewidth = 1.1, colour = "#ad354e") +
  labs(title = "Elevation and presence–background score",
       x = "Elevation (m)",
       y = "Fitted presence–background score (0–1)") +
  theme_minimal()








Change: Substitute bio_1 for elevation in the glm() formula. Create a new prediction grid for temperature. What differs in the direction and shape of the response? Remember to save the new model under a different name so you do not overwrite glm_elev.




Many ecological relationships are not straight lines. A quadratic term allows a GLM to fit a curved response, although the resulting curve is not necessarily hump-shaped—its shape depends on the data and fitted coefficients.

glm_elev_poly <- glm(
  pa ~ poly(elevation, 2),
  data = sdm_df_train,
  family = binomial(link = "logit")
)

elev_seq$score_quadratic <- predict(
  glm_elev_poly, newdata = elev_seq, type = "response"
)

# AIC compares training-set fit while penalising additional parameters.
AIC(glm_elev, glm_elev_poly)

              df      AIC
glm_elev       2 602.7098
glm_elev_poly  3 581.6366



ggplot(sdm_df_train, aes(x = elevation, y = pa)) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.035, width = 0,
              alpha = 0.2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(data = elev_seq, aes(y = score_linear),
            colour = "#ad354e", linewidth = 1.1,
            linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = elev_seq, aes(y = score_quadratic),
            colour = "#287c57", linewidth = 1.1) +
  labs(title = "Compare straight and curved elevation responses",
       subtitle = "Dashed: linear; solid: quadratic",
       x = "Elevation (m)",
       y = "Fitted presence–background score (0–1)") +
  theme_minimal()








Inspect: Does the quadratic model actually turn downward at higher elevations? Does the model predict an optimum within the observed range? Compare the AIC values but also consider whether the shape is ecologically plausible.
Change: Try a quadratic temperature response instead. Does the curve imply an environmental optimum? How might a biased presence sample create a misleading apparent optimum?






NoteWhat does poly(x, 2) mean?





poly(x, 2) fits a quadratic relationship using orthogonal polynomial terms. This can improve numerical behaviour, but its coefficient values are not as easy to interpret directly as the coefficients in x + I(x^2).
For this practical, focus on the predicted response curve, not on interpreting each polynomial coefficient separately. A lower training AIC is not proof that a model predicts new locations better.






Core practical. A species may respond to several ecological factors together. We now extend the example to the three environmental predictors prepared in the preceding chapters: bio_1 (annual mean temperature), bio_12 (annual precipitation) and elevation.
These three variables are used to keep the exercises manageable; they are not presented as an automatically optimal predictor set for lesser horseshoe bats or for other species.


Check correlations in the training subset before fitting or selecting model formulas. Correlation does not prove that two predictors measure the same ecological mechanism.

predictor_cor <- stats::cor(
  sdm_df_train[, model_predictors, drop = FALSE]
)
round(predictor_cor, 2)

          bio_1 bio_12 elevation
bio_1      1.00  -0.65     -0.82
bio_12    -0.65   1.00      0.74
elevation -0.82   0.74      1.00


Inspect: Which pair is most strongly correlated? If elevation and temperature are associated, what might happen when both enter the GLM? Should ecological relevance or the numerical correlation alone determine predictor choice?



We fit a model with three linear terms, then a model that allows each environmental response to curve. Both models are fitted to the same training data.

glm_multi_1 <- glm(
  pa ~ elevation + bio_1 + bio_12,
  data = sdm_df_train,
  family = binomial(link = "logit")
)

glm_multi <- glm(
  pa ~ poly(elevation, 2) + poly(bio_1, 2) +
    poly(bio_12, 2),
  data = sdm_df_train,
  family = binomial(link = "logit")
)

To show how the multivariable model responds to temperature, we vary bio_1 while holding precipitation and elevation at their training-data median values. This is a model-based illustration, not a controlled experiment and not a causal effect estimate.

temperature_grid <- data.frame(
  bio_1 = seq(min(sdm_df_train$bio_1),
              max(sdm_df_train$bio_1), length.out = 200),
  bio_12 = median(sdm_df_train$bio_12),
  elevation = median(sdm_df_train$elevation)
)
temperature_grid$score <- predict(
  glm_multi, newdata = temperature_grid, type = "response"
)

ggplot(temperature_grid, aes(x = bio_1, y = score)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#287c57", linewidth = 1.1) +
  labs(title = "Modelled temperature response",
       subtitle = "Precipitation and elevation held at training medians",
       x = "Annual mean temperature (°C)",
       y = "Fitted presence–background score (0–1)") +
  theme_minimal()








Change: Replace bio_1 with bio_12 as the varying predictor and keep the other two predictors constant. Describe how the response changes.




The environmental data prepared in Chapter 4 contain the same three predictor names used by the GLM. We can now apply the fitted model to those rasters, estimating a value for each cell with complete environmental data. This is spatial prediction; it does not, by itself, demonstrate how well the model predicts new observations.

stopifnot(all(model_predictors %in% names(proj_stack)))

# Predict from the training-fitted model on the current climate grid.
glm_suitability_map <- terra::predict(
  proj_stack, glm_multi, type = "response", na.rm = TRUE
)
names(glm_suitability_map) <- "relative_suitability"

plot(glm_suitability_map,
     main = "Relative suitability — GLM presence/background score")








Inspect: Do the areas with higher fitted scores correspond to locations where the sampled environments resemble those associated with recorded presences? Why might high suitability appear in places with few or no records?
Important: The map is conditional on the study region, background-sampling procedure, occurrence-data quality, climate baseline and fitted model. It is not a map of verified occupancy, population abundance, or future colonisation.






NoteInterpreting suitability maps





The colour gradient represents variation in a modelled presence-versus-background score. Its numbers lie between 0 and 1 because of the inverse-logit transformation, not because the sampled data establish the true probability of species occurrence in each cell.
To assess whether the model generalises, we need to compare predictions against observations not used for fitting. We will do this in the Assessment and Projection chapter. Spatially separated evaluation may be needed to investigate transferability beyond sampled locations.








Deviance and AIC describe aspects of model fit, but they are not substitutes for independent predictive assessment. McFadden’s pseudo-(R^2) is one descriptive measure based on the improvement over an intercept-only model; it should not be interpreted like the ordinary least-squares (R^2).

cat("Residual deviance:", glm_multi$deviance, "\n")

Residual deviance: 391.7235 

cat("Null deviance:", glm_multi$null.deviance, "\n")

Null deviance: 598.8792 

cat("Training AIC:", AIC(glm_multi), "\n")

Training AIC: 405.7235 

pseudo_r2 <- 1 - glm_multi$deviance / glm_multi$null.deviance
cat("McFadden's pseudo-R²:", round(pseudo_r2, 3), "\n")

McFadden's pseudo-R²: 0.346 








TipResearch extension: inspect residuals and model complexity





More complex models can reproduce patterns in the training sample without necessarily generalising. Inspect residuals and compare ecologically motivated formulas before making conclusions.

# Optional diagnostic views: not required for the core PC lab.
plot(glm_multi, which = c(1, 2))

# AIC-based stepwise selection is an exploratory procedure,
# not a substitute for ecological predictor selection or validation.
glm_step <- stats::step(glm_multi, direction = "both", trace = FALSE)
summary(glm_step)

If you explore stepwise selection, perform it using training data only, describe your selection process and avoid repeatedly tuning decisions against the held-out test set. For independent research, consider spatial validation and quantify sensitivity to alternative model specifications.









TipFurther research: a small logistic regression demonstration





An intercept-only binomial GLM is a useful way to see how the logit works, independent of the ecological example.

set.seed(42)
y <- rbinom(100, size = 1, prob = 0.2)
intercept_model <- glm(y ~ 1, family = binomial())
mean(y)
stats::plogis(coef(intercept_model))

How does the observed fraction of 1 labels compare with the fitted value? Why is this more directly interpretable as an event probability than the labels assigned to our background locations?









TipOptional: save your GLM work for the next chapter





You can save the fitted model and the training/test data to revisit them later without fitting the GLM again. The corresponding environmental raster is saved separately as a GeoTIFF. These are checkpoints, not replacements for the code in your own R script.

dir.create("data/checkpoints", recursive = TRUE,
            showWarnings = FALSE)

saveRDS(
  list(
    sdm_df_train = sdm_df_train,
    sdm_df_test = sdm_df_test,
    glm_multi_1 = glm_multi_1,
    glm_multi = glm_multi,
    model_predictors = model_predictors
  ),
  "data/checkpoints/glm_chapter6_results.rds"
)

terra::writeRaster(
  proj_stack,
  "data/checkpoints/SDM_predictors_current.tif",
  overwrite = TRUE
)

# In a later R session, after loading the required packages:
# glm_results <- readRDS("data/checkpoints/glm_chapter6_results.rds")
# sdm_df_test <- glm_results$sdm_df_test
# glm_multi <- glm_results$glm_multi
# proj_stack <- terra::rast("data/checkpoints/SDM_predictors_current.tif")

The held-out test observations remain unused for model fitting. In the next chapter, we will apply the trained model to those observations to assess discrimination. This random split is a first demonstration, not a substitute for spatially separated validation in independent research.













NoteCore practical — before moving to assessment




Fit the elevation-only GLM and explain the sign of its coefficient in your own R script.
Compare straight and curved elevation responses. Which curve better represents the observed training data? Is the more flexible curve necessarily preferable?
Fit the three-predictor GLM and plot its relative-suitability map.
Explain why the fitted scores are not confirmed occupancy probabilities and why the test subset has not been used to choose the model.




Compare one or more ecologically defensible GLM formulas using training data only.
Inspect how predictor correlation and the choice of background locations change the fitted responses.
Refit a model after centering or scaling predictors; compare prediction curves and coefficient interpretation.
Plan a spatially blocked validation scheme for a research dataset with clustered occurrences, keeping model tuning separate from final assessment.

text:
Keep adding the code and your own explanatory comments to the R script you created for the workshop. If you just completed Background and Pseudo-Absence Data, the objects sdm_df_clean and proj_stack should already be available in your R session.

NoteWhat is in the model data?





sdm_df_clean is a table containing:



Column
Meaning




pa = 1
Recorded presence of the focal species


pa = 0
Sampled background location, not a confirmed absence


bio_1

bio_12

elevation

proj_stack is a three-layer raster with the same predictor names. We will later apply the fitted model to each grid cell using these layers.
Note: Because the background points have artificially assigned zero labels, the GLM’s fitted numbers are not automatically the absolute probability that a bat occurs at a given location. They are scores representing the contrast between the supplied presence and background samples. Their values depend on the sampling design and presence–background ratio.

title: Fitting your first species distribution model - GLMs
text:
Core practical. Before fitting the GLMs, we will set aside some records for later evaluation. This helps avoid presenting model performance measured on the same observations that were used to fit it.
For a first teaching example, we use a 70% training / 30% test split, retaining records from both labelled groups. The test observations will not be used to choose the model formula or fit its coefficients.

set.seed(2026)
presence_rows <- which(sdm_df_clean$pa == 1L)
background_rows <- which(sdm_df_clean$pa == 0L)
stopifnot(length(presence_rows) >= 5L,
          length(background_rows) >= 5L)

trainIndex <- sort(c(
  sample(presence_rows, floor(0.7 * length(presence_rows))),
  sample(background_rows, floor(0.7 * length(background_rows)))
))

sdm_df_train <- sdm_df_clean[trainIndex, , drop = FALSE]
sdm_df_test <- sdm_df_clean[-trainIndex, , drop = FALSE]

# Compare the numbers of presence/background labels in both subsets
table(Training = sdm_df_train$pa)

Training
  0   1 
216 216 

table(Test = sdm_df_test$pa)

Test
 0  1 
93 93 


Inspect: Which subset is used for fitting models? Why should you avoid repeatedly checking the test results and then altering the model to improve them?
Research connection: Random splitting is easy to demonstrate but does not account for spatial autocorrelation or neighbouring observations that share environmental conditions. Independent SDM research should assess whether spatially separated validation is appropriate. We return to this in Assessment and Projection.

title: Fitting your first species distribution model - GLMs
text:
A binomial GLM models a binary response using a mathematical transformation called the logit link. A simple model has the form:
[ () = _0 + _1,. ]
Here, (p) is the model’s fitted probability of the training label pa = 1, given the particular presence–background sampling design. In our example, it must not be described as the species’ true occupancy probability.
The fitted intercept describes the log-odds at elevation zero. The slope describes how the log-odds change with elevation; neither coefficient is directly an ordinary probability.



Conceptual illustration of bat observations and environmental predictors. This is a schematic teaching illustration, not the workshop’s actual survey design.



glm_elev <- glm(
  pa ~ elevation,
  data = sdm_df_train,
  family = binomial(link = "logit")
)

summary(glm_elev)

    data = sdm_df_train)

(Intercept) 
  0.5140947

elevation 
0.9669322 


Inspect: Is the elevation coefficient positive or negative? What does the odds ratio for a 100-m elevation change suggest about the sampled contrast between presences and background locations? Does it establish that elevation causes the observed distribution?






NoteGLM refresher: Understanding predictions from a binomial GLM





When we fit a binomial GLM with a logit link (family = binomial(link = "logit")), we are using logistic regression. The model estimates how the response changes in relation to an environmental predictor, such as elevation. The fitted coefficients describe this relationship on the log-odds scale.
Using predict() with type = "response" converts the model’s predictions into values between 0 and 1. By calculating these predictions across a range of elevation values, we can draw a response curve showing how the fitted relationship changes along the environmental gradient.
In our workshop, we compare species presence records (pa = 1) with randomly selected background locations (pa = 0), rather than confirmed absences. Therefore, the predicted values should be interpreted as relative presence–background suitability scores, not as the actual probability that the species occurs at a particular location.
The model intercept represents the fitted log-odds when elevation equals 0 m. If this is not representative of the sampled locations, we can centre elevation around its mean to make the intercept easier to interpret.






Visualising the fitted response helps connect an R model to an ecological question. Here, the horizontal axis is elevation and the vertical axis is the fitted presence–background score.

elev_seq <- data.frame(
  elevation = seq(min(sdm_df_train$elevation),
                  max(sdm_df_train$elevation),
                  length.out = 200)
)
elev_seq$score_linear <- predict(
  glm_elev, newdata = elev_seq, type = "response"
)

ggplot(sdm_df_train, aes(x = elevation, y = pa)) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.035, width = 0,
              alpha = 0.25, colour = "grey35") +
  geom_line(data = elev_seq,
            aes(x = elevation, y = score_linear),
            linewidth = 1.1, colour = "#ad354e") +
  labs(title = "Elevation and presence–background score",
       x = "Elevation (m)",
       y = "Fitted presence–background score (0–1)") +
  theme_minimal()

To show how the multivariable model responds to temperature, we vary bio_1 while holding precipitation and elevation at their training-data median values. This is a model-based illustration, not a controlled experiment and not a causal effect estimate.

temperature_grid <- data.frame(
  bio_1 = seq(min(sdm_df_train$bio_1),
              max(sdm_df_train$bio_1), length.out = 200),
  bio_12 = median(sdm_df_train$bio_12),
  elevation = median(sdm_df_train$elevation)
)
temperature_grid$score <- predict(
  glm_multi, newdata = temperature_grid, type = "response"
)

ggplot(temperature_grid, aes(x = bio_1, y = score)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#287c57", linewidth = 1.1) +
  labs(title = "Modelled temperature response",
       subtitle = "Precipitation and elevation held at training medians",
       x = "Annual mean temperature (°C)",
       y = "Fitted presence–background score (0–1)") +
  theme_minimal()








Change: Replace bio_1 with bio_12 as the varying predictor and keep the other two predictors constant. Describe how the response changes.

title: Fitting your first species distribution model - GLMs
text:
The environmental data prepared in Chapter 4 contain the same three predictor names used by the GLM. We can now apply the fitted model to those rasters, estimating a value for each cell with complete environmental data. This is spatial prediction; it does not, by itself, demonstrate how well the model predicts new observations.

stopifnot(all(model_predictors %in% names(proj_stack)))

# Predict from the training-fitted model on the current climate grid.
glm_suitability_map <- terra::predict(
  proj_stack, glm_multi, type = "response", na.rm = TRUE
)
names(glm_suitability_map) <- "relative_suitability"

plot(glm_suitability_map,
     main = "Relative suitability — GLM presence/background score")








Inspect: Do the areas with higher fitted scores correspond to locations where the sampled environments resemble those associated with recorded presences? Why might high suitability appear in places with few or no records?
Important: The map is conditional on the study region, background-sampling procedure, occurrence-data quality, climate baseline and fitted model. It is not a map of verified occupancy, population abundance, or future colonisation.






NoteInterpreting suitability maps





The colour gradient represents variation in a modelled presence-versus-background score. Its numbers lie between 0 and 1 because of the inverse-logit transformation, not because the sampled data establish the true probability of species occurrence in each cell.
To assess whether the model generalises, we need to compare predictions against observations not used for fitting. We will do this in the Assessment and Projection chapter. Spatially separated evaluation may be needed to investigate transferability beyond sampled locations.

title: Fitting your first species distribution model - GLMs
text:
Deviance and AIC describe aspects of model fit, but they are not substitutes for independent predictive assessment. McFadden’s pseudo-(R^2) is one descriptive measure based on the improvement over an intercept-only model; it should not be interpreted like the ordinary least-squares (R^2).

cat("Residual deviance:", glm_multi$deviance, "\n")

Residual deviance: 391.7235 

cat("Null deviance:", glm_multi$null.deviance, "\n")

Null deviance: 598.8792 

cat("Training AIC:", AIC(glm_multi), "\n")

Training AIC: 405.7235 

pseudo_r2 <- 1 - glm_multi$deviance / glm_multi$null.deviance
cat("McFadden's pseudo-R²:", round(pseudo_r2, 3), "\n")

McFadden's pseudo-R²: 0.346 








TipResearch extension: inspect residuals and model complexity





More complex models can reproduce patterns in the training sample without necessarily generalising. Inspect residuals and compare ecologically motivated formulas before making conclusions.

# Optional diagnostic views: not required for the core PC lab.
plot(glm_multi, which = c(1, 2))

# AIC-based stepwise selection is an exploratory procedure,
# not a substitute for ecological predictor selection or validation.
glm_step <- stats::step(glm_multi, direction = "both", trace = FALSE)
summary(glm_step)

If you explore stepwise selection, perform it using training data only, describe your selection process and avoid repeatedly tuning decisions against the held-out test set. For independent research, consider spatial validation and quantify sensitivity to alternative model specifications.









TipFurther research: a small logistic regression demonstration





An intercept-only binomial GLM is a useful way to see how the logit works, independent of the ecological example.

set.seed(42)
y <- rbinom(100, size = 1, prob = 0.2)
intercept_model <- glm(y ~ 1, family = binomial())
mean(y)
stats::plogis(coef(intercept_model))

How does the observed fraction of 1 labels compare with the fitted value? Why is this more directly interpretable as an event probability than the labels assigned to our background locations?









TipOptional: save your GLM work for the next chapter





You can save the fitted model and the training/test data to revisit them later without fitting the GLM again. The corresponding environmental raster is saved separately as a GeoTIFF. These are checkpoints, not replacements for the code in your own R script.

dir.create("data/checkpoints", recursive = TRUE,
            showWarnings = FALSE)

saveRDS(
  list(
    sdm_df_train = sdm_df_train,
    sdm_df_test = sdm_df_test,
    glm_multi_1 = glm_multi_1,
    glm_multi = glm_multi,
    model_predictors = model_predictors
  ),
  "data/checkpoints/glm_chapter6_results.rds"
)

terra::writeRaster(
  proj_stack,
  "data/checkpoints/SDM_predictors_current.tif",
  overwrite = TRUE
)

# glm_results <- readRDS("data/checkpoints/glm_chapter6_results.rds")
# sdm_df_test <- glm_results$sdm_df_test
# glm_multi <- glm_results$glm_multi
# proj_stack <- terra::rast("data/checkpoints/SDM_predictors_current.tif")

The held-out test observations remain unused for model fitting. In the next chapter, we will apply the trained model to those observations to assess discrimination. This random split is a first demonstration, not a substitute for spatially separated validation in independent research.

NoteCore practical — before moving to assessment




Fit the elevation-only GLM and explain the sign of its coefficient in your own R script.
Compare straight and curved elevation responses. Which curve better represents the observed training data? Is the more flexible curve necessarily preferable?
Fit the three-predictor GLM and plot its relative-suitability map.
Explain why the fitted scores are not confirmed occupancy probabilities and why the test subset has not been used to choose the model.




Compare one or more ecologically defensible GLM formulas using training data only.
Inspect how predictor correlation and the choice of background locations change the fitted responses.
Refit a model after centering or scaling predictors; compare prediction curves and coefficient interpretation.

title: Fitting and Comparing Algorithms
text:
In Fitting your first species distribution model, we used a generalised linear model (GLM) to examine the relationships between lesser horseshoe bat (Rhinolophus hipposideros) records and environmental predictors. In Assessment and Projection, we introduced held-out model assessment and the limitations of presence–background predictions.
GLMs remain widely used in ecological research because their assumptions and coefficients can be examined and explained. However, a quadratic GLM is only one way to describe a curved ecological response. Other methods can represent more flexible shapes, thresholds and interactions. Comparing methods helps us understand how modelling assumptions affect results, rather than demonstrating that one algorithm is universally best.






TipLearning outcomes — optional research extension



This chapter extends the four-hour core practical. You can complete the earlier GLM exercises without fitting all the algorithms shown here.
By working through the examples, you should be able to:

Explain the main differences between GLMs, GAMs, Random Forests, Boosted Regression Trees (BRTs), MaxEnt and simple environmental envelopes.
Fit alternative models to the same training data and predictors.
Compare predictions on the same held-out test observations using ROC/AUC.
Examine how model structure changes environmental response curves and maps.
Explain why sampling bias, background selection and spatial validation matter even when an algorithm appears to predict well.

The GAM, Random Forest and simple envelope examples include executable R code. The more computationally demanding BRT and MaxEnt examples are also provided, but are not run automatically on this page. Copy them into your own RStudio script if you choose to investigate those methods.




Continue using your own annotated .R script in the RStudio project you created for this workshop. Do not create a new random split for every algorithm: the comparison only makes sense when all methods are trained and assessed on consistent data.
If you have just completed Chapter 6 or 7, keep sdm_df_train, sdm_df_test, proj_stack and glm_multi in the current R session. The setup below can also reconstruct the standard Chapter 5/6 teaching inputs if you open this page independently. If you changed the occurrence-cleaning or background-sampling strategy, rerun your own preceding code instead of using the standard recovery script.

library(terra)
library(ggplot2)
library(pROC)

predictors <- c("bio_1", "bio_12", "elevation")

# Reuse existing training and test data when continuing the tutorial.
has_train <- exists("sdm_df_train", inherits = FALSE)
has_test <- exists("sdm_df_test", inherits = FALSE)
if (xor(has_train, has_test)) {
  stop("Only one of the training/test objects exists. ",
       "Restore both from Chapter 6, or rerun your own earlier code.")
}
if (has_train && !exists("proj_stack", inherits = FALSE)) {
  stop("The training/test data exist but proj_stack is missing. ",
       "Restore the matching raster or rerun Chapter 6.")
}

# If needed, reproduce the standard teaching inputs from Chapter 5.
if (!has_train) {
  if (!exists("sdm_df_clean", inherits = FALSE) ||
      !exists("proj_stack", inherits = FALSE)) {
    source("scripts/prepare_glm_inputs.R")
  }

  # Exactly the same stratified 70/30 split used in Chapter 6.
  set.seed(2026)
  clean_labels <- suppressWarnings(
    as.integer(as.character(sdm_df_clean$pa))
  )
  stopifnot(!anyNA(clean_labels), all(clean_labels %in% 0:1))
  presence_rows <- which(clean_labels == 1L)
  background_rows <- which(clean_labels == 0L)
  stopifnot(length(presence_rows) >= 5L,
            length(background_rows) >= 5L)
  training_rows <- sort(c(
    sample(presence_rows, floor(0.7 * length(presence_rows))),
    sample(background_rows, floor(0.7 * length(background_rows)))
  ))
  sdm_df_train <- sdm_df_clean[training_rows, , drop = FALSE]
  sdm_df_test <- sdm_df_clean[-training_rows, , drop = FALSE]
}

# Make independent copies to avoid changing objects used in other pages.
model_train <- as.data.frame(sdm_df_train[, c("pa", predictors)])
model_test <- as.data.frame(sdm_df_test[, c("pa", predictors)])
for (part in c("model_train", "model_test")) {
  d <- get(part)
  d$pa <- suppressWarnings(as.integer(as.character(d$pa)))
  stopifnot(!anyNA(d$pa), all(d$pa %in% 0:1),
            all(stats::complete.cases(d)))
  assign(part, d)
}
stopifnot(
  all(c(0L, 1L) %in% model_train$pa),
  all(c(0L, 1L) %in% model_test$pa),
  inherits(proj_stack, "SpatRaster"),
  all(predictors %in% names(proj_stack))
)

# Retain Chapter 6's fitted model when available. Otherwise fit its
# documented quadratic GLM formula, using TRAINING DATA ONLY.
if (exists("glm_multi", inherits = FALSE) && !has_train) {
  stop("A previous glm_multi is present without its matching training ",
       "set. Rerun Chapter 6 or restart R before reconstructing inputs.")
}
if (!exists("glm_multi", inherits = FALSE)) {
  glm_multi <- stats::glm(
    pa ~ poly(elevation, 2) + poly(bio_1, 2) +
      poly(bio_12, 2),
    data = model_train,
    family = binomial(link = "logit")
  )
}
stopifnot(inherits(glm_multi, "glm"))

Training

Test
